The thesis makes one very large model, LTX-2.3, smaller and faster on Intel hardware without breaking its videos. The sixteen papers in this atlas each solve one piece of that. This tab gives the ideas they all take for granted: diffusion, transformers, number formats and quantization, hardware, the OpenVINO stack and quality metrics, then a map of how the papers fit together.

Reading guide

Welcome to the atlas. The thesis asks one practical question: how can LTX-2.3, a model that turns a text prompt into a video with sound, be made smaller and faster on an Intel CPU and an Intel Arc GPU without spoiling its output? The answer will come from sixteen papers, and this first tab gives the vocabulary they all assume. It moves in order from the pipeline, to diffusion, to transformers, to number formats and quantization, to hardware, to the OpenVINO software stack, to quality metrics and other speed-ups, and ends with a map of all sixteen papers and a glossary. Every paper tab after this one follows the same pattern: a header, a short Before reading section, the big picture, the problem, the method, every equation and figure, the results, and a closing box on what it means for the thesis.

§1The thesis in one picture

A prompt goes in; a short video with its soundtrack comes out. One part, the diffusion transformer, is called again and again, so that is where memory and time go.

§2How diffusion makes a video

Diffusion starts from pure noise and removes a little of it at every step. The model never paints the video in one go.

(1)\[ \hat{v} \;=\; v_\theta(x_t,\emptyset) \;+\; s\,\big(v_\theta(x_t,c) - v_\theta(x_t,\emptyset)\big) \]

Classifier-free guidance: \(v_\theta\) is the transformer's prediction, \(x_t\) the noisy latent, \(c\) the prompt, \(\emptyset\) an empty prompt, \(s\) the guidance scale. Two calls per step (three with LTX-2's extra modality term).

Guide

This is the guidance rule in one line. v hat is the final prediction used for the step. v theta of x t and empty is the model's answer without the prompt, v theta of x t and c is the answer with the prompt c, and s is the guidance scale. The bracket is the difference the prompt makes, stretched by s. Both terms need their own transformer call, which is the cost shown in the figure above.

§3Transformers in 5 minutes

A transformer is mostly two operations repeated many times: linear layers (matrix multiplies) and attention.

(2)\[ \text{FLOPs}_{\text{attention}} \approx 4\,N^2 d \qquad\qquad \text{FLOPs}_{\text{linear}} \approx 2\,N\,d_{\text{in}}\,d_{\text{out}} \]

Per layer, for \(N\) tokens and width \(d\): attention (\(QK^\top\) plus scores times \(V\)) grows with \(N^2\); a linear layer grows only with \(N\). For long videos attention takes a growing share of each step.

Guide

Two rough cost formulas, per layer. Attention needs about four times N squared times d operations, where N is the number of tokens and d the model width. A linear layer needs about two times N times d in times d out. The key difference is N squared versus N: longer or higher-resolution videos make attention grow much faster than the linear layers, which is where FlashAttention-style kernels matter.

§4Numbers and quantization from zero

Quantization stores numbers with fewer bits. Fewer bits mean less memory and less data to move, at the cost of rounding error.

Weight memory at each precision (1 GB = 10⁹ bytes). INT4 adds about 0.13 bits per weight for one FP16 scale per group of 128.
PrecisionBitsBytes / paramDiT 19BGemma-3 12BWhere it appears
FP3232476 GB48 GBtraining, reference math
BF16 / FP1616238 GB24 GBreleased model, PyTorch reference
INT88119 GB12 GBNNCF INT8 weights; W8A8
INT4 (group 128)4≈ 0.52≈ 9.8 GB≈ 6.2 GBNNCF INT4 weight compression
Guide

This table turns bit-widths into gigabytes for the two big components of LTX-2.3. Read across a row: bits, bytes per parameter, then memory for the 19 billion parameter transformer and the 12 billion parameter Gemma encoder. The highlighted INT4 row includes a small overhead for one 16-bit scale per group of 128 weights, giving about 9.8 gigabytes for the transformer. These are weight sizes only; activations and runtime buffers come on top.

(3)\[ \text{memory} \;\approx\; N_{\text{params}} \times \text{bytes per parameter} \qquad 19\times10^{9} \times 0.5\ \text{B} \approx 9.5\ \text{GB} \]

The first estimate for every row of the table; scales, activations and runtime buffers come on top.

Guide

The first estimate to always make. Memory is about the number of parameters times the bytes per parameter. For the transformer at 4 bits, 19 billion times half a byte gives about 9.5 gigabytes. Scales, activations and buffers add to this, so use it as a lower bound and compare it with the IR size on disk and the measured peak memory.

(4)\[ s = \frac{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}{q_{\max} - q_{\min}} \qquad z = \operatorname{round}\!\Big(q_{\min} - \frac{x_{\min}}{s}\Big) \]

Scale \(s\) is the real-valued size of one integer step; zero-point \(z\) is the integer that stands for real 0. For INT4 asymmetric, \(q_{\min}=0\), \(q_{\max}=15\). Symmetric quantization fixes \(z\) at 0.

Guide

How the grid is chosen. The scale s is the real-valued size of one integer step: the range of the data, x max minus x min, divided by the number of steps, q max minus q min. The zero-point z is the integer that stands for real zero. For asymmetric INT4, q runs from 0 to 15. Symmetric schemes fix z at zero, which is simpler but wastes levels when the data is lopsided.

(5)\[ q = \operatorname{clamp}\!\Big(\operatorname{round}\!\big(\tfrac{x}{s}\big) + z,\; q_{\min},\; q_{\max}\Big) \]

Quantize: divide by the step, round to the nearest level, shift by the zero-point, and clip anything outside the grid.

Guide

Quantizing one number. Divide x by the scale s, round to the nearest integer, add the zero-point z, and clamp the result between q min and q max. Rounding causes the small, everyday error; clamping causes the large error for values outside the chosen range. Every quantization method in the atlas is, in some way, a smarter choice of s, z or the rounding.

(6)\[ \hat{x} = s\,(q - z) \qquad \lvert x - \hat{x}\rvert \le \tfrac{s}{2}\ \text{ inside the range} \]

Dequantize: the value the model actually computes with. The rounding error is at most half a step; values outside the range get the larger clipping error.

Guide

Dequantizing, which gives the value the model actually computes with. x hat equals s times q minus z. Inside the range, the error between x and x hat is at most half a step. Outside the range, clipping can make it much larger. This trade-off between step size and clipping is exactly what the worked example below shows with real numbers.

§5Hardware, and why speed is not just FLOPs

Chips are often waiting for data rather than doing arithmetic. Whether a layer gets faster depends on which of the two limits it.

§6The software stack

The project code path: a Hugging Face model becomes an OpenVINO model, gets compressed, and is compiled for a device.

§7How quality is measured

Papers disagree on metrics because they measure different things. Know which question each metric answers.

§8Speeding up without fewer bits

Quantization makes each step cheaper. The other levers cut the number of steps or the work inside a step, and they stack.

Five groups, left to right: what gets compressed, the LLM tools, their diffusion versions, other speed-ups, and how to judge the result.

§10Glossary

Glossary

Activation
The numbers flowing between layers for a given input; they change with every prompt and step.
AdaLN
Adaptive layer norm: the timestep sets a scale, shift and gate inside each DiT block.
Attention
The operation where every token weighs every other token using queries, keys and values.
BF16 / FP16
16-bit floating-point formats; BF16 keeps FP32's range with less precision.
Calibration data
A small set of real inputs used to measure value ranges before quantizing.
CFG (classifier-free guidance)
Running the model with and without the prompt and mixing the results to follow the text better.
Compute-bound
Limited by how fast the chip can do arithmetic.
Custom op
An operation the runtime does not provide, so someone must write its kernel.
Distillation
Training a model to reproduce a bigger or slower one, for example with fewer steps.
DiT
Diffusion transformer: the denoising network, built from transformer blocks.
Fused kernel
One kernel doing several operations so intermediates stay on chip.
GEMM
General matrix multiply, the core computation of every linear layer.
Group size
How many weights share one scale in group-wise quantization, for example 128.
INT4 / INT8
4-bit and 8-bit integers: 16 or 256 levels, used with a scale.
IR (OpenVINO)
Intermediate representation: the .xml graph plus .bin weights that OpenVINO compiles.
Kernel
A compiled routine that runs one operation on a CPU or GPU.
Latent
The compressed representation produced by a VAE, where diffusion happens.
Memory-bound
Limited by how fast data can be moved from memory, not by arithmetic.
Mixed precision
Different bit-widths for different layers, keeping sensitive layers higher.
NNCF
Neural Network Compression Framework: Intel's library for quantizing and compressing OpenVINO models.
Optimum Intel
The Hugging Face library that exports and runs Transformers and diffusers models with OpenVINO.
Outlier
A value or channel far larger than the rest, which stretches a shared scale.
Per-channel / per-group / per-token
Which numbers share one scale: a row, a block of a row, or one token's activations.
PTQ
Post-training quantization: quantize a finished model without retraining.
QAT
Quantization-aware training: retrain with simulated rounding so the model adapts.
Roofline
A plot showing whether an operation is capped by memory bandwidth or by compute.
Salient channel
A channel whose errors hurt the output most, often found from activation size.
Scale and zero-point
The step size and integer offset that map integers back to real values.
Step caching
Reusing a previous step's result when the model output barely changes.
Tensor Core
NVIDIA's matrix-multiply units for low-precision math.
Timestep
The noise level of the current denoising step.
Token
One unit the transformer processes: a word piece for text, or a patch of latent video.
VAE
Variational autoencoder: compresses pixels or sound into latents and decodes them back.
VBench
A benchmark that scores generated videos on 16 separate dimensions.
Vocoder
The network that turns a decoded spectrogram into an audio waveform.
W4A16, W8A8…
Bits of weights (W) and activations (A); W4A16 is 4-bit weights, 16-bit activations.
Weight-only quantization
Only the weights are stored in low bits; math still runs in 16-bit.
WWB
Who What Benchmark: an OpenVINO GenAI tool that scores how similar optimized outputs are to reference outputs.
XMX
Xe Matrix Extensions: the matrix engines in Intel Arc GPUs.
Guide

Keep this glossary open while reading. It lists the terms that appear across many papers, in alphabetical order, each with a one-line definition in plain words. When a paper tab uses an unfamiliar word, such as salient channel, roofline or AdaLN, come back here first. Target models

LTX-Video: Realtime Video Latent Diffusion

Y. HaCohen, N. Chiprut, B. Brazowski, D. Shalem, … O. Bibi · Lightricks · arXiv:2501.00103, Dec 2024

LTX-Video is the ancestor of LTX-2.3. Its video autoencoder squeezes every 32×32×8 block of pixels into a single 128-channel latent “token” (1:192 compression). That leaves the diffusion transformer (DiT) with very few tokens, so it can run full 3-D attention fast. The VAE decoder also does the final denoising step, so fine detail comes back without a separate upsampler.

VAE compression
1:192
Pixels per token
32×32×8 = 8192
Latent channels
128 (no patchifier)
DiT
1.9B · 28 blocks · d=2048
Speed (H100)
121 fr 768×512 in 2 s
Human win rate
85% T2V · 91% I2V
Reading guide

LTX-Video asks how to make a video diffusion model fast enough to generate faster than real time without losing quality. Its answer is to compress the video so hard in the autoencoder that the transformer only has a few thousand tokens to attend over, and to let the decoder finish the last denoising step. The result is a 1.9 billion parameter model that makes five seconds of video in about two seconds on an H100, and wins most human comparisons. The tab opens with the big picture, then three problems, the method steps, every equation, every figure, the results tables, and finally a thesis box. This is the first of sixteen papers and the first of the two target-model papers, followed by LTX-2. It describes the ancestor architecture of LTX-2.3, so it explains what the thesis will be compressing before the quantization and caching papers explain how.

§0Before reading

This paper builds on three ideas: a video autoencoder (VAE) squeezes pixels into a small grid of “latent” tokens, a diffusion transformer (DiT) removes noise from that grid step by step, and attention cost grows with the square of the number of tokens. LTX-Video is here because it is the direct ancestor of LTX-2.3: the VAE, DiT and denoising decoder that the thesis compresses are all introduced in this paper.

Terms used in this paper

Diffusion model
A generator that starts from random noise and removes it step by step until a clean image or video remains.
VAE (video autoencoder)
A network pair: the encoder compresses pixels into a small latent, the decoder turns a latent back into pixels. LTX-Video compresses by 1:192.
Latent / token
The latent is the compressed grid; each cell of that grid is one token, a vector of 128 numbers that the transformer processes.
Patchify
Grouping neighbouring cells into one token to reduce the token count. LTX-Video does all of this inside the VAE, so its transformer patch size is 1.
DiT (diffusion transformer)
The transformer that does the denoising. In LTX-Video it has 28 blocks and about 1.9 billion parameters, and it is where most compute happens.
Self- and cross-attention
Self-attention lets every video token look at every other one; cross-attention lets video tokens look at the text tokens of the prompt.
Timestep \( t \)
The current noise level, from 1 (pure noise) to 0 (clean). The network is told \( t \) at every step, and in LTX-Video each token can have its own \( t \).
Rectified flow / velocity
A diffusion variant where the noisy latent is a straight-line blend of clean data and noise. The network predicts the velocity, the direction of that line.
T5-XXL
A large pretrained language model from Google used only as a text encoder: it turns the prompt into text tokens for cross-attention.
RoPE
Rotary positional embedding: tells attention where each token is (position in the frame and in time) by rotating its query and key vectors.
AdaLN
Adaptive layer normalisation: the timestep is turned into a scale and shift that modulate each transformer block.
Nvidia H100
A data-centre GPU with Tensor Cores and high-bandwidth memory, far more powerful than an Intel laptop CPU or Arc GPU. The paper’s “2 seconds” is measured on it.
Win rate
The human-study score: wins divided by wins plus losses in side-by-side comparisons, with ties left out.
Guide

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The most important are latent and token, the diffusion transformer, the timestep, and rectified flow, because the whole method is built from them. T5, RoPE and AdaLN are parts of the transformer that appear in the architecture figure. The H100 entry is a reminder that the paper's two second speed is measured on a data centre GPU, not on Intel hardware.

§2Big picture

Two ideas carry the paper. (1) A deep VAE that compresses hard and dense (32×32×8 pixels → one 128-channel token), so the DiT has few tokens and can attend over all space and time. (2) A decoder that is itself a one-step diffusion model, so it can regenerate the fine detail that such heavy compression throws away.

§3The problem

  • Token count: usual 1:48–1:96 VAEs plus a 2×2 patchifier still leave far too many tokens for full 3-D attention at high resolution.
  • Naive patchify does not remove redundancy. It only regroups latent pixels (Fig. 3). The VAE has to learn a decorrelated latent itself.
  • Hard compression loses high frequencies: L2 blurs, LPIPS adds texture artifacts, and a Patch-GAN cannot tell depth-of-field blur from a fake.

§4Method

  1. Patchify at the VAE input, not the DiT input. A causal 3-D conv encoder maps a video of h×w×f to a latent of h/32 × w/32 × (f+7)/8 with 128 channels. The first frame gets its own latent frame. The DiT patch size is 1×1×1.
  2. Train the VAE with four losses: MSE, 3-D video DWT (L1 over 8 wavelet sub-bands), LPIPS, and Reconstruction-GAN. Plus uniform log-variance and per-channel learned noise injection in the decoder.
  3. Make the decoder a denoiser. D(zt, t) is conditioned on t through AdaNorm scale/shift and trained on noise levels t ∈ [0, 0.2], so it maps a slightly noisy latent straight to clean pixels.
  4. DiT = PixArt-α block with RMSNorm, QK-RMSNorm, 3-D RoPE on normalised fractional coordinates (pixels and seconds, relative to a max size, with exponentially spaced frequencies), T5-XXL text via cross-attention, and AdaLN timestep modulation.
  5. Per-token timestep for image-to-video: conditioning-frame tokens get a small tc, all others t = 1. No extra parameters.
  6. Rectified-flow training with velocity prediction. A log-normal t-sampler is shifted towards high noise as the token count grows, with the pdf clamped at the 0.5 and 99.9 percentiles. Multi-resolution batches keep a roughly constant token count (0–20% random token dropping), and images are trained jointly as 1-frame clips.
Guide

This is the recipe in order. First the VAE takes over patchifying and compresses each 32 by 32 by 8 pixel block into one 128-channel latent, trained with four reconstruction losses. Then the decoder is made a small denoiser so it can finish the last step. The transformer is a PixArt-style block with normalisation and rotary positions, and image-to-video works by giving conditioning tokens their own small timestep. Training uses rectified flow with a noise schedule shifted for many tokens.

The paper has no Algorithm box. The pseudo-code below is reconstructed from §2.1.1, §2.4 and §2.5.

LTX-Video inference (reconstructed, not an Algorithm box of the paper) input : prompt p, optional first frame I, schedule 1 = t_N > ... > t_2 > t_1 c ← T5-XXL(p) # text tokens, via cross-attn z ← N(0, I) shape (128, (f+7)/8, h/32, w/32) tau ← 1 for every token if I given: # image-to-video z_c ← CausalVAE.Enc(I) # 1 latent frame z[frame 0] ← (1-t_c) z_c + t_c · eps ; tau[frame 0] ← t_c # t_c small, e.g. 0 for k = N .. 2: # latent-to-latent steps v ← DiT(z, tau, c) # RoPE, QK-norm, AdaLN(tau per token) z ← z - (t_k - t_{k-1}) · v (only on non-conditioning tokens) x0 ← VAE.DenoisingDecoder(z, t_1) # final latent-to-pixel denoising return x0
Guide

This pseudo-code is reconstructed by the tab, not copied from the paper. The logic is simple: encode the prompt once with T5, start from pure noise, and if an image is given, place its latent in frame zero with a small timestep. Then loop the transformer, each time subtracting a velocity step from the noisy tokens only. Finally the denoising decoder turns the slightly noisy latent into pixels. The loop body is the part the thesis will quantize and possibly cache.

§5Every equation

The paper has no numbered equations. Below is all of its display and inline math in paper order (u1–u10), plus two lines (u11–u12) that spell out the compression arithmetic behind Table 1.

(u1)\[ z_{t_i} = (1-t_i)\,z_0 + t_i\,\epsilon,\qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I) \]

Rectified-flow forward noising (§2.1.1, §2.5.1): a straight line between the clean latent and Gaussian noise, with t ∈ [0,1].

Guide

This is how noise is added in rectified flow. z sub t i is the noisy latent at noise level t i, z zero is the clean latent, and epsilon is Gaussian noise. The noisy latent is simply a straight-line blend: one minus t times the clean latent plus t times the noise. At t equal to 0 it is clean, at t equal to 1 it is pure noise. Every later equation builds on this line.

(u2)\[ f^{\theta}(z_{t_i}, t_i) = z_0 \]

The ideal denoiser recovers the clean latent. In practice fθ predicts an intermediate quantity (the velocity) from which z0 follows in closed form (footnote 3).

Guide

The goal of the denoiser in one line. f theta is the neural network with weights theta, and given the noisy latent z sub t i and its noise level t i, it should return the clean latent z zero. In practice the network predicts a velocity, from which the clean latent follows directly, as equation u8 defines. Quantizing theta perturbs exactly this prediction.

(u3)\[ \{t_N, t_{N-1}, t_{N-2}, \dots, t_2, t_1\} \]

Decreasing noise levels used when iteratively refining z0, starting from pure noise.

Guide

The sampling schedule: a decreasing list of noise levels, from t N at pure noise down to t one, the lowest level. Generation refines the latent one level at a time along this list. In LTX the transformer covers t N down to t two, and the last level t one is handled by the decoder, as equation u6 states. Fewer levels means fewer transformer passes, which is the other lever on speed.

(u4)\[ z_0 = \mathcal E(x_0),\qquad x_0 = \mathcal D(z_0) \]

Standard latent diffusion: the encoder compresses the sample x0 and the decoder maps the latent back to pixels.

Guide

Standard latent diffusion in two halves. The encoder, script E, compresses a video x zero into a latent z zero, and the decoder, script D, maps a latent back to pixels. Diffusion happens only on the small latent. LTX keeps this structure but changes the decoder, which is what equation u5 introduces next.

(u5)\[ x_0 = \mathcal D(z_{t_i}, t_i) = \mathcal D\big((1-t_i)\,z_0 + t_i\,\epsilon,\; t_i\big) \]

Denoising decoder: 𝒟 is trained as a diffusion model that maps noisy latents to clean pixels, with ti ∈ [0, 0.2] during training.

Guide

The key change: the decoder also takes a noise level. It receives a noisy latent, the blend of clean latent and noise from equation u1, together with t i, and must output clean pixels x zero. It is trained on noise levels from 0 to 0.2 only, so it learns to clean up small residual noise while decoding. This is the fix for the leftover-noise problem in Problem B.

(u6)\[ x_0 = \mathcal D(z_{t_1}, t_1) \]

Because 𝒟 changes dimensionality it cannot be iterated. It performs only the final step, from the lowest latent noise level t1 to pixels.

Guide

How the denoising decoder is used at inference. Because the decoder changes the size of the data, from latent to pixels, it cannot be applied repeatedly. So it performs exactly one step, taking the latent at the lowest noise level t one and producing the final video x zero. The paper sets t one to 0.05.

(u7)\[ t\sim\mathcal U(0,1) \]

Original timestep sampling during training. LTX instead uses a shifted log-normal (SD3), clamped at the 0.5 and 99.9 percentiles (Fig. 10).

Guide

The baseline way to pick training noise levels: t drawn uniformly between 0 and 1. LTX replaces this with a shifted log-normal sampler from Stable Diffusion 3 that favours higher noise when there are more tokens, and clamps the tails at the 0.5 and 99.9 percentiles. Figure 10 draws the resulting distributions.

(u8)\[ v = \epsilon - z_0 \]

Velocity target (SD3). This regression task is more evenly difficult across t than noise prediction.

Guide

The training target. v is the velocity, epsilon is the noise, and z zero is the clean latent, so v equals noise minus clean latent: the direction of the straight line in equation u1. The transformer learns to predict v. This target is about equally hard at every noise level, which makes training more even than predicting noise.

(u9)\[ z_{t-\Delta t} = z_t - \Delta t\; v^{\theta}_t \]

Euler sampling step: move from pure noise z1 towards clean z0 along the predicted velocity.

Guide

One sampling step. The next latent, at noise level t minus delta t, equals the current latent z t minus delta t times the predicted velocity v theta. It walks back along the straight line from noise towards the clean latent. Each such step is one full transformer pass, so step count times DiT cost is the inference budget the thesis attacks.

(u10)\[ \text{win rate} = \frac{\text{wins}}{\text{wins} + \text{losses}} \]

Human-survey metric for Table 2 and Fig. 15. Skipped votes are excluded.

Guide

The human-survey metric. The win rate is the number of wins divided by wins plus losses, with skipped votes left out. So 85 percent means that in comparisons where raters expressed a preference, LTX was preferred 85 times out of 100. Table 2 and Figure 15 report this number.

(u11)\[ \frac{32\cdot 32\cdot 8\cdot 3}{128} = 192,\qquad \frac{8\cdot 8\cdot 4\cdot 3}{16}=48,\qquad \frac{8\cdot 8\cdot 8\cdot 3}{16}=96 \]

Total VAE compression = (pixel values per latent cell × 3 RGB) / latent channels (Table 1; arithmetic made explicit).

Guide

Total VAE compression made explicit. Take the pixels covered by one latent cell, times three colour values, and divide by the number of latent channels. For LTX that is 32 times 32 times 8 times 3 over 128, which is 192. Typical VAEs reach 48 or 96. So LTX's latent is two to four times smaller in raw numbers, as Table 1 lists.

(u12)\[ \underbrace{32\times 32\times 8}_{\text{LTX, patch }1\times1\times1} = 8192 \quad\text{vs.}\quad \underbrace{(8\cdot 2)\times(8\cdot 2)\times 4}_{\text{typical, patch }2\times2\times1}=1024 \]

Pixels per transformer token: LTX has 4–8× fewer tokens for the same video.

Guide

Pixels per transformer token, which is what really sets the token count. LTX has 32 by 32 by 8, so 8192 pixels per token, because its transformer patch size is one. A typical model has an 8 by 8 by 4 VAE plus a 2 by 2 patch, so 1024 pixels per token. That is why LTX sees four to eight times fewer tokens for the same video.

Image-to-video20%47%35%91%
Guide

The headline result: human preference in pairwise tests over 1,000 prompts per task and 20 raters. LTX wins 85 percent for text-to-video and 91 percent for image-to-video, far above Open-Sora Plan, CogVideoX 2B and PyramidFlow. All models ran at the same resolution, length and 40 steps. So speed did not cost quality.

Denoising-decoder study (§4.4, no numbers given): in an internal user study, decoding with t = 0.05 (the decoder denoises) was “strongly preferred” over t = 0.0 (no denoising), especially for high-motion videos. rGAN (§4.3.1) and RoPE spacing (§4.3.2) ablations are Figs. 16–17.

§8Why it matters for this thesis

LTX-Video → LTX-2.3 on OpenVINO / NNCF

  • The dense latent leaves no slack for error. Fig. 3 shows all 128 channels carry decorrelated information, and each token stands for 8192 pixels. A small error in the DiT’s velocity output (for example INT4 weight noise) is not averaged away by redundant channels; the decoder spreads it over a whole 32×32×8 block. Expect it to show up as blocky or temporal artifacts, and measure quality per frame and over time (FVD/VBench-type metrics), not just a single-image PSNR.
  • Compute sits in the DiT’s linear layers. 28 blocks at d=2048 with self-attn, cross-attn and a 4× FFN: these are the MatMuls that NNCF compress_weights (INT8/INT4 weight-only, data-free or AWQ/GPTQ-style with calibration) targets. Few tokens (about 6k for a 5-s 768×512 clip) means inference is closer to weight-bandwidth-bound on CPU/Arc, which is where weight-only compression pays off most.
  • Activation ranges depend on the timestep. AdaLN scale/shift (and in LTX a per-token t) change activation ranges from step to step. Any activation quantization (W8A8) or calibration set must sample latents from all timesteps, not only t≈1. QK-RMSNorm helps by keeping attention logits bounded (fewer outliers).
  • Keep the denoising VAE decoder at higher precision to start. It is a conv-heavy 3-D network (Conv3D, PixelNorm, noise injection) whose job is to rebuild high frequencies. Quantization noise here goes straight to pixels. Its last-step denoising (t≈0.05) may partly absorb small DiT errors, which is worth measuring. OpenVINO supports 3-D convolution natively; decoding 121 frames at full resolution is memory-heavy on CPU, so plan for temporal/spatial tiling.
  • The text encoder is big too. T5-XXL’s encoder has more parameters than the 1.9B DiT, but it runs only once per prompt, so INT8 weight compression there is a cheap memory win. Check what LTX-2.3 actually uses and what carries over (audio branch, larger DiT): this paper describes the v0.9 design, not 2.3.
Guide

Use this box as the plan of attack. Target the DiT's linear layers with NNCF weight-only INT8 or INT4 compression first, since with only about six thousand tokens the model is close to weight-bandwidth bound on CPU and Arc. Calibrate across all timesteps, keep the denoising decoder at higher precision at first, and compress T5 cheaply. Judge quality with temporal video metrics, and confirm which of these design points still hold in LTX-2.3.

Target models

LTX-2: Efficient Joint Audio-Visual Foundation Model

Y. HaCohen, B. Brazowski, N. Chiprut, Y. Bitterman, … Z. Farbman (Lightricks) · Technical report, arXiv:2601.03233 · January 2026 · weights and code: github.com/Lightricks/LTX-2

LTX-2 makes a video and its soundtrack together from one text prompt. A big video transformer and a smaller audio transformer run side by side and talk to each other at every layer, so lips, footsteps and music line up in time. This is the model the thesis compresses: almost all of its weight sits in two parts, the 19B dual-stream DiT and the 12B Gemma-3 text encoder.

Reading guide

LTX-2 asks whether one open model can generate a video and its soundtrack together from a single text prompt, with lips, footsteps and music in sync. Its answer is an asymmetric dual-stream transformer: a 14 billion parameter video stream and a 5 billion parameter audio stream that exchange information at every layer, conditioned on a frozen Gemma-3 12B text encoder. This is the exact model family the thesis compresses, so the tab is written as a map of where the weights and the compute sit. It moves from the big-picture component map, to the problem of joint generation and memory, to the method, every equation, every figure, the results, and a closing thesis box. Among the sixteen papers it is the second target-model paper, after LTX-Video, and everything that follows, from GPTQ to TeaCache to VBench, is a tool applied to it.

§0Before reading

LTX-2 is a latent diffusion transformer: it never touches pixels or sound waves while generating, only compact latent tokens that a denoiser cleans up step by step. It builds on three ideas: latents, self- versus cross-attention, and classifier-free guidance. It is in the atlas because it is the model family of the thesis model, LTX-2.3, so this report shows where the weights and the compute are.

Terms used in this paper

DiT (diffusion transformer)
A transformer used as the denoiser in a diffusion model. It works on a sequence of latent tokens instead of an image grid of pixels.
VAE latent
The compact code a variational autoencoder makes from video or audio. The encoder compresses, the decoder turns latents back into frames or sound.
Denoising step, timestep \(\sigma\)
One call of the denoiser. \(\sigma\) is the noise level: 1 means pure noise, 0 means a clean sample. Fewer steps means faster generation.
Rectified flow / flow matching
A training recipe where the model learns the straight-line direction (a velocity) from noise to data, so good samples need fewer steps.
Mel spectrogram
A picture of sound: time on one axis, frequency bands spaced like human hearing on the other, loudness as brightness.
Vocoder (HiFi-GAN)
A small network that turns a mel spectrogram back into an audio waveform. LTX-2 uses a HiFi-GAN style vocoder for 24 kHz stereo.
Cross-attention
Attention where queries come from one sequence and keys and values from another, for example video tokens reading text or audio tokens.
RoPE
Rotary position embedding: rotates queries and keys by an angle that depends on position, so attention knows where tokens are (3D for video, 1D time for audio).
AdaLN
Adaptive layer normalisation: small layers compute a scale, a shift and a gate from the timestep and apply them inside each block.
CFG (classifier-free guidance)
Running the model with and without a condition and extrapolating away from the unconditioned result. Stronger adherence, but extra forward passes.
Gemma-3 12B
An open decoder-only language model from Google. LTX-2 keeps it frozen and uses its hidden states from all layers as the text encoding.
BF16
A 16-bit floating-point format (2 bytes per number) with the same range as FP32 but fewer precision bits. The usual full-precision baseline here.
NVIDIA H100
A data-centre GPU from NVIDIA's Hopper generation, where the paper measures speed. It has far more memory and bandwidth than an Intel Arc card, so its timings will not transfer directly.
Wan 2.2
An open video generation model family from Alibaba. The paper compares its 14B version against LTX-2 for speed per step.
Guide

These fourteen terms cover what the report takes for granted. The most important are the diffusion transformer, the VAE latent, the timestep sigma and classifier-free guidance, because they explain where compute goes. RoPE and AdaLN appear inside every block, and AdaLN layers are small ones likely to stay in high precision. The H100 is the NVIDIA data-centre GPU used for the speed numbers, which will not transfer directly to Intel hardware.

§1Big picture: the full component map

The model has three parts: modality-specific causal VAEs, a text pipeline built on Gemma-3, and an asymmetric dual-stream DiT that denoises audio and video latents together. Because the DiT runs at every step, it dominates compute. Gemma-3 runs once per prompt but holds more than a third of the weights.

§2The problem

  • Silent T2V models and sequential T2V→V2A (or A2V) pipelines cannot model the joint distribution. The paper's fix is one model with two streams.
  • Symmetric twin backbones (e.g. Ovi: two 5B Wan streams) waste capacity, since audio carries less information than video. The fix is an asymmetric 14B/5B split.
  • Decoder-only LLM encoders use causal attention, and their last layer alone is a weak conditioning signal. The fix is to extract features from all layers and refine them bidirectionally.

§3Method

  1. Encode. Video goes through a spatiotemporal causal VAE (the LTX-Video latent space). Audio is converted to stereo 16 kHz, each channel becomes a mel spectrogram, the two are stacked as 2 channels, and a causal audio VAE turns them into 1D tokens (128-d, one per ≈1/25 s).
  2. Text. Gemma-3 12B stays frozen. Hidden states from all L layers are mean-centred and scaled per layer, flattened to D·L and projected by W to D. W is trained once, early, with the diffusion MSE loss, then frozen.
  3. Connectors. Each stream gets its own connector: bidirectional transformer blocks. Learnable "thinking tokens" replace the padding positions. A caption projection then feeds the result to the DiT by cross-attention.
  4. Dual-stream block (×depth), run per stream: self-attention (3D RoPE for video, 1D for audio) → text cross-attention → AV cross-attention (temporal RoPE only, AdaLN on Q and on K/V, output gate driven by the other modality's timestep) → FFN. RMSNorm sits between the operations.
  5. Sample with modality-aware CFG (§4.1). Video uses st=3, sm=3; audio uses st=7, sm=3.
  6. Multi-scale, multi-tile. Generate a base latent at ≈0.5 MP, upscale it in latent space, split it into overlapping spatial and temporal tiles, refine each tile with the same model, blend in latent space, then VAE-decode.
  7. Decode. The video VAE decoder produces frames. The audio VAE decoder produces a stereo mel, and a HiFi-GAN vocoder (2× channels) turns it into a 24 kHz stereo waveform.
Guide

The pipeline runs in a clear order. First, video and audio are compressed into latents, audio as one 128-dimensional token per twenty-fifth of a second. Next, the frozen Gemma model turns the prompt into features that are merged across all its layers and refined by one connector per stream. Then the dual-stream blocks denoise both latents together, guided by modality-aware guidance, optionally refined tile by tile at high resolution, and finally decoded into frames and 24 kilohertz stereo sound.

Inference loop (atlas summary of §3 and §4, not an Algorithm box from the paper)

e_V, e_A = ConnectorV(FeatExt(Gemma3(prompt))), ConnectorA(FeatExt(Gemma3(prompt))) # once z_V, z_A = noise(video_latent_shape), noise(audio_latent_shape) for σ in schedule (N steps): for stream s in {V, A}: # both run inside one DiT call full = M_s(z_s, e_s, m = other stream) no_txt = M_s(z_s, ∅, m = other stream) no_mod = M_s(z_s, e_s, m = ∅) v_s = full + s_t(full − no_txt) + s_m(full − no_mod) z_s = Euler(z_s, v_s, σ) if multiscale: z_V = LatentUpscaler(z_V); z_V = blend(refine(tile) for tile in tiles(z_V)) frames = VideoVAE.decode(z_V); wav24k = Vocoder(AudioVAE.decode(z_A))
Guide

The whole inference loop fits in a few lines. The text is encoded once into one embedding per stream. Then, for every noise level, each stream computes three predictions, full, without text and without the other modality, mixes them with the guidance weights and takes an Euler step. After optional upscaling and tile refinement, the latents are decoded. Note that this is the tab author's summary, not an algorithm box from the paper.

This table is a compression plan. Each row is a component with its role, parameter count, how often it runs per clip, and a suggested precision. §4Every equation

The paper has no numbered equations and only one display equation, the modality-aware CFG. The other entries below are written out from the paper's prose and are marked as such.

(§4.1)\[ \hat{\mathcal{M}}(x,t,m)=\mathcal{M}(x,t,m)+s_t\big(\mathcal{M}(x,t,m)-\mathcal{M}(x,\varnothing,m)\big)+s_m\big(\mathcal{M}(x,t,m)-\mathcal{M}(x,t,\varnothing)\big) \]

The paper's only display equation. x is this stream's latent, t the text condition, m the other modality's features. st scales text guidance and sm scales cross-modal guidance. With st=sm=0 it reduces to one conditional pass.

Guide

The paper's only displayed equation is its guidance rule. M hat is the guided prediction for one stream, where x is that stream's noisy latent, t is the text condition and m is the other modality's features. It starts from the fully conditioned prediction, then adds s t times its difference from the text-dropped prediction and s m times its difference from the modality-dropped prediction. With both weights zero it reduces to one ordinary pass; otherwise it costs three.

(§4.1 values)\[ \text{video: } s_t=3,\; s_m=3 \qquad\qquad \text{audio: } s_t=7,\; s_m=3 \]

Guidance weights used for all reported results. Larger sm improves sync and semantic coherence.

Guide

These are the guidance weights behind every reported result. Video uses a text weight s t of three and a cross-modal weight s m of three; audio uses a stronger text weight of seven and the same cross-modal weight of three. The paper says a larger s m improves synchronisation and semantic coherence. When benchmarking on CPU or Arc, keep these settings fixed so the quality and speed numbers are comparable to the paper's.

(§3.2.1*)\[ \tilde h_\ell=\operatorname{scale}\!\big(h_\ell-\mu_\ell\big),\quad h_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times D};\qquad e=\big[\tilde h_1\,\Vert\,\cdots\,\Vert\,\tilde h_L\big]\,W,\quad W\in\mathbb{R}^{(D\cdot L)\times D} \]

*Written from the three prose steps: mean-centre and scale each layer over (T, D), flatten to [B,T,D·L], project with a learned dense W to D. ‖ is concatenation. The paper does not specify the exact scaling statistic.

Guide

This equation reconstructs the feature extractor from the paper's prose; the paper gives no formula. For each Gemma layer l, the hidden state h l is centred by subtracting its mean mu l and then scaled. All L layers are concatenated side by side and multiplied by the learned matrix W, which maps width times L down to width D, giving the embedding e. The exact scaling statistic is not specified, so treat the details as approximate.

(A1*)\[ z_\sigma=(1-\sigma)\,z_0+\sigma\,\epsilon,\qquad \mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{z_0,\epsilon,\sigma}\big\lVert v_\theta(z_\sigma,\sigma,c)-(\epsilon-z_0)\big\rVert_2^2 \]

*Standard rectified-flow form. Fig. A1 only says "match their velocity fields using a flow-matching loss", applied to both the audio and video latents. The exact sign and time conventions are not given.

Guide

Training uses the standard rectified-flow objective, written here in its usual form because the paper only names it. The noisy latent z sigma is a straight-line blend of the clean latent z zero and Gaussian noise epsilon, weighted by the noise level sigma. The network v theta, given the condition c, is trained to predict the velocity, epsilon minus z zero, with a squared-error loss, separately for audio and video. Signs and time conventions may differ in the real code.

LTX-2 is about eighteen times faster per step than Wan 2.2, despite having more parameters. On an H100 at 720p with 121 frames, Wan 2.2 with 14 billion parameters takes 22.3 seconds per step for video only, while LTX-2 with 19 billion takes 1.22 seconds for audio and video. The paper credits its compact latent space. Note that guidance was off, so real runs with modality guidance cost up to three times more.

That is ≈18× faster with more parameters and an extra modality. The speed comes from LTX-Video's highly compressed latent space, which produces far fewer tokens. The paper says the gap grows with resolution and duration, and that LTX-2 is also faster than Ovi (two 5B Wan-2.2 streams), but gives no number for Ovi.

§7Why it matters for this thesis

LTX-2(.3) on Intel CPU / Arc with OpenVINO + NNCF

  • Compress the transformer first. The 19B dual-stream DiT runs N steps × up to 3 CFG passes, plus tile refinements, so it dominates both latency and memory (≈38 GB BF16). NNCF weight-only INT8, or INT4 (e.g. nncf.compress_weights with a group size and mixed INT4/INT8 ratio), runs with standard OpenVINO ops and needs no custom kernels. Data-free methods need no calibration. AWQ, scale estimation or GPTQ need a few denoising-step activations, collected across several σ values.
  • Compress Gemma-3 12B second. It runs only once per prompt, so compressing it frees memory (24 → ≈6 GB at INT4) more than it saves time. LLM-style INT4 weight compression is mature. Validate on the feature-extractor output, which depends on all layers, not only the last one. Errors in early layers matter here.
  • Keep the small parts in FP16/BF16. VAE decoders, vocoder, connectors, the timestep/AdaLN modulation and gate linears, and the patchify and output projections have few weights but are precision-sensitive. Exclude them with an NNCF ignored_scope, and compare Fig. A2's scale/shift/gate paths before and after. The video VAE decoder is activation-bound at 1080p, so tiling matters more than bit-width for it.
  • Reduce passes before shrinking bits. Modality-CFG means 3 forward passes per step (§4.1), so caching or skipping guidance passes on some steps is a cheap extra speed-up that stacks with quantization. Table 1's 1.22 s/step used CFG = 1 on an H100. Report CPU and Arc numbers under the same stated settings (frames, resolution, steps, CFG).
  • Check the paper against the exports. This report describes LTX-2, not 2.3, and it contradicts itself on parameter counts (14B+5B in the abstract and §3.1, 13B+3B in the conclusion). Sum the weight constants in each exported IR (text_encoder, transformer, connectors, video/audio VAE, vocoder, and the upscaler if multi-scale is used) and publish that as the thesis parameter table.
Guide

Act on this in four steps. First, compress the 19 billion parameter transformer with NNCF weight-only INT8 or INT4, calibrating data-aware methods on activations from several noise levels. Second, compress Gemma for memory and check the feature-extractor output. Third, keep the decoders, vocoder, connectors and the AdaLN modulation layers in sixteen bit with an ignored scope, and reduce guidance passes with caching. Finally, count parameters in the actual exported models, since the paper describes LTX-2, not 2.3.

Quantization foundations (LLMs)

GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers

Elias Frantar, Saleh Ashkboos, Torsten Hoefler, Dan Alistarh · IST Austria, ETH Zurich, NeuralMagic · ICLR 2023 (arXiv 2210.17323)

GPTQ quantizes a trained model's weights to 3–4 bits, one layer at a time, using a small calibration set. Every time a column of weights is rounded, the rounding error is pushed onto the columns that are still in full precision, weighted by second-order (Hessian) information. Three engineering tricks — one shared column order, lazy block updates and a Cholesky form of the inverse Hessian — make this fast enough for 175B-parameter models.

Bits (weights only)
4 / 3 (2, ternary w/ groups)
Largest model
OPT-175B, BLOOM-176B
Quantization time
≈4 GPU-h for 175B
OPT-175B Wiki2 PPL
8.34 → 8.37 (4b)
Calibration
128 × 2048 C4 tokens
Speed-up (3b kernel)
3.24× A100, 4.53× A6000
Reading guide

GPTQ asks whether a huge trained language model can have its weights squeezed to three or four bits in a few GPU hours, without retraining and without losing quality. Its answer is yes: round the weights one column at a time and push each rounding error onto the columns not yet rounded, guided by second-order information from a small calibration set. The tab opens with the big picture, then the problem of plain rounding and slow exact solvers, then the method and its three speed tricks, every equation, the paper's figures, the result tables, and finally a box on what this means for the thesis. Among the sixteen papers, GPTQ is the first of three quantization foundations for large language models, followed by SmoothQuant and AWQ. The diffusion quantization papers later in the atlas, and NNCF's int4 weight compression, build directly on its error compensation idea.

§0Before reading

GPTQ builds on three ideas: what it means to store a weight in 4 or 3 bits, why a layer's inputs decide which rounding errors hurt (the Hessian), and why low-bit weights make text generation faster. GPTQ is in the atlas because its error-compensating weight quantization is the method behind NNCF's data-aware int4 compression, the tool most likely to be used on LTX-2.3.

Terms used in this paper

Post-training quantization (PTQ)
Converting an already trained model to fewer bits without retraining it. GPTQ only needs a small calibration set and a few GPU hours.
Weight-only quantization
Only the stored weights become low-bit; activations stay FP16. The paper's "3-bit" and "4-bit" always mean weights only (W3A16, W4A16).
Round-to-nearest (RTN)
The baseline: snap every weight to its closest grid level independently. Simple and data-free, but it breaks down at 3 bits on large models.
Calibration set
A few real inputs run through the model to record layer inputs \(\mathbf{X}\). GPTQ uses 128 random text segments of 2048 tokens from C4.
Hessian
Here \(\mathbf{H}=2\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^\top\): a matrix built from the calibration inputs that says which combinations of weight errors change the layer output most.
OBS / OBQ
Optimal Brain Surgeon and Optimal Brain Quantizer: older second-order methods that quantize one weight at a time and correct the others. Accurate, but far too slow for billions of weights; GPTQ is their fast version.
Cholesky decomposition
A standard, numerically stable way to factor a symmetric positive matrix into a triangular one. GPTQ uses it to get all needed inverse-Hessian rows at once.
Group size (g128)
Instead of one scale per row, every block of 128 consecutive weights gets its own scale and zero point. Costs a fraction of a bit, recovers most 4-bit accuracy.
Perplexity (PPL)
How surprised a language model is by real text; lower is better. The paper's main quality metric, measured on WikiText2, PTB and C4.
WikiText2, PTB, C4
Standard text corpora: Wikipedia articles, Penn Treebank news text, and a large cleaned web crawl. Used to measure perplexity.
LAMBADA, ARC, PIQA
Zero-shot benchmarks: predict a story's last word, answer school science questions, and pick the sensible solution to an everyday physical task.
OPT, BLOOM
Two open families of GPT-style language models, up to about 175 billion parameters. GPTQ's test subjects.
NVIDIA A100, A6000
A100: a datacenter GPU (80 GB version used here). A6000: a cheaper 48 GB workstation GPU with lower memory bandwidth. Neither is Intel hardware; speed-ups must be measured on the target Intel devices.
Guide

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. The most important are round to nearest, the simple baseline GPTQ beats; the Hessian, built from calibration inputs, which ranks weight errors; group size, the per block scales that recover most four bit accuracy; and perplexity, the language model quality score where lower is better. The hardware entries are NVIDIA GPUs, not Intel devices, so treat the paper's speed numbers as context, not as predictions.

§1Big picture

Only weights are quantized; activations stay FP16. The model is stored as low-bit integers plus a scale (and zero point) per row or group, and dequantized on the fly.

§2The problem

  • Prior LLM quantizers (ZeroQuant, LLM.int8(), nuQmm) all just round to nearest: fine at 8 bits, not at 3–4.
  • Accurate post-training methods (AdaRound, BRECQ, OBQ) take ≈1 h for a 25M-parameter ResNet-50 — hopeless for 175B.
  • Activation outliers are not the issue here: GPTQ is weight-only.

§3Method

Background: OBS → OBQ

OBQ (Optimal Brain Quantization) adapts the classic OBS (Optimal Brain Surgeon) pruning rule to quantization: each row is solved separately; quantize one weight at a time (greedy), then update the rest with Eq. (2) and shrink \(\mathbf{H}^{-1}\) with Eq. (3).

Step 1 — arbitrary (shared) order

Step 2 — lazy batch updates

Step 3 — Cholesky reformulation

Whole-model pipeline

  1. Run 128 random 2048-token C4 segments to the current block; for each linear layer build \(\mathbf{H}=2\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^\top\).
  2. Damp (\(+\lambda\mathbf{I}\), \(\lambda\) = 1% of mean diagonal), invert, take the upper Cholesky factor.
  3. Sweep columns in blocks of B = 128: round column j to the per-row asymmetric min-max grid (or per-group grid, with group params fitted on the current updated weights), push the scaled error into the rest of the block.
  4. After each block, apply one GEMM update to all remaining columns.
  5. Re-run the block with quantized weights to get inputs for the next block.
Guide

The recipe walks through the network one block at a time. Each linear layer gets its Hessian, which is damped, inverted and turned into a Cholesky factor once. Then the columns are swept in blocks of one hundred twenty-eight: round, push the error inside the block, and after the block update everything else in one go. Grid parameters are fitted on the already updated weights. Finally, the quantized block produces inputs for the next.

Algorithm 1 Quantize W given inverse Hessian H⁻¹ = (2XXᵀ + λI)⁻¹ and blocksize B. Q ← 0_{d_row × d_col} // quantized output E ← 0_{d_row × B} // block quantization errors H⁻¹ ← Cholesky(H⁻¹)ᵀ // Hessian inverse information for i = 0, B, 2B, … do for j = i, …, i + B − 1 do Q[:, j] ← quant(W[:, j]) // quantize column E[:, j−i] ← (W[:, j] − Q[:, j]) / [H⁻¹]_jj // quantization error W[:, j:(i+B)] ← W[:, j:(i+B)] − E[:, j−i] · H⁻¹[j, j:(i+B)] // update weights in block end for W[:, (i+B):] ← W[:, (i+B):] − E · H⁻¹[i:(i+B), (i+B):] // update all remaining weights end for
Guide

Algorithm 1 is the entire quantizer for one layer, and it combines all three tricks. It takes the damped inverse Hessian, replaces it by its Cholesky factor once, and then loops over blocks of B columns. Inside a block it rounds each column, divides the error by the diagonal entry, and subtracts that error times the matching Cholesky row from the remaining columns of the block. The saved block errors then update all later columns with one matrix multiply.

§4Every equation

(1)\[ \operatorname{argmin}_{\widehat{\mathbf{W}}}\ \lVert \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}-\widehat{\mathbf{W}}\mathbf{X}\rVert_2^2 \]

Layer-wise reconstruction: find quantized weights \(\widehat{\mathbf{W}}\) (on a fixed grid) whose outputs on calibration inputs \(\mathbf{X}\) (m samples) match the FP layer \(\mathbf{W}\).

Guide

Equation one is the goal for each layer. Find quantized weights W hat, restricted to the grid, that minimise the squared difference between W times X and W hat times X, where W is the full-precision weight matrix and X holds the layer inputs from the calibration samples. It matches layer outputs, not weights, so errors on unimportant directions are cheap. Every later equation is a way to solve this problem approximately and quickly.

§3\[ \mathbf{H}_F = 2\,\mathbf{X}_F\mathbf{X}_F^{\top} \]

Hessian of the per-row quadratic objective restricted to the set \(F\) of still full-precision weights. Depends only on inputs, not on weights.

Guide

H sub F equals two times X sub F times X sub F transposed. This is the Hessian, the curvature, of the layer objective for one row, restricted to F, the set of weights still in full precision. It tells how costly an error in each direction is. The key point is that it depends only on the inputs, not on the weights, which is why all rows can share it once the column order is fixed.

(2)\[ w_q=\operatorname{argmin}_{w_q}\frac{(\operatorname{quant}(w_q)-w_q)^2}{[\mathbf{H}_F^{-1}]_{qq}},\qquad \boldsymbol{\delta}_F=-\frac{w_q-\operatorname{quant}(w_q)}{[\mathbf{H}_F^{-1}]_{qq}}\cdot(\mathbf{H}_F^{-1})_{:,q} \]

OBQ: greedily pick the weight whose rounding costs least, then shift all remaining weights by \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_F\) to cancel its error. \(\operatorname{quant}\) = round to nearest grid point.

Guide

Equation two is the OBQ rule that GPTQ inherits. The first part picks the weight whose rounding error squared, divided by its diagonal entry of the inverse Hessian, is smallest. The second part, delta F, shifts all remaining weights by minus that scaled error times the matching column of the inverse Hessian, cancelling its effect on the output. Quant means rounding to the nearest grid point. GPTQ keeps the update but drops the greedy choice.

(3)\[ \mathbf{H}^{-1}_{-q}=\Big(\mathbf{H}^{-1}-\frac{1}{[\mathbf{H}^{-1}]_{qq}}\,\mathbf{H}^{-1}_{:,q}\mathbf{H}^{-1}_{q,:}\Big)_{-p} \]

Remove row/column \(q\) directly in the inverse via one Gaussian-elimination step (subscript printed as \(-p\) in the paper; it means \(-q\)).

Guide

Equation three removes a quantized weight from the problem without inverting a new matrix. It subtracts from the inverse Hessian an outer product of its q-th column and q-th row, divided by the q-th diagonal entry, which is one step of Gaussian elimination, and then drops row and column q. The paper prints the subscript as minus p but means minus q. Repeated use of this update is what drifts numerically at scale.

§3\[ O(d_{\text{row}}\cdot d_{\text{col}}^{3})\ \longrightarrow\ O\big(\max\{d_{\text{row}}\cdot d_{\text{col}}^{2},\ d_{\text{col}}^{3}\}\big) \]

OBQ cost vs. GPTQ cost with a shared column order: a \(\min\{d_{\text{row}},d_{\text{col}}\}\) speed-up.

Guide

This line is the cost argument in one step. OBQ costs on the order of rows times columns cubed per layer. With a shared column order GPTQ costs the larger of rows times columns squared and columns cubed. That is a speed-up by a factor of the smaller dimension, thousands of times for large models, and it is what makes one hundred seventy-five billion parameters feasible in hours.

(4)\[ \boldsymbol{\delta}_F=-(\mathbf{w}_Q-\operatorname{quant}(\mathbf{w}_Q))\,([\mathbf{H}_F^{-1}]_{QQ})^{-1}\,(\mathbf{H}_F^{-1})_{:,Q} \]

Multi-weight (block) version of (2): compensation for quantizing a whole index set \(Q\) (e.g. B = 128 columns) at once.

Guide

Equation four is the block version of the update in equation two. Instead of one weight, a whole index set Q, such as one hundred twenty-eight columns, is quantized together. The correction delta F is minus the block error times the inverse of the Q by Q sub-block of the inverse Hessian, times the matching columns. This is the lazy batch update that applies once per block in Algorithm 1.

(5)\[ \mathbf{H}^{-1}_{-Q}=\Big(\mathbf{H}^{-1}-\mathbf{H}^{-1}_{:,Q}\,([\mathbf{H}^{-1}]_{QQ})^{-1}\,\mathbf{H}^{-1}_{Q,:}\Big)_{-Q} \]

Multi-row removal from the inverse; repeated use accumulates round-off and motivates the Cholesky reformulation.

Guide

Equation five removes many rows and columns from the inverse Hessian at once, the block version of equation three. It subtracts the Q columns times the inverse of the Q by Q sub-block times the Q rows. Applied over and over through a large layer, it accumulates round-off error and can make the matrix indefinite, as figure four shows. That failure is why GPTQ switches to the Cholesky form.

§4\[ \mathbf{H}\leftarrow\mathbf{H}+\lambda\mathbf{I},\qquad \lambda=0.01\cdot\operatorname{mean}\big(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{H})\big) \]

Dampening: add 1% of the average diagonal to keep \(\mathbf{H}\) well-conditioned.

Guide

Dampening adds lambda times the identity to the Hessian, with lambda equal to one percent of the average diagonal value. This small boost keeps the matrix well-conditioned, so inverting it and taking a Cholesky factor stay stable even when some input directions are almost never used. It is a cheap safety step and a setting worth keeping in mind in NNCF's GPTQ options.

§4\[ \big[\operatorname{Cholesky}(\mathbf{H}^{-1})^{\top}\big]_{q,\,q:}=\frac{[\mathbf{H}^{-1}_{F_q}]_{q,\,q:}}{\big([\mathbf{H}^{-1}_{F_q}]_{qq}\big)^{1/2}} \]

Row \(q\) of the upper Cholesky factor equals the needed row of \(\mathbf{H}^{-1}_{F_q}\) (from the diagonal on), just scaled; so all rows can be precomputed stably.

Guide

This identity is the heart of the Cholesky trick. Row q of the upper Cholesky factor of the inverse Hessian, from the diagonal onward, equals the row GPTQ needs from the shrinking inverse, divided by the square root of its diagonal entry. So instead of updating the inverse column after column, one Cholesky factorisation computed at the start gives every needed row, stably. Algorithm 1 uses exactly these rows.

Alg. 1\[ \mathbf{H}^{-1}=(2\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1} \]

Input to Algorithm 1: the damped inverse Hessian of the layer, computed once per layer.

Guide

The input to Algorithm 1 is H inverse, the inverse of two X X transposed plus lambda times the identity. X is the layer's calibration inputs and lambda the one percent dampening. It is computed once per layer, then replaced by its Cholesky factor. Its size depends only on the number of input columns, which keeps the cost modest even on a CPU.

§5\[ \bar b\approx b+\frac{16+b}{g} \]

Average bits/weight with grouping (FP16 scale + b-bit zero point per group of g): 3-bit g1024 ≈ +0.02, g128 ≈ +0.15; 2-bit g128 ≈ 2.2, g32 ≈ 2.6 (derived from the text).

Guide

Grouping costs a few extra bits. The average bits per weight, b bar, is about b plus sixteen plus b, divided by g, because each group of g weights stores a sixteen-bit scale and a b-bit zero point. Three-bit with groups of one thousand twenty-four adds about 0.02 bits, groups of one hundred twenty-eight add about 0.15, and two-bit ranges from about 2.2 to 2.6 bits. These figures are derived from the text.

A.2.1\[ \operatorname{PPL}=\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\log p(x_t\mid x_{\lt t})\Big) \]

Perplexity as used in all language-generation tables: non-overlapping 2048-token segments, exponentiated mean next-token negative log-likelihood (described in words in the paper).

Guide

Perplexity is the language quality score in all the tables, and lower is better. It is the exponential of minus the average log probability the model gives each true next token, over N tokens, using non-overlapping segments of two thousand forty-eight tokens. A perplexity of eight means the model is roughly as unsure as choosing among eight words. The paper describes it in words; the formula is the standard one.

GPTQ357.8059.7761.8163.9769.2675.37
Guide

StoryCloze accuracy for BLOOM, higher being better, closes the appendix. Four-bit GPTQ stays within about half a point of FP16 on the largest model, and three-bit GPTQ gets 75.37 against 48.50 for RTN. Across all these tasks the conclusion is the same: GPTQ keeps large models usable at three bits.

§7Why it matters for this thesis

GPTQ → LTX-2.3 on OpenVINO / NNCF

  • It is already in the toolchain. NNCF's data-aware int4 weight compression (nncf.compress_weights(..., mode=INT4_SYM/INT4_ASYM, group_size=128, dataset=..., gptq=True), optionally with scale_estimation=True) applies GPTQ-style error compensation. The output is ordinary compressed weights (int4 + scale/zero point) in OpenVINO IR, which run on OpenVINO's standard weight-compressed MatMul kernels on CPU and Arc GPU. No custom kernels are needed.
  • It needs calibration data, and for a diffusion model that data must cover the timesteps. \(\mathbf{H}=2\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^\top\) comes from real layer inputs. For LTX-2.3, collect DiT inputs across prompts and across denoising steps (early, noisy steps and late steps differ), for both the video and the audio streams. Otherwise the error compensation is fitted to the wrong input statistics.
  • Grouping is the lever the paper recommends. Fig. 4 and Table 5 show that g128 recovers most of the 4-bit loss. This matches NNCF's int4 group_size. Keep sensitive layers (embeddings, final projection, possibly adaLN/timestep MLPs) in int8 or FP16 using NNCF's ratio or ignored scopes, as GPTQ keeps embeddings and the output layer in FP16.
  • Expect memory savings more than latency gains for video. GPTQ's speed-ups come from memory-bound matrix-vector products at batch 1 (Table 6). A video DiT processes thousands of tokens per step, so it is mostly compute-bound. int4 weights will mainly cut RAM/VRAM and load time, and speed-ups on Intel hardware must be measured, not assumed. Pair it with caching or activation int8 for compute savings.
  • The compute cost is modest. GPTQ needs one \(d_{\text{col}}\times d_{\text{col}}\) Hessian per linear layer plus a Cholesky factorization, so it is feasible on a workstation CPU. Budget the extra compression time and report RTN (NNCF data-free) vs GPTQ vs AWQ/scale-estimation as an ablation.
Guide

Treat GPTQ as a ready-made option in NNCF rather than something to implement. Turn on the GPTQ flag in int4 weight compression with group size one hundred twenty-eight, and feed it calibration inputs gathered across prompts, denoising timesteps, and both the video and audio streams of LTX-2.3. Keep sensitive layers in int8 or FP16. Expect memory savings more than speed, measure latency on the Intel hardware, and report RTN, GPTQ and AWQ side by side as an ablation.

Quantization foundations (LLMs)

SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models

Guangxuan Xiao, Ji Lin, Mickael Seznec, Hao Wu, Julien Demouth, Song Han · MIT & NVIDIA · ICML 2023 (PMLR 202) · arXiv:2211.10438

Weights of big transformers are easy to quantize, but their activations have a few huge “outlier” channels that ruin INT8. SmoothQuant divides each activation channel by a factor \(s_j\) and multiplies the matching weight row by the same \(s_j\) — the product is unchanged, but now both operands are smooth enough for plain INT8 × INT8 matrix multiplication (W8A8). It is training-free, done offline from a small calibration set.

Format
W8A8 (INT8 GEMM + BMM)
Key knob
α = 0.5 (OPT/BLOOM), 0.75 (GLM)
OPT-175B avg acc.
66.8% vs 66.9% FP16
Speed-up
up to 1.56× (FasterTransformer)
Memory
≈ 2× less (1.96×)
Calibration
512 Pile sentences, once
Reading guide

SmoothQuant asks why large transformers break when both weights and activations are cast to eight-bit integers, and how to fix that without retraining. Its answer is to divide each troublesome activation channel by a scale and multiply the matching weight row by the same scale, so the product stays identical but both sides become easy to quantize. That gives W eight A eight, meaning eight-bit weights and eight-bit activations, running on ordinary integer matrix kernels. The tab moves from the big picture, to the outlier problem, to the smoothing method and its equations, then every figure from the paper, the results tables, and a closing box on what this means for LTX-2.3 with NNCF. Among the sixteen papers it is the second of three language-model quantization foundations, after GPTQ and before AWQ. GPTQ and AWQ compress weights only, while SmoothQuant is the one that makes activations quantizable too.

§0Before reading

SmoothQuant builds on three ideas: how rounding to 8-bit integers works (one step size for many numbers), the difference between quantizing only the weights and quantizing the activations too, and which numbers share a step size. The paper is in the atlas because it is the classic fix for activation outliers, and its “smoothing” trick reappears in NNCF and in almost every diffusion quantizer that follows.

Terms used in this paper

Activation
The numbers flowing between layers for one input, the \(\mathbf{X}\) in \(\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{XW}\). Unlike weights they change with every input, so they are only known at run time.
Outlier channel
A feature dimension of \(\mathbf{X}\) whose values are far larger (up to about 100 times) than the rest. In LLMs above about 6.7B parameters these channels stay the same across tokens.
W8A8
Weights stored in 8-bit integers and activations cast to 8-bit integers, so the matrix multiply itself runs in INT8. Compare W4A16: 4-bit weights, activations left in FP16.
Step size (scale)
The gap \(\Delta\) between neighbouring integer levels, usually \(\max|x|/127\) for INT8. Every value is divided by it and rounded.
Per-tensor / per-token / per-channel
How many values share one step size: the whole matrix, each token row, or each channel column.
Static vs dynamic
Static: activation scales fixed once from calibration data (cheapest). Dynamic: scales computed on the fly from each input. SmoothQuant-O3 is static per-tensor; O1 is dynamic per-token.
Calibration set
A small batch of real inputs run once through the model to record activation ranges. Here: 512 random sentences from the Pile text corpus.
GEMM / BMM
General matrix multiply (a linear layer) and batched matrix multiply (the two matmuls inside attention). They dominate compute, so they are what should go to INT8.
A100
NVIDIA's Ampere-generation data-centre GPU, used here in its 80 GB version. Its Tensor Cores run INT8 matrix multiplies faster than FP16 ones.
Tensor Core
NVIDIA's dedicated matrix-multiply units. Intel's rough counterparts are XMX engines on Arc GPUs and VNNI/AMX instructions on recent Xeon CPUs.
FasterTransformer
NVIDIA's optimised C++/CUDA inference library for transformers. The paper's biggest speed-ups (up to 1.56 times) are measured inside it.
LLM.int8()
The main competitor: it keeps outlier channels in FP16 and the rest in INT8. Accurate, but the mixed-precision split makes it slower than plain FP16 in most of the paper's tests.
OPT, BLOOM, GLM-130B
Open large language models used as test subjects, up to 175 billion (OPT) and 176 billion (BLOOM) parameters.
LAMBADA, WikiText
Language benchmarks. LAMBADA: accuracy at predicting the last word of a passage (higher is better). WikiText-2: perplexity, how surprised the model is by real text (lower is better).
Guide

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The most important are outlier channel, W eight A eight, the difference between static and dynamic scales, and per-tensor versus per-token versus per-channel granularity. The hardware and benchmark names matter too: the results come from NVIDIA A100 GPUs and the FasterTransformer library, and accuracy is measured on language tasks such as LAMBADA and WikiText, not on images or video.

§2Big picture

SmoothQuant is a per-input-channel rescaling \(\mathbf{Y}=(\mathbf{X}\,\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{s})^{-1})(\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{s})\mathbf{W})\). The scale is folded into the previous op offline, so at runtime only plain INT8 GEMMs run. One knob, \(\alpha\), sets how much difficulty moves to the weights.

§3The problem

  • Activations >> weights in difficulty. Weights are flat (INT8 or even INT4 weight-only is fine); activation outliers are ~100× larger than typical values.
  • Outliers persist in fixed channels across all tokens; variation within a channel is small (Fig. 4).
  • Existing W8A8 baselines (naive, ZeroQuant, Outlier Suppression) give near-random OPT-175B; LLM.int8() keeps accuracy by running outliers in FP16 but is slower than FP16.

§4Method

  1. Calibrate. Run 512 random Pile sentences; record per-input-channel \(\max|\mathbf{X}_j|\) for each smoothed linear (and static step sizes \(\Delta\) for O3).
  2. Pick α. Quick grid search on a Pile validation subset: 0.5 for OPT/BLOOM, 0.75 for GLM-130B, 0.8–0.9 for Llama/Mistral (Tables 6–7).
  3. Compute s per channel with Eq. (4).
  4. Fold. Divide the producer (LayerNorm \(\gamma,\beta\) or previous linear) by \(\mathbf{s}\); multiply the weight rows by \(\mathbf{s}\) (Eq. 3). No runtime op added.
  5. Quantize all linear weights and BMM inputs to INT8 (Fig. 6), choose O1/O2/O3 granularity (Table 2).
  6. Run with off-the-shelf INT8 GEMM kernels (CUTLASS); dequantize with Eq. (2).
Guide

The recipe runs in five stages, all offline except the last. First, measure the largest absolute value of every input channel on 512 calibration sentences. Then pick alpha by a quick search, which gives about one half for OPT and BLOOM and higher values for Llama-style models. From alpha, compute the scales, fold them into the previous operation and the weights, quantize every linear layer and attention product to eight bits, and finally run on standard integer kernels.

Procedure SmoothQuant (summary of Sec. 4–5; the paper has no Algorithm box) input : FP16 transformer, calibration set D (512 Pile sentences), α for each block: for each smoothed linear L with input X (QKV after LN1, FC1 after LN2): a_j ← max over D, tokens of |X[:, j]| # per input channel w_j ← max over out-channels of |W[j, :]| # rows of all layers sharing X s_j ← a_j^α / w_j^(1−α) # Eq. (4) producer(X) ← producer(X) · diag(s)^−1 # e.g. LN γ,β ÷ s W ← diag(s) · W # Eq. (3) quantize every Linear / BMM: W → INT8 (per-tensor), X → INT8 (O1/O2/O3) keep LayerNorm, Softmax, ReLU/GELU, residual adds in FP16 # Fig. 6
Guide

The procedure as pseudocode written by the tab, since the paper has no algorithm box. For each smoothed linear layer, the attention QKV input and the first feed-forward input, it collects activation channel maxima and weight row maxima, turns them into a scale with equation 4, and folds that scale in with equation 3. Then every matrix multiply is quantized to eight bits, while LayerNorm, Softmax, activation functions and residual adds stay in FP16.

§5Every equation

(1)\[ \bar{\mathbf{X}}^{\text{INT8}} = \left\lceil \frac{\mathbf{X}^{\text{FP16}}}{\Delta} \right\rfloor, \qquad \Delta = \frac{\max(|\mathbf{X}|)}{2^{N-1}-1} \]

Symmetric uniform quantizer: step \(\Delta\) from the absolute max, \(\lceil\cdot\rfloor\) = round, \(N=8\). \(\Delta\) from calibration = static; from runtime stats = dynamic. Asymmetric case adds a zero-point.

Guide

The basic symmetric quantizer used throughout the paper. X bar, the integer version of the floating-point activation X, is X divided by the step size delta and rounded. Delta is the largest absolute value in X divided by two to the power N minus one, minus one, which is 127 for eight bits. Delta from calibration is called static, delta measured at run time is dynamic. Because the largest value sets delta, outliers hurt everything else.

(–)\[ \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\cdot\mathbf{W},\quad \mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times C_o},\ \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times C_i},\ \mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{C_i\times C_o} \]

Linear layer: \(T\) tokens, \(C_i\) input channels (the summed, inner dim), \(C_o\) output channels (batch omitted).

Guide

The shape bookkeeping for a linear layer. Y equals X times W, where X has T rows, one per token, and C i columns, the input channels. W has C i rows and C o columns, the output channels. The important detail is that C i is the inner dimension that gets summed over, so later arguments about which scales can leave the kernel all refer back to these three names.

(–)\[ \text{effective levels of channel } i = 2^{8}\cdot \frac{m_i}{m} \]

\(m_i\) = max of channel \(i\), \(m\) = max of the whole matrix. With outliers ~100×, non-outlier channels get only 2–3 levels (Sec. 3).

Guide

A back-of-the-envelope count of how many integer levels a channel really uses. It is two to the eighth, or 256, times m i over m, where m i is that channel's maximum and m is the maximum of the whole matrix. When outliers are about a hundred times larger, ordinary channels get only two or three levels. This is the numeric form of the grid picture in P1 and the reason naive W8A8 collapses.

(2)\[ \mathbf{Y} = \operatorname{diag}\!\left(\mathbf{\Delta}_{\mathbf{X}}^{\text{FP16}}\right)\cdot\left(\bar{\mathbf{X}}^{\text{INT8}}\cdot\bar{\mathbf{W}}^{\text{INT8}}\right)\cdot\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\mathbf{\Delta}_{\mathbf{W}}^{\text{FP16}}\right) \]

Vector-wise INT8 GEMM: per-token scales (length \(T\)) and per-output-channel scales (length \(C_o\)) are applied after the integer matmul. Scales along \(C_i\) cannot be.

Guide

How an eight-bit matrix multiply is dequantized. The integer product of X bar and W bar is computed first, then multiplied on the left by a diagonal matrix of per-token step sizes, delta X, and on the right by a diagonal matrix of per-output-channel step sizes, delta W. Both scales sit on the outer dimensions, so they can be applied after the integer kernel. A scale along the inner input-channel dimension cannot, which is the constraint SmoothQuant is designed around.

(3)\[ \mathbf{Y} = \left(\mathbf{X}\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})^{-1}\right)\cdot\left(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})\mathbf{W}\right) = \hat{\mathbf{X}}\hat{\mathbf{W}} \]

Smoothing: \(\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{C_i}\) divides activation channels and multiplies the matching weight rows; exact equivalence. \(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})^{-1}\) is fused into the previous op offline.

Guide

The smoothing identity, the heart of the method. X is multiplied by the inverse of diag of s, which divides each activation channel j by s j, and W is multiplied by diag of s, which multiplies weight row j by the same s j. The two cancel, so Y equals X hat times W hat exactly. Because the division can be folded into the previous operation offline, the model gains easier activations at no runtime cost.

(–)\[ \mathbf{s}_j = \max(|\mathbf{X}_j|),\quad j=1,2,\dots,C_i \qquad\text{vs.}\qquad \mathbf{s}_j = 1/\max(|\mathbf{W}_j|) \]

The two extremes: left pushes all difficulty into the weights (every \(\hat{\mathbf{X}}\) channel has max 1); right pushes it all into the activations. Both hurt accuracy (Fig. 10).

Guide

The two extreme choices of scale, shown side by side. Setting s j to the maximum of activation channel j makes every smoothed activation channel peak at one and dumps all the difficulty into the weights. Setting s j to one over the maximum of weight row j does the opposite and leaves everything in the activations. Figure 10 shows that both extremes lose accuracy, which motivates the balanced formula in equation 4.

(4)\[ \mathbf{s}_j = \max(|\mathbf{X}_j|)^{\alpha} \,/\, \max(|\mathbf{W}_j|)^{1-\alpha} \]

Migration strength \(\alpha\in[0,1]\): \(j\) = input channel, \(\mathbf{X}_j\) = activation column \(j\) (over calibration tokens), \(\mathbf{W}_j\) = weight row \(j\). \(\alpha=0.5\) balances; larger \(\alpha\) moves more to weights.

Guide

The paper's scale formula. For each input channel j, s j equals the maximum absolute activation in that channel raised to the power alpha, divided by the maximum absolute weight in row j raised to the power one minus alpha. Alpha, the migration strength, runs from zero to one: one half splits the difficulty evenly, and larger values push more of it into the weights. This single knob is what the steps block tunes and what Figure 10 sweeps.

(Fig. 5)\[ \mathbf{s} = \sqrt{\max|\mathbf{X}| \,/\, \max|\mathbf{W}|},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{X}\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})^{-1},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{W}} = \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})\mathbf{W} \]

Eq. (4) at \(\alpha=0.5\), as annotated in Fig. 5 (channel-wise max over tokens for \(\mathbf{X}\), over output channels for \(\mathbf{W}\)).

Guide

Equation 4 at alpha equal to one half, written the way Figure 5 annotates it. The scale is the square root of the activation channel maximum divided by the weight row maximum. X hat is X with each channel divided by its scale, and W hat is W with each row multiplied by it. Applied to the toy example this gives scales of 1, 4, 1 and 3.

(derived)\[ \max|\hat{\mathbf{X}}_j| = \max|\mathbf{X}_j|^{1-\alpha}\max|\mathbf{W}_j|^{\alpha},\qquad \max|\hat{\mathbf{W}}_j| = \max|\mathbf{X}_j|^{\alpha}\max|\mathbf{W}_j|^{1-\alpha} \]

Not printed in the paper; follows from (3)–(4). At \(\alpha=0.5\) both equal \(\sqrt{\max|\mathbf{X}_j|\max|\mathbf{W}_j|}\) — “same quantization difficulty”.

Guide

A derived line the tab adds, not printed in the paper. After smoothing, the maximum of activation channel j becomes the old activation maximum to the power one minus alpha times the old weight maximum to the power alpha, and the weight maximum is the mirror image. At alpha one half both equal the square root of the product, which is what the paper means by giving weights and activations the same quantization difficulty.
