Appendix A (text only): weight-only methods such as GPTQ dequantize to FP16 on the fly and shine at batch-1 generation (memory-bound); W8A8 wins in the context stage and with batching (compute-bound), and also shrinks the KV cache. The authors see the two as orthogonal (GPTQ-style weights + SmoothQuant activations → possibly W4A4).

§8Why it matters for this thesis

SmoothQuant → LTX-2.3 on OpenVINO / NNCF

  • It is only needed for the INT8-activation path. Weight-only INT8/INT4 (nncf.compress_weights) never quantizes activations, so outliers there are harmless and SmoothQuant does not apply. It matters when trying full W8A8 with nncf.quantize(..., model_type=nncf.ModelType.TRANSFORMER), where NNCF runs its SmoothQuant step before inserting FakeQuantize nodes (per-MatMul α via AdvancedSmoothQuantParameters; default for MatMul is high, ~0.95 in recent releases — check the installed version and sweep it as in Fig. 10).
  • No custom kernels. Everything is plain ops: a per-channel Multiply (or a folded LayerNorm/linear) plus a rescaled weight constant, then OpenVINO's standard INT8 MatMul (VNNI/AMX on Xeon, XMX/DP4A on Arc). This is exactly the “off-the-shelf INT8 GEMM” argument of Eq. (2).
  • Calibration must cover the diffusion timesteps. Static per-tensor activation scales (O3-style, what OpenVINO FakeQuantize uses) are tuned to calibration statistics; in a DiT the activation ranges drift with timestep and adaLN modulation, so the calibration set should sample prompts × several denoising steps, not just one step.
  • Fold targets differ in a DiT. LTX-style blocks use adaLN (LN(x)·(1+scale(t))+shift(t)), so \(1/\mathbf{s}\) cannot simply be folded into a static LayerNorm γ; NNCF's explicit Multiply node sidesteps this at a small element-wise cost. Attention BMMs and FFN inputs are the natural candidates (Fig. 6).
  • Why W8A8 can pay off for video. A video DiT processes thousands of latent tokens per step — the compute-bound “context stage” regime where the paper's speed-ups appear (Appendix A), whereas weight-only compression mainly saves bandwidth/memory. Compare both on Arc/CPU before choosing.
Guide

Use SmoothQuant only when trying full eight-bit activations for LTX-2.3; weight-only compression with nncf compress weights does not need it. With nncf quantize and the transformer model type, NNCF already applies smoothing, so sweep its alpha as in Figure 10 rather than trusting the default. Calibrate on several prompts times several denoising steps, expect explicit Multiply nodes around adaptive LayerNorm, and benchmark W8A8 against weight-only on Arc and CPU before choosing.

Quantization foundations (LLMs)

AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for On-Device LLM Compression and Acceleration

Ji Lin, Jiaming Tang, Haotian Tang, Shang Yang, Wei-Ming Chen, Wei-Chen Wang, Guangxuan Xiao, Xingyu Dang, Chuang Gan, Song Han — MIT / SJTU / NVIDIA / Tsinghua / MIT-IBM / UMass. MLSys 2024 (Best Paper Award).

Only about 1% of weight channels really matter, and they are found by looking at the activations, not at the weights. AWQ protects them by multiplying those channels by a scale before 4-bit rounding (and dividing the activations by the same scale), so every weight stays in one simple INT4 format. The companion runtime TinyChat turns the 4× smaller weights into about 3× faster token generation on edge GPUs and CPUs.

Format
W4A16 / W3A16, g128
Salient channels
~0.1–1%, by |activation|
Search
1 scalar α, grid of 20
Calibration
16 seqs ≈ enough (10× < GPTQ)
Speed-up (TinyChat)
3.2–3.3× avg, up to 3.9×
Llama-2-7B INT4 PPL
5.60 (FP16 5.47)
Reading guide

AWQ asks how to squeeze a large language model's weights down to four or three bits without retraining and without losing accuracy. Its answer: only about one percent of weight channels really matter, they are found by looking at activation sizes, and they are protected by scaling them up before rounding, so every weight stays in one simple INT4 format. The tab moves from a big picture diagram to the problem, the method and its kernels, every equation and figure, the result tables, and a thesis box. This is the fifth of sixteen papers and the last of the three language model foundations, after GPTQ and SmoothQuant. It is the most directly usable for the LTX-2.3 study, because NNCF offers AWQ as an option in INT4 weight compression. The diffusion papers that follow adapt these ideas to image and video transformers.

§0Before reading

To follow AWQ, three ideas are needed: what weight-only 4-bit storage with one scale per group of 128 weights looks like, what an "input channel" of a linear layer is and why a large activation there magnifies that weight's rounding error, and why generating text one token at a time is limited by memory traffic rather than arithmetic. AWQ is in the atlas because it is the method NNCF offers as its awq option for INT4 weight compression, the exact tool used on LTX-2.3 in this project.

Terms used in this paper

Weight-only quantization (W4A16, W3A16)
Only the weights are stored in low precision (4 or 3 bits); activations stay FP16. Saves memory and bandwidth without needing integer activation kernels.
Group size (g128)
How many consecutive weights share one scale. Smaller groups follow the data more closely but store more scales; 128 is the common default and the one AWQ uses.
RTN (round-to-nearest)
The plain baseline: compute each group's scale from its largest value and round every weight to the nearest level. No calibration data.
Salient channel
An input channel whose activations are consistently large, so errors on its weights matter most. AWQ finds about 0.1 to 1 percent of them from activation averages.
Calibration set
A small batch of ordinary inputs run through the model only to measure statistics. AWQ uses a few samples from the Pile, a large public text dataset, and needs no labels or gradients.
Perplexity (PPL), WikiText-2
Perplexity measures how surprised a language model is by real text; lower is better. WikiText-2 is a standard set of Wikipedia articles used to compute it.
Instruction-tuned and multimodal models
Vicuna is a chat-tuned Llama; OpenFlamingo, VILA and LLaVA take images plus text. AWQ shows it works on them because it does not overfit the calibration data.
Context vs. generation stage
Context (prefill) reads the whole prompt in one pass; generation (decode) then produces one token per step, which is the slow, memory-bound part.
Arithmetic intensity, roofline
Arithmetic intensity is computation per byte moved from memory. A roofline plot shows whether a workload is limited by memory speed (low intensity) or by compute (high intensity).
Kernel, kernel fusion
A kernel is one compiled routine that runs on the GPU or CPU, such as a matrix multiply. Fusion merges several small ones so data stays on chip instead of going back to memory.
TinyChat
The authors' own inference engine for AWQ models, with kernels that unpack INT4 weights inside the matrix multiply. It is the source of the reported speed-ups.
RTX 4090, RTX 4070 laptop
NVIDIA consumer GPUs: a desktop card and a laptop chip (the paper's has 8 GB of memory). Used to show speed on ordinary PCs.
Jetson Orin
NVIDIA's embedded computer for robots and edge devices, with CPU and GPU sharing one memory. The paper's main "on-device" GPU.
Raspberry Pi 4B
A small, cheap single-board computer with an ARM CPU. The paper runs a 7B model on its CPU to show deployment on very weak hardware.
Guide

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. The most important are weight-only quantization with group size one twenty eight, salient channels, and the calibration set, a few text samples used only to measure activation sizes. Perplexity on WikiText-2 is the main accuracy score, where lower is better. The hardware names, RTX 4090, Jetson Orin and Raspberry Pi, mark the range of devices from desktop GPU down to a tiny ARM computer.

§2Big picture

Error from rounding a weight is multiplied by its input activation, so channels with big activations dominate the error. AWQ scales those weight channels up (smaller relative rounding error) and the activations down by the same factor, which is folded into the previous op. No retraining, no mixed precision, no custom data format.

§3The problem

  • Plain RTN collapses at 3 bits (OPT-1.3B: PPL 14.62 → 119).
  • Keeping the 1% of channels with large activations in FP16 recovers most of it; picking by weight norm is no better than random (Table 1).
  • But mixed FP16/INT storage needs irregular kernels; GPTQ-style reconstruction can overfit the calibration domain.
  • On-device decoding (batch 1) is memory-bound: weight bytes, not FLOPs, set the speed (Fig. 3).

§4Method

A. Activation-aware scaling search

  1. Run a small generic calibration set (Pile) through the model; cache each linear layer's input X.
  2. Per input channel, compute the average activation magnitude sX.
  3. For α on a 20-point grid in [0,1], set s = sXα, quantize W·diag(s) (INT4/INT3, g128) and measure the output error ‖Q(W·diag(s))(X/s) − WX‖; keep the best α.
  4. Apply weight clipping chosen to minimise quantization MSE.
  5. Fold diag(s)−1 into the preceding operator; store uniform low-bit weights + FP16 group scales. No backprop, no weight reconstruction.
Guide

The procedure is deliberately cheap. It only needs forward passes on a small generic calibration set, to cache each layer's inputs and measure how large each channel's activations are. From that it tries twenty strengths of scaling, quantizes, and keeps whichever gives the smallest output error. Clipping is then set, the inverse scale disappears into the previous operator, and plain low bit weights are stored with FP16 group scales. There is no backpropagation and no weight reconstruction, which is why AWQ generalizes well across domains.

AWQ per linear layer (reconstructed from §3.2 / §5.1 — the paper has no Algorithm box) input : FP16 weight W, cached calibration inputs X (small Pile subset), bits N, group 128 s_X ← mean_over_tokens |X| # per input channel best ← ∞ for α in {0, 1/20, 2/20, …, 1}: # grid size 20 s ← s_X ^ α Wq ← Q_N,g128( W · diag(s) ) # Eq. (1) L ← ‖ Wq · (diag(s)^-1 · X) − W · X ‖ # Eq. (4) if L < best: best, s* ← L, s W' ← clip( W · diag(s*) ) with clip range chosen to minimise MSE of quantisation fold diag(s*)^-1 into the preceding op (LayerNorm / previous Linear) store Q(W') as INT4/INT3 g128 + FP16 group scales
Guide

The tab reconstructs this box from sections 3.2 and 5.1, since the paper has none. For each linear layer it measures the mean activation size per input channel, then tries twenty values of alpha from zero to one, using the statistic raised to alpha as the scale, quantizing the scaled weights and measuring output error against full precision. The best scale wins, clipping is applied, the inverse scale is folded into the preceding operator, and weights are stored at four or three bits in groups of 128.

B. TinyChat runtime

§5Every equation

—\[ y = \mathbf{w}\mathbf{x}, \qquad y = Q(\mathbf{w})\mathbf{x} \]

A group/block of weights \(\mathbf{w}\) applied to input \(\mathbf{x}\), and its weight-quantized counterpart (activations stay FP16).

Guide

This sets up the notation. y equals w times x is a normal linear operation, where w is a group of weights and x is the input. The second form, y equals Q of w times x, is the same operation with only the weights quantized, Q being the quantizer, while the activations x stay in FP16. This is weight only quantization, the W4A16 setting that the rest of the paper and NNCF's INT4 compression use.

(1)\[ Q(\mathbf{w}) = \Delta \cdot \operatorname{Round}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{w}}{\Delta}\right), \qquad \Delta = \frac{\max(|\mathbf{w}|)}{2^{N-1}} \]

Symmetric absmax round-to-nearest with \(N\) bits; \(\Delta\) is the step size of the group (g128 in the paper).

Guide

Equation one is the basic quantizer. Q of w equals delta times the rounded value of w divided by delta, so weights are snapped to a grid of evenly spaced levels. Delta, the step size, is the largest absolute weight in the group divided by two to the power N minus one, where N is the number of bits. Because delta depends on the group maximum, a group of 128 weights shares one step size, which is the detail equation two exploits.

(2)\[ Q(w\cdot s)\cdot\frac{x}{s} = \Delta' \cdot \operatorname{Round}\!\left(\frac{ws}{\Delta'}\right)\cdot x \cdot \frac{1}{s} \]

Scale one weight \(w\) up by \(s\gt 1\) and its input \(x\) down by \(s\): mathematically the same product; \(\Delta'\) is the new group step size.

Guide

Equation two is the key trick. Multiply one weight w by a scale s greater than one, and divide its input x by the same s. Mathematically the product is unchanged, but now the weight is rounded at a larger size, so after dividing by s its rounding error is relatively smaller. Delta prime is the group's new step size, which may differ slightly from delta if the scaled weight becomes the group maximum.

—\[ \mathtt{RoundErr}(\cdot) \sim 0.25, \qquad \Delta' \approx \Delta \]

Empirical facts: rounding error is ~uniform on [0, 0.5] (mean 0.25); scaling one element rarely changes the group max; \(\Delta\), \(x\) are FP16 (no error).

Guide

These are two empirical facts that make the argument work. First, the rounding error of a single weight is spread roughly evenly between zero and one half, so its average is about 0.25 and does not depend on scaling. Second, scaling one weight rarely changes the group maximum, so delta prime is about equal to delta. The step size and the input are FP16 and add no error. Equation three and the ratio that follows rely on both facts.

(3)\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Err}\big(Q(w)x\big) &= \Delta \cdot \mathtt{RoundErr}\!\left(\frac{w}{\Delta}\right)\cdot x \\ \operatorname{Err}\!\left(Q(w\cdot s)\left(\frac{x}{s}\right)\right) &= \Delta' \cdot \mathtt{RoundErr}\!\left(\frac{ws}{\Delta'}\right)\cdot x \cdot \frac{1}{s} \end{aligned} \]

Output error before and after scaling; the error is proportional to \(|x|\), which is why large-activation channels are salient.

Guide

Equation three writes out the output error before and after scaling. Before, it is delta times the rounding error of w over delta, times x. After, it is delta prime times the rounding error of the scaled weight, times x, times one over s. The first line shows why saliency comes from activations: the error grows with the size of x, so channels with large inputs contribute most. The second line shows the extra factor one over s that scaling adds.

—\[ \frac{\operatorname{Err}_{\text{new}}}{\operatorname{Err}_{\text{orig}}} = \frac{\Delta'}{\Delta}\cdot\frac{1}{s} \]

With \(\Delta'\approx\Delta\) and \(s\gt 1\), the salient weight's relative error shrinks by ~\(1/s\); non-salient channels in the group are amplified by \(\Delta'/\Delta\) (Table 2).

Guide

Dividing the two errors gives the ratio: new error over original error equals delta prime over delta, times one over s. With delta prime about equal to delta and s greater than one, the salient weight's error shrinks by roughly one over s. The catch is the other weights in the group, which see their step size grow by delta prime over delta. Table 2 measures exactly this trade off.

(4)\[ \mathbf{s}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{s}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{s}), \qquad \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{s}) = \big\lVert Q\big(\mathbf{W}\cdot\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})\big)\big(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})^{-1}\cdot\mathbf{X}\big) - \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X} \big\rVert \]

Per-input-channel scale that minimizes a layer's output error after quantization; \(\mathbf{X}\) = cached calibration inputs; \(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})^{-1}\) is fused into the previous operator.

Guide

Equation four turns the idea into an optimization. The best scale vector s star is the one that minimizes L of s, the size of the difference between the quantized layer output and the full precision output W times X. Here W is the weight matrix, X is the cached calibration input, and diag of s is a diagonal matrix of per input channel scales whose inverse is folded into the previous operator. Because Q is not differentiable, the paper solves it by the simple search in equation five.

(5)\[ \mathbf{s} = \mathbf{s_X}^{\alpha}, \qquad \alpha^* = \arg\min_{\alpha} \mathcal{L}\big(\mathbf{s_X}^{\alpha}\big) \]

Search space: \(\mathbf{s_X}\) = per-channel average activation magnitude; one scalar \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) (grid of 20) trades salient vs non-salient protection (0 = no scaling).

Guide

Equation five shrinks the search to one number. The scale is s X raised to the power alpha, where s X is the average activation size per input channel. Alpha between zero and one sets how strongly salient channels are protected: zero means no scaling, one means scaling fully by activation size. The best alpha is found by trying twenty grid points and keeping the one with the lowest loss from equation four.

—\[ \text{AI}_{\text{gen, FP16}} \approx 1\ \tfrac{\text{FLOP}}{\text{Byte}} \;\Rightarrow\; 1\ \text{TFLOPS}; \qquad \text{AI}_{\text{gen, W4A16}} \approx 4 \;\Rightarrow\; 4\ \text{TFLOPS}; \qquad \text{AI}_{\text{ridge}} = \tfrac{165\ \text{TFLOPS}}{1\ \text{TB/s}} = 165 \]

Roofline numbers (§4.1, RTX 4090): below 165 FLOP/Byte a workload is memory-bound, so cutting weight bytes 4× raises attainable throughput ~4×.

Guide

These roofline numbers explain the speed up. Arithmetic intensity is operations done per byte loaded. On an RTX 4090, with 165 TFLOPS and one terabyte per second, anything below 165 operations per byte is memory bound. FP16 token generation sits near one, reaching about one TFLOPS; four bit weights raise it to about four, so throughput rises about four times. A video diffusion transformer processes many tokens at once and sits much higher, so expect a smaller latency gain.

—\[ \text{index offset of adjacent packed weights} = \tfrac{1}{8}\times 2^{n} \quad (2^{n}\text{-bit SIMD register}) \]

Packing rule (§4.2): a 128-bit NEON register holds 16 bytes, so pairs are (wi, wi+16); on GPUs 8 weights are packed as w{0,2,4,6,1,3,5,7}.

Guide

This is the packing rule from section 4.2. For a SIMD register of two to the n bits, weights that share a byte should be one eighth of two to the n positions apart. For a 128 bit ARM NEON register this means pairing weight i with weight i plus 16, and on GPUs eight weights are stored in the interleaved order zero, two, four, six, one, three, five, seven. It is an engineering detail that makes unpacking cheap; Figure 4 illustrates it.

§8Why it matters for this thesis

AWQ → LTX-2.3 on OpenVINO / NNCF

  • Directly available: nncf.compress_weights(model, mode=INT4_SYM|INT4_ASYM, group_size=128, ratio=…, dataset=calib, awq=True) runs this algorithm on an OpenVINO IR. It needs a calibration dataset (activation statistics), but no training and no custom kernels: the OpenVINO CPU/GPU plugins dequantize INT4 weights inside their own matmul kernels, i.e. they play TinyChat's role.
  • Folding constraint: the inverse scale diag(s)−1 must be absorbed by a preceding op. NNCF only applies AWQ where it finds such a pattern (e.g. a MatMul/Multiply feeding the next MatMul, as in gated MLPs); other layers get plain data-aware INT4. Check which DiT linears (attention out-projection, FFN down-projection, adaLN) are actually matched.
  • Calibration for a diffusion transformer: activation magnitudes in a DiT change with the denoising timestep and with prompt/audio-video modality. Build the NNCF calibration set from latents sampled across many timesteps and prompts, otherwise sX reflects only one noise level. AWQ's low data need (Fig. 8) keeps this cheap.
  • Speed expectation differs from LLMs: AWQ's 3× speed-up relies on batch-1 decoding being memory-bound (arithmetic intensity ≈1, Fig. 3). A video DiT processes thousands of latent tokens per step, so it is mostly compute-bound: INT4 weight-only will mainly cut memory and model size (fits Arc / laptop RAM), with smaller latency gains. Measure it, and compare against INT8 weight+activation (W8A8) for compute-bound layers.
  • Mixed precision in practice: use AWQ INT4 for the bulk of linears and keep sensitive layers (first/last projections, timestep/text embedding, adaLN modulation) in INT8 or FP16 via NNCF's ratio / ignored scope. AWQ can be combined with NNCF's scale estimation or GPTQ options, just as the paper combines AWQ with GPTQ (Table 9).
Guide

Use AWQ through NNCF by calling compress weights with an INT4 mode, group size 128, a calibration dataset, and awq set to true, then check which transformer linears it actually matched, since AWQ needs a preceding operation to absorb the inverse scale. Calibrate on many denoising timesteps and prompts, because activation sizes change with noise level. Expect mainly memory savings, since a video diffusion transformer is largely compute bound; compare against W8A8 and keep sensitive layers in INT8 or FP16.

Quantizing diffusion models

Q-Diffusion: Quantizing Diffusion Models

Xiuyu Li, Yijiang Liu, Long Lian, Huanrui Yang, Zhen Dong, Daniel Kang, Shanghang Zhang, Kurt Keutzer · ICCV 2023 (arXiv 2302.04304v3)

Standard post-training quantization (PTQ) breaks on diffusion models for two reasons: the same U-Net sees very different activations at different denoising steps, and U-Net skip concatenations glue together channels with wildly different ranges. Q-Diffusion fixes the first with time-step-aware calibration (sample calibration inputs uniformly across all steps, then BRECQ/AdaRound block reconstruction) and the second with shortcut-splitting quantization (separate quantizers for the two concatenated halves). Result: 4-bit weights, 8-bit activations with near-FP quality, no training.

Precision
W4A8 (also W8A8, W4A32)

None (data-free PTQ)
Reading guide

Q-Diffusion asks why ordinary post-training quantization, which works well on classifiers, falls apart on diffusion models, and how to fix it without any retraining. Its answer: calibrate on inputs sampled evenly across every denoising step, and give the two halves of each U-Net skip concatenation their own quantizers. With these two changes, four-bit weights and eight-bit activations, called W four A eight, stay within about 2.3 FID points of full precision, while naive quantization collapses. The tab starts with a big-picture drawing, then the two problems, the method with its algorithms, every equation and figure, the result tables, and a box on what this means for the thesis. Among the sixteen papers, this is the first of the diffusion-specific quantization group, after the general LLM methods GPTQ, SmoothQuant and AWQ, and it is the ancestor that PTQ4DiT, ViDiT-Q, SVDQuant and the later video methods build on.

§0Before reading

To follow this paper, three ideas are needed: a diffusion model makes an image by running the same network over many denoising steps, quantization uses a small calibration set to choose its scales, and a U-Net copies features through skip connections. Q-Diffusion is in the atlas because it was the first to make post-training quantization work on diffusion models, and its step-aware calibration recipe is what the thesis reuses when building the NNCF calibration set for LTX-2.3.

Terms used in this paper

Denoising step (timestep)
One pass of the network in the sampling loop. Generation starts from pure noise at the highest step \(t=T\) and removes a little noise per step until \(t=0\) gives the image.
DDPM and DDIM
DDPM is the classic diffusion model and training recipe. DDIM is a faster sampler for the same trained network that needs far fewer steps; the paper samples its CIFAR-10 model with 100 DDIM steps.
U-Net
The convolutional network that predicts the noise in these models. An encoder shrinks the image, a decoder grows it back, and skip connections copy encoder features across to the decoder.
Latent diffusion model (LDM)
A diffusion model that works in the small latent space of an autoencoder instead of on pixels; a decoder turns the final latent into an image. LTX-2.3 is also a latent model.
Stable Diffusion
A widely used text-to-image latent diffusion model. The paper quantizes version 1.4 and generates 512 by 512 images from text prompts.
Classifier-free guidance
At each step the model runs twice, with and without the prompt, and the two noise predictions are mixed. This is why calibration stores both branches.
Post-training quantization (PTQ)
Converting a trained model to low-bit numbers without retraining it, using only a small set of example inputs. NNCF works this way.
Calibration set
The example inputs fed through the model during PTQ so the quantizer can measure value ranges and set its scales. Q-Diffusion builds it from the model's own intermediate steps, so no training data is needed.
W4A8
Weights stored with 4 bits (16 levels) and activations with 8 bits (256 levels). W4A32 means only the weights are quantized.
BRECQ, AdaRound, LSQ
The PTQ recipe the paper builds on. BRECQ tunes the quantized model one block at a time to match the full-precision block output; AdaRound learns whether each weight rounds up or down; LSQ learns the activation step sizes.
FID
Fréchet Inception Distance: compares feature statistics of generated and real images using an Inception network. Lower is better; it is the paper's main quality metric.
Inception Score and CLIP score
Inception Score rewards images that are clearly recognisable and varied (higher is better). CLIP score measures how well an image matches its text prompt (higher is better).
CIFAR-10, LSUN, MS-COCO
Benchmark datasets: CIFAR-10 has tiny 32 by 32 images in ten classes, LSUN Bedroom and Church are scene photos at 256 by 256, and MS-COCO captions provide the text prompts for Stable Diffusion.
Bit operations (Bops)
A hardware-free estimate of compute: the number of multiply-adds weighted by the bit widths used. The paper reports Bops and model size, not measured speed on any device.
Guide

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The most important are post-training quantization, which compresses a trained model without retraining, the calibration set that sets the scales, and W4A8. For results, remember that FID compares generated and real images and lower is better, while CLIP score measures how well an image matches its prompt. Note that the paper reports model size and bit operations, not measured speed on hardware.

§2Big picture

Same weights, one quantized U-Net, reused at every step. Calibrate it on inputs from all steps, and never share one quantizer across a skip concatenation.

§3The problem

  • Error accumulation: INT4 linear quantization gives MSE that climbs to ~100 by the last steps (Fig. 3).
  • Timestep-varying activations: ranges shrink from about ±5 at t=100 to ±2 at t=1 (Fig. 5). Calibrating on only part of the trajectory raises W4 FID to 6–99 (Fig. 4).
  • Shortcut outliers: input activations of DDIM shortcut convs are up to 200× larger than neighbouring layers (Fig. 6), because deep and shallow features are concatenated.
  • Traditional calibration data (training images, random noise, ZeroQ-style synthesis) does not match the noisy intermediate xt the network really sees (Fig. 1a).

§4Method

  1. Pick sampler (DDIM 100 steps, LDM 200/500, PNDM 50 for SD) and calibration interval c, per-step count n (Table 4).
  2. Run the FP model from random noise; at every step with t mod c = 0 store n intermediate inputs xt (plus time embedding, and for SD both conditional and unconditional text features).
  3. Split every skip-concatenation conv into two quantizer pairs (Eqs. 6–8).
  4. Block-wise reconstruction (BRECQ): for each residual / transformer block, learn AdaRound rounding and weight clipping to minimise output MSE vs FP; other layers per-layer.
  5. If activations are quantized: calibrate activation step sizes block by block with LSQ.
  6. Keep SoftMax, SiLU, GroupNorm in FP; for SD W8A8/W4A8, attention scores in INT16 (q, k, v still 8-bit).
Guide

The recipe runs in a fixed order. First choose the sampler and the calibration interval, then run the full-precision model and collect inputs at the chosen steps, including time embeddings and, for Stable Diffusion, both conditional and unconditional text features. Next, split the shortcut layers, then reconstruct weights block by block with AdaRound, and only afterwards calibrate activation step sizes. Fragile operations like SoftMax, SiLU and GroupNorm stay in full precision, and Stable Diffusion attention scores use sixteen-bit integers.

Algorithm 1 — Q-Diffusion Calibration

Require: pretrained FP model and quantized model [W_θ, Ŵ_θ] Require: empty calibration dataset D Require: number of denoising sampling steps T Require: calibration sampling interval c, amount of calibration data per step n for t = 1, ..., T time step do if t % c = 0 then Sample n intermediate inputs x_t^(1), ..., x_t^(n) randomly at t from W_θ and add them to D end if end for for all i = 1, ..., N blocks do Update the weight quantizers of the i-th block in Ŵ_θ with D and W_θ end for if do activation quantization then for all i = 1, ..., N blocks do Update the activation quantizers step sizes of the i-th block with Ŵ_θ, W_θ, D end for end if
Guide

Algorithm 1 is the unconditional version of time-step-aware calibration. The first loop walks through the denoising steps and, whenever the step number is a multiple of c, stores n intermediate inputs from the full-precision model. The second loop visits the blocks one by one and fits the weight quantizers against the full-precision outputs. An optional third loop then fits activation step sizes. The key design choice is that calibration data comes from the model's own trajectory, so no training images are needed.

Algorithm 2 — Q-Diffusion Calibration for Text-guided Image Generation (App. A.2)

Require: pretrained FP model and quantized model [W_θ, Ŵ_θ] Require: empty calibration dataset D Require: number of denoising sampling steps T Require: calibration sampling interval c, amount of calibration data per step n for t = 1, ..., T time step do if t % c = 0 then Sample 2n intermediate inputs (x_t^(1), c_t^(1), t_t^(1)), (x_t^(1), uc_t^(1), t_t^(1)), ..., (x_t^(n), c_t^(n), t_t^(n)), (x_t^(n), uc_t^(n), t_t^(n)) randomly at t from W_θ and add them to D end if end for for all i = 1, ..., N blocks do Update the weight quantizers of the i-th block in Ŵ_θ with D and W_θ end for if do activation quantization then for all i = 1, ..., N blocks do Update the activation quantizers step sizes of the i-th block with Ŵ_θ, W_θ, D end for end if
Guide

Algorithm 2 is the same procedure for text-to-image models like Stable Diffusion. The only change is in the sampling loop: each stored sample is a triple of latent, text feature and time step, and it is stored twice, once with the prompt's conditional features and once with the unconditional ones, because classifier-free guidance runs both branches at inference. That is why Table 4 lists twice as many Stable Diffusion samples as prompts. This is the version that maps onto LTX-2.3, which also uses guidance.

ct = conditional text feature, uct = unconditional (empty-prompt) feature, tt = time embedding: classifier-free guidance runs the U-Net on both, so both go into calibration.

§5Every equation

(1)\[ q(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \mathbf{x}_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_t;\ \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,\mathbf{x}_{t-1},\ \beta_t \mathbf{I}\right) \]

Forward diffusion: add Gaussian noise with variance schedule \(\beta_t \in (0,1)\); as \(T\to\infty\), \(\mathbf{x}_T\) becomes isotropic Gaussian.

Guide

Equation 1 is the forward diffusion step, which adds noise. It says x t, the image at step t, is drawn from a Gaussian centred at the square root of one minus beta t times the previous image x t minus one, with variance beta t times the identity. Beta t is the noise schedule, a small number between zero and one. After enough steps, x T is pure Gaussian noise. This is background; it is not quantized, but it defines what the U-Net sees.

(2)\[ p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{t-1} \mid \mathbf{x}_t) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t-1};\ \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\theta,t}(\mathbf{x}_t),\ \tilde{\beta}_t \mathbf{I}\right) \]

Learned reverse step, starting from \(\mathbf{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\). Its output is the next step's input, which is why quantization errors accumulate.

Guide

Equation 2 is the learned reverse step, the part the network performs. P theta of x t minus one given x t is a Gaussian with mean mu tilde, computed by the network, and variance beta tilde times the identity. Sampling starts from pure noise x T and applies this step repeatedly. The important point for quantization is that each output becomes the next input, which is exactly why errors accumulate, as Figure 2 and Figure 3 show.

(3)\[ \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\theta,t}(\mathbf{x}_t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(\mathbf{x}_t - \frac{1-\alpha_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta,t}\right) \]

Mean from the predicted noise \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta,t}\) (the U-Net output that gets quantized).

Guide

Equation 3 shows where the network enters the reverse step. The mean mu tilde equals one over the square root of alpha t, times the current image x t minus a scaled copy of epsilon theta, the noise predicted by the U-Net. The scaling factor is one minus alpha t over the square root of one minus alpha bar t. Epsilon theta is the quantized part, so any quantization error in the predicted noise flows straight into the next image.

(4)\[ \tilde{\beta}_t = \frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\cdot \beta_t, \qquad \alpha_t = 1-\beta_t,\quad \bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{i=1}^{t}\alpha_i \]

Reverse-step variance; the definitions of \(\alpha_t, \bar{\alpha}_t\) follow the equation in the paper.

Guide

Equation 4 gives the variance of the reverse step and defines the helper symbols. Beta tilde t equals one minus alpha bar at t minus one, divided by one minus alpha bar at t, times beta t. Alpha t is one minus beta t, and alpha bar t is the product of all alphas up to step t. These are fixed schedule constants, not learned and not quantized; they complete the diffusion background before the paper turns to quantization.

(5)\[ \hat{w} = s\cdot \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{w}{s}\right),\ c_{\min},\ c_{\max}\right) \]

Uniform quantize/de-quantize: scale \(s\), clipping bounds \(c_{\min}, c_{\max}\); round is nearest (linear-quant baseline) or adaptive (AdaRound/BRECQ in Q-Diffusion).

Guide

Equation 5 is the basic uniform quantizer used for both weights and activations. Divide w by the step size s, round to an integer, clip between c min and c max, then multiply by s again to get w hat, the de-quantized value. With four bits there are only sixteen integers available. Plain linear quantization uses round-to-nearest; Q-Diffusion keeps the same form but lets AdaRound learn whether each weight rounds up or down, and learns the clipping range too.

(6)\[ \mathcal{Q}_X(X) = \mathcal{Q}_{X_1}(X_1) \oplus \mathcal{Q}_{X_2}(X_2) \]

Split activation quantizer: quantize deep part \(X_1\in\mathbb{R}^{w\times h\times c_1}\) and shallow part \(X_2\in\mathbb{R}^{w\times h\times c_2}\) separately, then concatenate (\(\oplus\)).

Guide

Equation 6 splits the activation quantizer of a shortcut layer. Q X of X, the quantized input, is formed by quantizing X1, the deep part with c1 channels, with its own quantizer, quantizing X2, the shallow part with c2 channels, with another, and then concatenating the two. This directly answers the range clash in Figure 3: the small shallow values now get a scale that fits them instead of being rounded to zero.

(7)\[ \mathcal{Q}_W(W) = \mathcal{Q}_{W_1}(W_1) \oplus \mathcal{Q}_{W_2}(W_2) \]

Split weight quantizer on the matching input-channel rows \(W_1\in\mathbb{R}^{c_1\times c_{out}}\), \(W_2\in\mathbb{R}^{c_2\times c_{out}}\).

Guide

Equation 7 applies the same split to the weights. The weight matrix W has one row per input channel, so it divides into W1, the c1 rows that multiply the deep features, and W2, the c2 rows that multiply the shallow features. Each part gets its own weight quantizer. This matters because Figure 7 shows the weights are bimodal too, with W1 small and W2 much larger, so one shared weight scale would waste precision.

(8)\[ \mathcal{Q}_X(X)\,\mathcal{Q}_W(W) = \mathcal{Q}_{X_1}(X_1)\,\mathcal{Q}_{W_1}(W_1) + \mathcal{Q}_{X_2}(X_2)\,\mathcal{Q}_{W_2}(W_2) \]

The layer output is the sum of two independently quantized partial products, so splitting costs no extra compute; \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{w\times h\times c_{in}}\), \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{c_{in}\times c_{out}}\), \(c_{in}=c_1+c_2\).

Guide

Equation 8 explains why splitting is free. The quantized input times the quantized weights equals the quantized X1 times the quantized W1, plus the quantized X2 times the quantized W2. The input has c in channels, equal to c1 plus c2. Because a matrix product over concatenated channels is just the sum of two smaller products, the layer computes the same amount of work with two scales instead of one, which is why the paper reports negligible overhead.

App. F.1\[ N_t = \frac{s_t}{\sum_{t} s_t}\,N \]

"Std" non-uniform sampling (did not beat uniform): draw calibration samples from step \(t\) in proportion to the pixel-wise std \(s_t\) of \(\mathbf{x}_t\) (estimated from 256 samples); \(N=5120\). "Norm Std" uses the std of \(\lVert \mathbf{x}_t\rVert_2\) instead.

Guide

This appendix equation defines a non-uniform alternative the authors tried and rejected. N t, the number of calibration samples taken from step t, is set to s t divided by the sum of s t over all steps, times the total N of 5,120. Here s t is the pixel-wise standard deviation of x t, so noisier steps get more samples. Table 7 shows it did slightly worse than plain uniform sampling, which supports the paper's simple choice.

Guide

Table 7 checks whether smarter, non-uniform sampling of calibration steps helps. Std draws more samples from steps with higher pixel standard deviation, as in the appendix equation; Norm Std uses the spread of the image norm; USL is another published strategy. All three give FIDs between 5.54 and 5.66 for four-bit weights on CIFAR-10, while plain uniform sampling gives 5.09. Simple uniform coverage wins, so there is no need for elaborate schemes.

  • 8-bit weights are almost free for everyone; the gap opens at 4-bit weights and when activations are also quantized.
  • Size column: 4-bit weights shrink DDIM from 143.2 Mb to 17.9 Mb (8×); Bops drop from 6597 G to 399 G per step at W4A8 (theoretical).
  • Stable Diffusion W4A8 is run with INT16 attention scores (App. A.1); Q-Diffusion quantizes q·k and attn·v matmuls to INT8 elsewhere, unlike PTQ4DM's FP16/32.
  • Changing the sampler after calibration (DPM-Solver++, Table 6) keeps W4A32 good but roughly doubles W4A8 FID: activation calibration is trajectory-specific.

§8Why it matters for this thesis

  • Calibration data recipe transfers directly. For LTX-2.3 in NNCF, build the nncf.Dataset by hooking the transformer's inputs (latent tokens, timestep/sigma embedding, text and audio conditioning, both cond and uncond branches if CFG is used) during full FP pipeline runs, keeping samples from every c-th step, not from a single step or random tensors. This is exactly Algorithm 2, and it is what Optimum-Intel's diffusion hybrid quantization does.
  • Weight-only int8/int4 is the easy half. Weight-only compression (nncf.compress_weights, INT4 group-wise or INT8) does not depend on activation ranges, so the timestep drift mainly bites when moving to W8A8 (nncf.quantize) on CPU/Arc. For A8, static per-tensor activation scales must cover all timesteps. Consider keeping sensitive layers (e.g. timestep/AdaLN modulation, final projection) in FP16 via the ignored_scope.
  • Shortcut splitting is U-Net specific. LTX-2.3 is a DiT with residual adds, not channel concatenation, so Eq. 6–8 rarely applies directly. The underlying lesson still applies: find tensors that mix sub-populations with different ranges (e.g. concatenated text/video/audio tokens in joint attention, AdaLN-modulated activations) and give them separate quantizers or leave them in higher precision.
  • No custom kernels needed. Split quantization is just two FakeQuantize nodes before a Concat, and BRECQ/AdaRound change only the stored integer weights, so the result runs on stock OpenVINO INT8 ops. NNCF has no AdaRound/BRECQ; its closest tools are SmoothQuant, bias correction, and for weights AWQ / scale estimation / GPTQ, all of which reuse the same multi-timestep calibration set.
  • Re-calibrate if the sampler or step count changes (Table 6): if the thesis also cuts steps or uses caching, generate calibration data with the final sampler schedule.
Guide

Act on this box when building the NNCF calibration set: hook the LTX-2.3 transformer's inputs during full pipeline runs and keep samples from many steps across the trajectory, including both guidance branches, exactly as in Algorithm 2. Weight-only int8 or int4 hardly depends on this, but W8A8 does. Shortcut splitting does not apply directly to a DiT, yet the lesson does: give mixed-range tensors separate quantizers or higher precision. And regenerate calibration data if the sampler or step count changes.

Quantizing diffusion models

PTQ4DiT: Post-training Quantization for Diffusion Transformers

Junyi Wu, Haoxuan Wang, Yuzhang Shang, Mubarak Shah, Yan Yan · NeurIPS 2024 · arXiv 2405.16005 · code: github.com/adreamwu/PTQ4DiT

Inside a Diffusion Transformer, a few input channels of each linear layer carry huge values (“salient channels”), and the activation ones grow and shift as denoising proceeds. PTQ4DiT notices that activation and weight outliers almost never sit in the same channel, so it rescales each channel to meet in the middle (geometric mean), picks the activation statistics by weighting timesteps with a Spearman-correlation score, and folds all scales into existing layers offline so inference costs nothing extra.

Reading guide

PTQ4DiT asks why standard post-training quantization breaks on Diffusion Transformers and how to fix it without retraining. Its answer: a few input channels carry huge values, activation outliers and weight outliers rarely share a channel, so each channel is rescaled to meet in the middle and choose the calibration timesteps carefully. On DiT-XL/2 for ImageNet, W eight A eight nearly matches full precision, and W four A eight reaches an FID of 7.09 where Q-Diffusion gets 15.31. The tab runs from the big picture and the problem, through the method, every equation and every figure, to the result tables and a thesis box on LTX-2.3 with NNCF. Among the sixteen papers it is the second diffusion-specific quantization paper, after Q-Diffusion and before ViDiT-Q. It borrows the SmoothQuant idea from the language-model group and adapts it to transformers with timesteps.

§0Before reading

To follow PTQ4DiT, three ideas are needed: what sits inside a Diffusion Transformer block (adaLN and its linear layers), why one very large channel ruins a low-bit quantization grid, and what a rank correlation measures. The paper is in the atlas because it is the first quantization method written for diffusion transformers, the family LTX-2.3 belongs to, and its balancing trick is the SmoothQuant idea that can be switched on in NNCF.

Terms used in this paper

Diffusion Transformer (DiT)
A diffusion model whose denoising network is a transformer working on patches of the latent image, instead of a convolutional U-Net. LTX-2.3 is a (video and audio) DiT.
DiT-XL/2
The largest model of the original DiT paper (Peebles and Xie), using 2×2 latent patches. It is the only model quantized in PTQ4DiT.
adaLN
Adaptive LayerNorm: LayerNorm followed by a per-channel scale \(\gamma\) and shift \(\beta\) computed from the timestep and class. It is how a DiT is told which step and which class it is on.
Timestep / sampling steps
Generation removes noise over many steps (250, 100 or 50 here). Activations change from step to step, so statistics from one step may not fit the others.
Post-training quantization (PTQ)
Converting a trained model to low-bit numbers without retraining, using only a small calibration set to choose ranges and scales.
Calibration set
A few inputs run through the full-precision model to record value ranges. Here: 32 generated samples at each of 25 (256 px) or 10 (512 px) timesteps.
W8A8 / W4A8
Weights at 8 or 4 bits, activations at 8 bits. Integer activations need a scale chosen in advance, which is why activation outliers matter so much.
Salient channel / salience
An input channel whose maximum absolute value is far above the rest. The paper calls that maximum the channel’s salience.
Geometric mean
\(\sqrt{a\cdot b}\). Balancing moves an activation channel with maximum 12 and its weight row with maximum 1 both to about 3.5; the product is unchanged.
Spearman’s ρ
A correlation computed on ranks rather than raw values; +1 means two lists are ordered the same, −1 means reversed.
ImageNet 256 / 512
Class-conditional generation: the model draws one of 1000 ImageNet classes (eagle, balloon…) at 256×256 or 512×512 pixels.
FID, sFID, IS, Precision
Image-quality scores from an Inception network. FID and sFID compare generated and real image statistics (lower is better); Inception Score and Precision reward sharp, recognisable, realistic images (higher is better).
PTQ4DM, Q-Diffusion, PTQD, RepQ*
The baselines: three PTQ methods for diffusion U-Nets and a ViT quantizer (RepQ-ViT) that the authors re-implemented for DiTs.
NVIDIA RTX A6000
The workstation GPU used for all experiments. The paper reports quality and model size, not measured speed-ups on it.
Guide

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The most important are adaptive layer norm, the timestep-driven scale and shift; salience, the largest value in a channel; W four A eight, the bit setting; and Spearman's rho, a correlation on ranks. For results, FID and sFID are lower is better, while Inception Score and Precision are higher is better. All experiments use DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet with an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU.

§2Big picture

Two DiT-specific problems: extreme salient channels, and activation salience that drifts over the ~250 denoising steps. CSB fixes the first by channel-wise balancing (SmoothQuant-style, fixed exponent ½); SSC fixes the second by choosing which timesteps to trust when estimating activation salience. Re-parameterization makes both free at inference.

§3The problem

  • Challenge 1 – salient channels. In both X and W of the attention/FFN linear layers, a handful of channels have max |value| an order of magnitude above the rest, and these channels carry most of the quantization MSE (Fig. 3).
  • Challenge 2 – temporal variation. s(X(t)) changes across the denoising trajectory (Fig. 4); W is fixed. Balancing scales tuned for one timestep are biased for others.
  • Lucky observation – complementarity. Extreme activation channels and extreme weight channels do not coincide, so they can trade magnitude without creating a new outlier.
  • Setup constraint: per-channel weight quantizers but per-tensor activation quantizers, so activation outliers hurt the whole tensor.

§4Method

  1. Build a calibration set: uniformly pick 25 timesteps (256×256) or 10 (512×512), 32 samples each, from the FP model’s own sampling trajectories.
  2. For every linear layer in MHSA/PF: per input channel j, record activation salience s(Xj(t)) = max|Xj(t)| at each timestep, and weight salience s(Wj) = max|Wj| (row j of W).
  3. Spearman’s ρ between the vectors s(X(t)) and s(W) for each t; ηt = softmax(−ρ) over t (Eq. 11).
  4. Temporal salience sρ = Σt ηt s(X(t)) (Eq. 10).
  5. Balanced salience s̃ρ,j = √(sρ,j·s(Wj)) (Eq. 14); BXρ = diag(s̃/sρ), BWρ = diag(s̃/s(W)) — exact inverses (Eq. 15).
  6. Fold BWρ into W, BXρ into adaLN MLP (Eqs. 13, 20–21) or the preceding matmul.
  7. Run standard PTQ (Q-Diffusion-style quantizer-parameter optimization): channel-wise uniform weights, tensor-wise uniform activations.
Guide

The recipe has three phases. First, collect statistics: sample 25 or 10 timesteps from the full-precision model's own trajectories, 32 samples each, and record per-channel maxima of activations at every timestep and of weights once. Second, compute the scales: rank-correlate the two, turn the negative correlations into softmax weights over timesteps, average the activation maxima with those weights, then take the geometric mean with the weight maxima. Third, fold the scales in and run a standard Q-Diffusion-style quantizer calibration.

Algorithm 1 Post-Training Quantization for Diffusion Transformers (PTQ4DiT) 1: Input: Pre-trained DiT model, Activation sequence X^(1:T) from calibration dataset 2: Output: Quantized DiT model with low-bit activations and weights 3: (1) Preparation: 4: Estimate activation salience s(X^(t)) at each timestep t ▷ Using Eq. (9) 5: Estimate weight salience s(W) ▷ Using Eq. (9) 6: (2) Spearman's rho-guided Salience Calibration: 7: Compute correlation coefficients {rho(s(X^(t)), s(W))}_{t=1..T} 8: Compute weighting factors {eta_t}_{t=1..T} ▷ Using Eq. (11) 9: Compute temporal salience s_rho(X^(1:T)) ▷ Using Eq. (10) 10: (3) Channel-wise Salience Balancing: 11: Compute balanced salience s~_rho(X_j^(1:T), W_j) for each channel j ▷ Using Eqs. (5), (14) 12: Construct refined Salience Balancing Matrices B^X_rho and B^W_rho ▷ Using Eqs. (6), (7) 13: (4) Re-Parameterization: 14: Integrate B^W_rho into the weight matrix of linear layers offline ▷ By W~ = B^W_rho W 15: Integrate B^X_rho into the MLPs before adaLN modules offline ▷ Using Eqs. (13), (20) 16: (5) Quantization: 17: Obtain X~ = X B^X_rho and W~ = B^W_rho W without extra computational demand during inference 18: Perform quantization on balanced activation X~ and weight W~
Guide

The algorithm is the same pipeline written as five stages. Preparation measures salience per channel, per timestep for activations and once for weights. The Spearman calibration stage decides how much each timestep counts and produces one blended activation salience per channel. Balancing turns that into the two diagonal matrices. Re-parameterization folds them into the weights and the adaLN MLP offline. Quantization then runs on the already balanced tensors, so the deployed model has the same structure and cost as a plain quantized DiT.

§5Every equation

(1)\[ (\boldsymbol{\gamma},\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \operatorname{MLPs}(\mathbf{c}),\qquad \operatorname{adaLN}(\mathbf{Z}) = \operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{Z})\odot(\mathbf{1}+\boldsymbol{\gamma})+\boldsymbol{\beta} \]

DiT conditioning: an MLP maps condition \(\mathbf c\) (timestep + class) to per-channel scale \(\boldsymbol\gamma\) and shift \(\boldsymbol\beta\) applied after LayerNorm.

Guide

This is how a DiT injects the timestep and class. An MLP maps the condition c to two vectors, gamma, a per-channel scale, and beta, a per-channel shift. The adaptive layer norm then normalizes the tokens Z, multiplies each channel by one plus gamma, and adds beta. This matters later because the output of adaLN is the input X to the QKV and feedforward layers, which gives the method a free place to hide its activation scale.

(2)\[ Q(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\left\lfloor \frac{\mathbf{x}}{\boldsymbol{\delta}} \right\rceil + \boldsymbol{\lambda},\ 0,\ 2^{b}-1\right) \]

Uniform asymmetric \(b\)-bit quantizer: step \(\boldsymbol\delta\), zero-point \(\boldsymbol\lambda\), round-to-nearest, clamp.

Guide

This is the standard uniform b-bit quantizer. Divide x by the step size delta, round to the nearest integer, add the zero point lambda, and clamp the result between zero and two to the power b minus one. The step size is set by the range being covered, so one huge value makes delta coarse for every other value. That is the failure shown in the problem figure, and every later equation is about shrinking the range before this quantizer is applied.

(3)\[ \widetilde{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf{W}} = \mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{W}}\mathbf{W} \]

CSB: diagonal balancing matrices rescale activation columns and weight rows (input channels).

Guide

Channel-wise salience balancing in one line. X tilde is the activation matrix multiplied on the right by a diagonal matrix B X, which rescales each input channel column. W tilde is the weight multiplied on the left by a diagonal matrix B W, which rescales the matching weight row. Choosing the two so they cancel keeps the layer output unchanged, as equation twelve shows, while reshaping what the quantizer sees.

(4)\[ s(\mathbf{X}_j) = \max(|\mathbf{X}_j|),\quad s(\mathbf{W}_j) = \max(|\mathbf{W}_j|),\quad \text{where}\ j = 1,2,\dots,d_{in} \]

Salience of channel \(j\) = its maximum absolute value (range drives quantization error).

Guide

Salience is simply the largest absolute value in a channel. For activation channel j, s of X j is the max of the absolute values in that column; for weights, s of W j is the max over row j. The index j runs over the d in input channels. The paper uses the maximum because the range is what sets the quantization step, and the problem figures show the channels with the biggest maxima also carry the biggest error.

(5)\[ \widetilde{s}(\mathbf{X}_j,\mathbf{W}_j) = \big(s(\mathbf{X}_j)\cdot s(\mathbf{W}_j)\big)^{\frac{1}{2}} \]

Balanced salience = geometric mean of activation and weight salience (SmoothQuant with \(\alpha=0.5\)).

Guide

The balanced salience of channel j is the geometric mean of its activation salience and its weight salience, the square root of their product. If activations peak at 12 and weights at 1 in that channel, both end up at about 3.5. This is exactly SmoothQuant with alpha equal to one half. It is the target value that the balancing matrices in equations six and seven are built to reach.

(6)\[ \mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}} = \operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{\widetilde{s}(\mathbf{X}_1,\mathbf{W}_1)}{s(\mathbf{X}_1)},\frac{\widetilde{s}(\mathbf{X}_2,\mathbf{W}_2)}{s(\mathbf{X}_2)},\dots,\frac{\widetilde{s}(\mathbf{X}_{d_{in}},\mathbf{W}_{d_{in}})}{s(\mathbf{X}_{d_{in}})}\right) \]

Activation balancing matrix: shrinks channels whose activation salience exceeds the balanced value.

Guide

The activation balancing matrix is diagonal, with entry j equal to the balanced salience divided by the activation salience of that channel. Where activations are loud, the ratio is below one and the channel is shrunk; where they are quiet, it is above one and the channel is enlarged. After multiplying, every activation channel has maximum equal to its balanced salience from equation five.

(7)\[ \mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{W}} = \operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{\widetilde{s}(\mathbf{X}_1,\mathbf{W}_1)}{s(\mathbf{W}_1)},\frac{\widetilde{s}(\mathbf{X}_2,\mathbf{W}_2)}{s(\mathbf{W}_2)},\dots,\frac{\widetilde{s}(\mathbf{X}_{d_{in}},\mathbf{W}_{d_{in}})}{s(\mathbf{W}_{d_{in}})}\right) \]

Weight balancing matrix; after (3), \(s(\widetilde{\mathbf X}_j)=s(\widetilde{\mathbf W}_j)=\widetilde s(\mathbf X_j,\mathbf W_j)\).

Guide

The weight balancing matrix mirrors equation six: entry j is the balanced salience divided by the weight salience of channel j. Multiplying the two entries gives s of X j times s of W j over the product of the same, which is exactly one, so the two matrices are inverses. After balancing, activation and weight channel j share the same maximum, the geometric mean. The exact inverse property is proven in equations fifteen and sixteen.

(8)\[ \max\big(s_o(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}),\,s_o(\widetilde{\mathbf{W}})\big) \le \max\big(s_o(\mathbf{X}),\,s_o(\mathbf{W})\big) \]

Overall salience (the larger of the two tensor ranges) never grows; it shrinks when outliers are complementary.

Guide

This inequality is the payoff of balancing. The overall salience of a tensor, s sub o, is its largest channel maximum. The larger of the two overall saliences after balancing is never bigger than before. When activation and weight outliers sit in different channels, it is much smaller, because each outlier is paired with a small partner. Since the quantization step follows the overall range, this means finer steps for both tensors at the same bit width.

—\[ s_o(\mathbf{X}) = \max\big(s(\mathbf{X}_1), s(\mathbf{X}_2),\dots,s(\mathbf{X}_{d_{in}})\big) \]

Unnumbered: overall salience of a tensor = max channel salience = range quantized together at the given granularity.

Guide

An unnumbered helper definition. The overall salience of a tensor is the maximum of all its channel saliences, so for X it is the largest value among s of X one up to s of X d in. With per-tensor activation quantization, this single number sets the step size for the whole tensor, which is why one loud channel hurts everyone. Equation eight is stated in terms of it.

(9)\[ \mathbf{s}(\mathbf{X}^{(t)}) = \big(s(\mathbf{X}^{(t)}_1), s(\mathbf{X}^{(t)}_2),\dots,s(\mathbf{X}^{(t)}_{d_{in}})\big),\qquad \mathbf{s}(\mathbf{W}) = \big(s(\mathbf{W}_1), s(\mathbf{W}_2),\dots,s(\mathbf{W}_{d_{in}})\big) \]

Salience vectors per timestep \(t\) of the activation sequence \(\mathbf X^{(1:T)}\); \(\mathbf s(\mathbf W)\) is timestep-independent.

Guide

Now time enters. For each timestep t, the activation salience vector collects the per-channel maxima s of X j at that step, one entry per input channel. The weight salience vector s of W does the same for weights and does not depend on t, since weights are fixed. These two vectors, compared step by step, are the inputs to the Spearman calibration in equations ten and eleven.

(10)\[ \mathbf{s}_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}) = (\eta_1,\eta_2,\dots,\eta_T)\cdot\big(\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{X}^{(1)}),\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{X}^{(2)}),\dots,\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{X}^{(T)})\big)^{\mathrm{T}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{in}} \]

Spearman’s \(\rho\)-calibrated temporal salience: weighted sum of per-timestep activation salience vectors.

Guide

The temporal salience s rho is a weighted average of the per-timestep activation salience vectors. Each timestep t contributes its vector times a weight eta t, and the result is one salience value per input channel. It replaces the single-timestep activation salience in the balancing formula, so the scales work across the whole denoising process rather than being tuned to one step. The weights come from equation eleven.

(11)\[ \eta_t = \frac{\exp\!\big[-\rho\big(\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{X}^{(t)}),\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{W})\big)\big]}{\sum_{\tau=1}^{T}\exp\!\big[-\rho\big(\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{X}^{(\tau)}),\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{W})\big)\big]} \]

Softmax of negative Spearman rank correlation: timesteps where activation and weight outliers are least aligned (most complementary) get more weight.

Guide

The timestep weights are a softmax of minus rho. Rho is Spearman's rank correlation between the activation salience vector at step t and the weight salience vector. Low or negative correlation means outliers sit in different channels, so balancing works well, and that timestep gets a larger weight. High correlation means outliers coincide and cannot be cancelled, so that step gets less say. The sum in the denominator just makes the weights add to one.

(12)\[ \widetilde{\mathbf{X}}\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf{W}} = (\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho})\cdot(\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{W}}_{\rho}\mathbf{W}) = \mathbf{X}\cdot\mathbf{W} \]

Balancing is exact: the layer output is unchanged in full precision.

Guide

Balancing is exact in full precision. X tilde times W tilde equals X times B X rho times B W rho times W, and since the two diagonal matrices multiply to the identity, this is just X times W. So the model is mathematically unchanged; only the ranges that the quantizers see are different. Equations fifteen and sixteen spell out the proof.

(13)\[ \widetilde{\mathbf{X}} = \widetilde{\operatorname{adaLN}}(\mathbf{Z}) = \operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{Z})\odot(\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho}+\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\gamma}})+\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\quad \text{where}\ \widetilde{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} = \boldsymbol{\gamma}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho},\ \ \widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \boldsymbol{\beta}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho} \]

Post-adaLN folding: \(\mathbf B^{\mathbf X}_\rho\) is absorbed into the scale/shift of adaLN (i.e. into the MLP that produces them).

Guide

This shows where the activation scale hides. Instead of an extra multiply, the adaLN output is rewritten: layer norm of Z times B X rho plus gamma tilde, plus beta tilde, where gamma tilde and beta tilde are gamma and beta already multiplied by B X rho. The constant one from equation one simply becomes B X rho. Because gamma and beta come from an MLP, the scaling can be baked into that MLP, as equations eighteen to twenty-one show.

(14)\[ \widetilde{s}_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{j},\mathbf{W}_{j}) = \big(s_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{j})\cdot s(\mathbf{W}_j)\big)^{\frac{1}{2}} \]

Appendix B: refined balanced salience using the SSC temporal salience \(s_\rho\) instead of a single-timestep \(s(\mathbf X_j)\).

Guide

From the appendix, this is the refined balanced salience actually used. It is the same geometric mean as equation five, but the activation salience is now the Spearman-weighted temporal salience s rho from equation ten rather than a value from one timestep. The square root of s rho of channel j times s of W j gives the target range for that channel across all denoising steps.

(15)\[ \begin{aligned} &\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho}\cdot\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{W}}_{\rho}\\ &= \operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{\widetilde{s}_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{1},\mathbf{W}_{1})}{s_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{1})},\dots,\frac{\widetilde{s}_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{d_{in}},\mathbf{W}_{d_{in}})}{s_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{d_{in}})}\right)\cdot\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{\widetilde{s}_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{1},\mathbf{W}_{1})}{s(\mathbf{W}_1)},\dots,\frac{\widetilde{s}_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{d_{in}},\mathbf{W}_{d_{in}})}{s(\mathbf{W}_{d_{in}})}\right)\\ &= \operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{\widetilde{s}_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{1},\mathbf{W}_{1})}{s_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{1})}\cdot\frac{\widetilde{s}_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{1},\mathbf{W}_{1})}{s(\mathbf{W}_1)},\dots,\frac{\widetilde{s}_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{d_{in}},\mathbf{W}_{d_{in}})}{s_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{d_{in}})}\cdot\frac{\widetilde{s}_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{d_{in}},\mathbf{W}_{d_{in}})}{s(\mathbf{W}_{d_{in}})}\right)\\ &= \operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{\big(s_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{1})\cdot s(\mathbf{W}_1)\big)^{\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2}}{s_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{1})\cdot s(\mathbf{W}_1)},\dots,\frac{\big(s_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{d_{in}})\cdot s(\mathbf{W}_{d_{in}})\big)^{\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2}}{s_{\rho}(\mathbf{X}^{(1:T)}_{d_{in}})\cdot s(\mathbf{W}_{d_{in}})}\right) = \mathbf{I} \end{aligned} \]

Appendix C proof: the two balancing matrices are exact inverses (product = identity).

Guide

This is the proof that the refined balancing matrices are exact inverses. Multiplying B X rho and B W rho entry by entry gives, for each channel, the balanced salience squared divided by s rho times s of W. Since the balanced salience is the square root of that same product, each entry equals one and the product is the identity matrix. This makes the equivalence in equation sixteen hold.

(16)\[ \widetilde{\mathbf{X}}\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf{W}} = (\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho})\cdot(\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{W}}_{\rho}\mathbf{W}) = \mathbf{X}\cdot(\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{W}}_{\rho})\cdot\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{X}\cdot\mathbf{W} \]

Hence mathematical equivalence of the balanced layer (Appendix C).

Guide

The equivalence stated fully. X tilde times W tilde is regrouped as X times the product of the two balancing matrices times W. Equation fifteen showed that product is the identity, so the result is X times W. In words, balancing changes nothing in full precision, and any quality change after quantization comes only from how well the new ranges quantize.

(17)\[ \mathbf{X} = \operatorname{adaLN}(\mathbf{Z}) = \operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{Z})\odot(\mathbf{1}+\boldsymbol{\gamma})+\boldsymbol{\beta} \]

Appendix D: adaLN on latent \(\mathbf Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_{in}}\) produces the linear layer’s input.

Guide

The appendix restates adaLN. The linear layer's input X is the layer norm of the latent tokens Z, multiplied channel-wise by one plus gamma and shifted by beta. Z has n tokens and d in channels. This is the starting point for showing that an activation-side scale can be absorbed upstream instead of being applied as an extra operation.

(18)\[ (\boldsymbol{\gamma},\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \operatorname{MLPs}(\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{W}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}},\mathbf{W}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) + (\mathbf{b}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}},\mathbf{b}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) \]

The scale/shift regressor is affine in \(\mathbf c\) (last layer), so right-multiplying by a diagonal matrix can be folded into it.

Guide

The scale and shift come from the last layer of the conditioning MLP, which is affine: c times weight matrices W gamma and W beta, plus biases b gamma and b beta. Because it is a linear map plus bias, multiplying its output by a diagonal matrix is the same as multiplying its weights and biases. That is what makes the offline fold in equations twenty and twenty-one possible.

(19)\[ \widetilde{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho} = \operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{Z})\odot(\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho}+\boldsymbol{\gamma}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho}) + \boldsymbol{\beta}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho} \]

Applying \(\mathbf B^{\mathbf X}_\rho\) to adaLN output distributes over the scale, the constant 1 and the shift (echoes Eq. 13).

Guide

Applying the activation scale to adaLN's output distributes over its three parts. X tilde, which is X times B X rho, equals layer norm of Z times the sum of B X rho and gamma times B X rho, plus beta times B X rho. The constant one becomes B X rho, and gamma and beta are each rescaled. This matches equation thirteen and sets up the weight edit that follows.

(20)\[ (\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}},\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = (\mathbf{W}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho},\,\mathbf{W}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho}),\qquad (\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}},\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = (\mathbf{b}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho},\,\mathbf{b}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho}) \]

Offline: scale the MLP weight columns and biases by \(\mathbf B^{\mathbf X}_\rho\).

Guide

The offline edit itself. Multiply the columns of the MLP weights W gamma and W beta, and the biases b gamma and b beta, by the diagonal activation scale B X rho. This is done once before deployment. The next equation checks that the edited MLP now outputs the already scaled gamma and beta.

(21)\[ \begin{aligned} \widetilde{\operatorname{MLPs}}(\mathbf{c}) &= \mathbf{c}\cdot(\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}},\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) + (\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}},\widetilde{\mathbf{b}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\\ &= \mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{W}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho},\mathbf{W}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho}) + (\mathbf{b}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho},\mathbf{b}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho})\\ &= \big(\mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{W}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}},\mathbf{W}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) + (\mathbf{b}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}},\mathbf{b}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\big)\cdot\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho}\\ &= (\boldsymbol{\gamma},\boldsymbol{\beta})\cdot\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho}\\ &= (\boldsymbol{\gamma}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho},\,\boldsymbol{\beta}\mathbf{B}^{\mathbf{X}}_{\rho}) \end{aligned} \]

The re-parameterized MLP directly outputs \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol\gamma},\widetilde{\boldsymbol\beta}\): no extra runtime multiply.

Guide

This verifies the fold. Running the condition c through the edited MLP gives c times the scaled weights plus the scaled biases, which factors into the original MLP output times B X rho, which is gamma and beta each times B X rho. So the modified adaLN produces the balanced activation directly, with no extra multiply at inference. This closes the argument that the method has zero runtime overhead.

Guide

The ablation table separates the two ideas at W4A8, 256 resolution, 250 steps. The baseline quantizer scores an FID of 22.54, worse than Q-Diffusion's 15.31. Channel balancing alone, calibrated at the midpoint timestep, cuts it to 8.17 and raises Inception Score from about 106 to 188. The full method with Spearman calibration reaches 7.09. So most of the gain is balancing, and timestep weighting adds a consistent final improvement.

Setup: DiT-XL/2 class-conditional, DDPM sampler 250/100/50 steps; 10k samples (256) / 5k (512); FID, sFID, IS, Precision via ADM toolkit; quantizer optimization follows Q-Diffusion; RepQ* = RepQ-ViT extended with temporal calibration. Sizes are model storage; no wall-clock latency is reported (all experiments are simulated/fake quantization on RTX A6000).

§8Why it matters for this thesis

PTQ4DiT → LTX-2.3 on OpenVINO / NNCF

  • CSB is SmoothQuant with α=0.5 and max-abs statistics, and NNCF already implements SmoothQuant for OpenVINO models (nncf.quantize with ModelType.TRANSFORMER; AdvancedQuantizationParameters(smooth_quant_alphas=...)). For a W8A8 track on LTX-2.3, the CSB half of this paper comes almost free: set α≈0.5 for MatMul layers and check which layers NNCF actually smooths.
  • SSC is only about the calibration set. Its idea is to pick which timesteps’ activation statistics to trust. In NNCF this is controlled through the calibration dataset: dump inputs to the LTX transformer from several denoising steps (the paper uses 10–25 timesteps × 32 samples), and optionally over-sample the steps where activation/weight salience is poorly correlated. Computing Spearman ρ per layer needs a short PyTorch hook script. No custom kernels are required.
  • Re-parameterization matches LTX’s DiT design. LTX-Video/LTX-2 blocks use adaLN-style scale/shift modulation (timestep-conditioned, AdaLN-single). Folding BX into that modulation (Eqs. 13, 19–21, with the constant “1” becoming BX) and BW into the Linear weights can be done in PyTorch before OpenVINO conversion, so the exported IR has no extra ops. It must be done carefully where modulation parameters are shared across blocks.
  • For the weight-only int8/int4 track (nncf.compress_weights), activations stay FP16, so CSB’s benefit for activations does not apply. But the weight-side insight still matters. Moving salience between X and W before compression is what NNCF’s data-aware AWQ and scale estimation options do, and they also need multi-timestep calibration data. PTQ4DiT’s W4A8 result (FID 7.09 vs 4.53 FP) shows how hard it is to get 4-bit DiT weights right.
  • Caveats: the paper covers image generation with DiT-XL/2 (~675M params), not text-to-video+audio at LTX scale. It reports no real latency, and it uses per-tensor activation and per-channel weight quantization. Present it as the “DiT-specific outlier + timestep” baseline motivating the calibration and smoothing choices, and compare with ViDiT-Q / Q-DiT for video DiTs.
Guide

The practical reading for the thesis: the balancing half of PTQ4DiT is SmoothQuant with alpha one half, which NNCF already offers, so a W8A8 run on LTX-2.3 can use it by setting the smooth quant alpha to about 0.5 and checking which MatMuls are smoothed. The timestep half becomes a calibration-set decision: collect transformer inputs from 10 to 25 denoising steps. For weight-only int4, look at NNCF's AWQ and scale estimation instead, and remember the paper covers images, not video with audio.

Quantizing diffusion models

ViDiT-Q: Efficient and Accurate Quantization of Diffusion Transformers for Image and Video Generation

Tianchen Zhao, Tongcheng Fang, Haofeng Huang, Rui Wan, Widyadewi Soedarmadji, Enshu Liu, Shiyao Li, Zinan Lin, Guohao Dai, Shengen Yan, Huazhong Yang, Xuefei Ning, Yu Wang · Tsinghua / Infinigence AI / Microsoft / SJTU · ICLR 2025 (arXiv 2406.02540v3)

Earlier quantizers break on text-to-video DiTs because the data inside one quantization group varies along tokens, CFG halves, timesteps and channels. ViDiT-Q fixes this in three steps: dynamic per-token activation scales, channel balancing that scales first and then rotates, and a mixed-precision search that measures each layer group with the metric it actually affects. The result is W8A8 and W4A8 video/image generation at about FP16 quality, with real CUDA-kernel gains.
