Reading guide

ViDiT-Q asks why quantizers that work for language models and image U-Nets fall apart on text-to-video diffusion transformers, and how to fix that. Its answer is that the numbers sharing one scale vary along tokens, the two classifier-free guidance halves, timesteps and channels, so it adds per-token dynamic activation scales, a two-stage channel balancing, and a mixed-precision search judged by the right quality metric per layer group. That gets W eight A eight and W four A eight video and image generation close to FP16 quality, with measured GPU speed-ups. The tab runs from the big picture and the problem, through the method, every equation and every figure, to the result tables and a thesis box. Among the sixteen papers it is the third diffusion quantization paper, after Q-Diffusion and PTQ4DiT and before SVDQuant, and the first built for video transformers like LTX.

§0Before reading

To follow ViDiT-Q, three ideas are needed: what it means to quantize a number to 8 or 4 bits with a scale, what happens inside one denoising step of a video diffusion transformer, and which group of numbers shares one scale. The paper is in the atlas because it is the first quantization method built for text-to-video transformers like LTX, and its layer-sensitivity search is the part most directly reusable with NNCF.

Terms used in this paper

Diffusion transformer (DiT)
A diffusion model whose denoiser is a transformer working on patch tokens instead of a convolutional U-Net. LTX-2.3 is one.
Timestep
One step of the denoising loop. The paper uses 20 steps, and activation statistics change from step to step.
Classifier-free guidance (CFG)
Each step runs the model with and without the text prompt and pushes the result towards the prompted one. The two halves have different activation ranges.
W8A8, W4A8, W4A8-MP
Weight bits and activation bits. MP means mixed precision: some layers use more bits than the headline number.
Scale and zero point
The step size \(s\) and offset \(z\) that map real numbers to integers. Everything in one group shares them.
Static vs dynamic quantization
Static fixes activation scales in advance from calibration data. Dynamic computes them at run time from the actual values, at a small cost.
Per-token, per-channel
Grouping choices: one scale per row of the activation (token) or per output channel of the weight. Both run along the matrix multiply's summation axis, so integer kernels can use them.
Outlier channel, incoherence
A channel with much larger values than the rest. The paper measures this as incoherence, roughly the largest value divided by the average.
Channel balancing
Moving outliers so all channels have similar ranges: SmoothQuant-style scaling (shift range from activations to weights) and Hadamard rotation (mix channels to spread outliers out).
adaLN
Adaptive layer norm. The timestep produces a scale and shift for each channel; in these models a learned constant table is added to it, which splits outliers into a static and a time-varying part.
OpenSORA, Latte, PixArt
Open models the paper tests. OpenSORA (STDiT blocks) and Latte generate video; PixArt-α and PixArt-Σ generate images.
CLIPSIM, VQA, FlowScore
Video metrics: CLIPSIM checks text match, DOVER VQA scores aesthetic and technical quality, and FlowScore uses optical flow to judge motion consistency.
FID, VBench
FID compares generated and real image statistics (lower is better). VBench scores videos on many separate dimensions such as consistency and motion.
A100 and INT8 GEMM kernels
The A100 is an NVIDIA data-centre GPU whose Tensor Cores run integer matrix multiplies fast. The paper's speed-ups come from custom CUDA kernels on it, which OpenVINO cannot use.
Guide

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. The most important are static versus dynamic quantization, per token and per channel grouping, and channel balancing, because the whole method is built from them. The metric names matter too: CLIPSIM for text match, VQA for visual quality, and FlowScore for motion. Keep in mind that the speed-ups come from custom GPU kernels on an A100, which OpenVINO cannot use.

§2Big picture

Only linear layers are quantized. Attention matmuls, norms, t/y embedding and the final layer stay FP16 (App. A.1). No retraining is needed. Calibration is needed only for the SmoothQuant scaling α and for the mixed-precision sensitivity runs.

§3The problem

  • Token-wise: visual tokens differ in both space and time (video).
  • Condition-wise: the conditional and unconditional CFG passes (batch of 2) have different ranges.
  • Timestep-wise: the same layer's activations shift across denoising steps.
  • Channel-wise, time-varying: outlier channels exist, and how strong they are changes with t.
  • Metric problem: a layer with low MSE can still ruin alignment or temporal consistency, so MSE alone is not a good enough objective for generation.

§4Method

4.1 Fine-grained grouping + dynamic quantization

4.2 Static-dynamic channel balancing

4.3 Metric-decoupled mixed precision: the sensitivity analysis to replicate

  1. Pick the aspects and one metric each: video → VQA (quality), CLIPSIM (text alignment), FlowScore (temporal); image → FID and CLIPScore (App. E.3.2 step 1).
  2. Group layers by operator type and draw the layer-type × metric heatmap (Fig. 20): relative metric drop (FP−Q)/FP, then z-score, then softmax over metrics. Each group should have one clearly dominant metric.
  3. Split the denoising trajectory into 4 equal time ranges (steps 0–5, 6–10, 11–15, 16–20) and run steps 4–6 separately for each range.
  4. Budget per group: quantize each whole group, measure the MSE of the output against the FP16 generation, and split the overall bit budget between groups (example: 5.54 / 4.05 / 4.34, average 5.00).
  5. Sensitivity per layer: inside a group, quantize one layer or block at a time and record that group's metric error against the FP16 video. This is done at two levels: between blocks, then between layers inside a block.
  6. Greedy allocation: start every layer at 4 bit and move the most sensitive to 8 bit until the group budget is used up.
Guide

The procedure moves from coarse to fine. First, the method picks one metric per quality aspect and confirms with a heatmap that each layer type mainly hurts one of them. Then, for each timestep range, it splits the total bit budget between groups using a cheap MSE test, ranks layers inside each group with their own metric, and greedily promotes the most sensitive layers from four to eight bits until the group budget is spent.

Algorithm A (reconstructed from Sec. 4.3 + App. E.3.2; the paper has no algorithm box) Metric-decoupled mixed precision for W4A8 input : FP16 DiT f, prompts P, avg-bit budget B, groups G = {SelfAttn+FFN: VQA, CrossAttn: CLIPSIM, TempAttn: FlowScore} V_fp ← f(P) # reference videos for range r in {0-5, 6-10, 11-15, 16-20}: # timestep ranges for g in G: e_g ← MSE( f[g→W4, only in r](P), V_fp ) B_g ← split B across groups by e_g # e.g. 5.54 / 4.05 / 4.34 for g in G: for layer (block, then intra-block) ℓ in g: sens[ℓ] ← |metric_g( f[ℓ→W4, only in r](P) ) − metric_g(V_fp)| bits[ℓ] ← 4 for all ℓ in g while avgbits(g) < B_g: ℓ* ← argmax sens over {ℓ : bits[ℓ]=4}; bits[ℓ*] ← 8 return bits (per layer, per time range) Algorithm B (inference path of one quantized linear, Sec. 4.1, 4.2, 5.1) x ← x · diag(s)⁻¹ # static SmoothQuant scale (folded into previous LN/GeLU/residual) x ← x · H # online Hadamard rotation (fused with the quant op) s_x, z_x ← minmax(x) per token # dynamic, computed on the fly x_int ← clamp(round(x/s_x)+z_x, 0, 2^8−1) y ← dequant( INT-GEMM(x_int, W_int) ) # W' = Hᵀ·diag(s)·W, per-out-channel INT8 or INT4
Guide

Two pieces of pseudocode, both reconstructed by the tab because the paper has no algorithm box. Algorithm A is the offline search: reference videos, per-group budgets from MSE, per-layer sensitivity from the group metric, then greedy promotion to eight bits, repeated per time range. Algorithm B is what one quantized linear layer does at run time: fixed scaling, Hadamard rotation, per-token quantization, an integer matrix multiply, and one rescale back to floating point.

§5Every equation

(1)\[ \min \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}(f_{FP}, f_q) \;\Rightarrow\; \min_{W_q, X_q} \sum_{l}^{L} \Big( \lVert W^{(l)} - Q(W^{(l)}) \rVert_2^2 + \lVert X^{(l)} - Q(X^{(l)}) \rVert_2^2 \Big) \]

The task loss between the FP and quantized network is replaced by a sum of layer-wise weight and activation quantization errors over L layers.

Guide

The usual quantization objective replaces the real task loss with a simpler proxy. On the left is the task loss between the full-precision network f FP and the quantized network f q. On the right is the sum over all L layers of the squared weight error, W minus Q of W, plus the squared activation error, X minus Q of X. The paper argues this layer-wise proxy is not enough for visual generation, which motivates its metric-decoupled search.

–\[ x \approx \hat{x} = s\,(x_{\text{int}} - z) \]

Dequantization: scale s and zero point z are shared by every element in a group \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^g\).

Guide

Dequantization maps an integer back to a real value. x hat, the approximation of x, equals the scale s times the integer x int minus the zero point z. The key point is that s and z are shared by every element in the group, so the whole design question is which elements should share them.

(2)\[ x_{\text{int}} = Q(x; s, z, b) = \operatorname{clamp}\!\Big( \Big\lfloor \frac{x}{s} \Big\rceil + z,\; 0,\; 2^b - 1 \Big) \]

b-bit uniform quantizer: round to nearest, then clamp to [0, 2b−1]. The error has two parts, clamping and rounding.

Guide

Equation two is the b-bit uniform quantizer. Divide x by the step s, round to the nearest integer, add the zero point z, then clamp to the range zero to two to the b minus one. Error comes from two places: clamping values that fall outside the range, and rounding the ones inside. The next equation shows that with min-max ranges only rounding is left.

–\[ s = \frac{\max(x) - \min(x)}{2^b - 1}, \qquad \text{rounding error} \in \Big[-\frac{s}{2}, \frac{s}{2}\Big] \]

Min-max scaling: nothing is clipped, so the error is set by s, which grows with the spread inside the group.

Guide

With min-max scaling the step s is the group's maximum minus its minimum, divided by two to the b minus one, so nothing is ever clipped. The rounding error then lies between minus half a step and plus half a step. The takeaway is that error grows directly with the spread inside a group, which is the central claim of the error analysis.

–\[ \max(x) \le \mu \frac{\lVert W \rVert_F}{\sqrt{g}} \]

μ-coherence (from QuIP): a group is harder to quantize when its largest element is far above the average magnitude. The paper writes ‖W‖F for the group's norm.

Guide

Mu-coherence, borrowed from QuIP, measures how spiky a group is. It says the largest element is at most mu times the group's Frobenius norm divided by the square root of the group size g, which is roughly mu times the average magnitude. A large mu means one value towers over the rest, making the group hard to quantize. The incoherence numbers in figures 3 and 8 are this idea in practice.

(3)\[ Y = \big(X \operatorname{diag}(s)^{-1}\big) \cdot \big(\operatorname{diag}(s) W\big) = \hat{X} \cdot \hat{W}; \qquad s_i = \frac{\max(|X_i|)^{\alpha}}{\max(|W_i|)^{1-\alpha}} \]

SmoothQuant channel scaling: the per-input-channel mask s moves difficulty between activation and weight, and α sets how much moves.

Guide

Equation three is SmoothQuant channel scaling. The output Y stays the same when the activations X are divided channel by channel by s and the weights W are multiplied by s. Each s i is the activation channel maximum to the power alpha, divided by the weight channel maximum to the power one minus alpha. Alpha decides how much difficulty moves from activations to weights. ViDiT-Q uses this as the static half of its balancing.

–\[ QQ^{T} = I,\; |Q| = 1, \qquad Y = XW^{T} = (XQ)(Q^{T}W) \]

Rotation (QuaRot/SpinQuant): an orthogonal Q leaves the output unchanged and spreads channel outliers. ViDiT-Q uses a Hadamard Q.

Guide

Rotation is the other balancing tool, used by QuaRot and SpinQuant. Q is an orthogonal matrix, so Q times Q transpose is the identity, and multiplying X by Q and the weights by Q transpose leaves the output unchanged. The rotation mixes channels, spreading an outlier's energy across many of them. ViDiT-Q uses a Hadamard matrix as Q, applied online as the dynamic half of its balancing.

–\[ \frac{f_Q - f_{FP}}{f_{FP}}, \qquad \text{score}_{\text{dyn}} = 1 - \frac{f_Q - f_{FP}}{f_{FP}} \]

App. C.1: VBench dynamic degree measured relative to FP16. Jitter raises the raw value, so the radar chart uses 1 − the relative change.

Guide

A small fix to how VBench's dynamic degree is read. The first term is the relative change of the quantized score f Q against the FP16 score f FP. Quantization jitter makes videos look more dynamic, so a higher raw value is not better. The radar chart in figure 10 therefore plots one minus this relative change, so that matching FP16 scores highest.

–\[ y = \sum_{i}^{C_{in}} w_i x_i \]

App. E.2 / Fig. 19: every output element sums over Cin, so the elements in that sum must share quantization parameters.

Guide

Each output element y is the sum, over the C in input channels, of weight w i times input x i. Because the integer kernel adds these products directly, all elements in the sum should share quantization parameters. This single line is the reason for the per-output-channel weight and per-token activation grouping in figure 19.

–\[ \begin{aligned} WX &= s_w (W_{\text{int}} - z_w)\, s_x (x_{\text{int}} - z_x) \\ &= s_w s_x W_{\text{int}} x_{\text{int}} - s_w z_w s_x x_{\text{int}} - s_w s_x z_x W_{\text{int}} + s_w z_w s_x z_x \end{aligned} \]

Quantized GEMM expansion: an integer GEMM Wintxint followed by one FP rescale swsx, plus zero-point correction terms.

Guide

Expanding the quantized product shows why the grouping is hardware friendly. Substitute the dequantized weight and activation, and the main term becomes s w times s x times an integer matrix multiply of W int and x int, followed by one floating-point rescale. The remaining three terms are zero-point corrections that can be precomputed or cheaply added. The integer multiply is where the speed-up comes from.

–\[ \Delta_{\ell,m} = \frac{\text{Metric}_{FP} - \text{Metric}_{Q}}{\text{Metric}_{FP}} \;\xrightarrow{\text{z-score}}\; \tilde{\Delta}_{\ell,m} \;\xrightarrow{\text{softmax over } m}\; \text{heat}_{\ell,m} \]

App. E.3.1 (stated in words in the paper): relative metric drop for layer type ℓ and metric m, standardized, then normalized so each layer type's column sums to 1 (Fig. 20).

Guide

This turns sensitivity runs into the heatmap of figure 20. For layer type l and metric m, delta is the relative drop, full-precision metric minus quantized metric, divided by the full-precision value. The drops are standardized with a z-score, then a softmax over metrics makes each layer type's column sum to one. The paper describes this in words, so the formula is the tab's reconstruction.

For the thesis, NNCF's built-in sensitivity metrics are MSE-like proxies, so this result is a reason to test a metric-based ranking against them.

§8Why it matters for this thesis

ViDiT-Q → LTX-2.3 on OpenVINO / NNCF

  • Copy the sensitivity method, not the kernels. For LTX-2.3, group the linear layers by role: video self-attn, text cross-attn, the audio branch, audio↔video cross-attn, and FFN. Give each group one metric (e.g. DOVER VQA, CLIPSIM, FlowScore/flicker, plus an audio metric), then quantize one layer at a time to int4 and rank the layers inside each group. This fits NNCF well: put the selected sensitive layers at int8 or in ignored_scope, and compress the rest with nncf.compress_weights (INT4 with ratio/group_size). NNCF's built-in sensitivity_metric options (weight error, Hessian/activation variance) are proxies for the MSE-style ranking that this paper shows hurts (Table 8), so it is worth comparing the two.
  • Cost of the analysis. It needs one generation per layer per timestep range, i.e. hundreds of runs. Use short, low-resolution clips and a small prompt set. LTX-2.3 runs few denoising steps, so the "4 time ranges" become coarse bins over those steps.
  • Weight-only vs W8A8. The thesis mainly targets weight-only int8/int4. The per-output-channel (or group-wise) weight scales and the mixed-precision finding carry over directly. The activation-side ideas (dynamic per-token quantization) matter only if A8 is also tried. NNCF's default nncf.quantize uses static per-tensor activation scales, which corresponds to Table 2's "Static & Tensor-wise" row, the one that collapsed at W4A8. The OpenVINO CPU/GPU plugins do have dynamic activation quantization for weight-compressed MatMuls (the DYNAMIC_QUANTIZATION_GROUP_SIZE hint); check support for the OpenVINO version in use.
  • Channel balancing on OpenVINO. The static scaling step is SmoothQuant, which NNCF offers (and AWQ/scale estimation for weight compression). The Hadamard rotation has no native NNCF pass. Using it would mean folding Hᵀ into the weights offline and inserting an explicit rotation MatMul on the activation, which costs latency, because LTX's adaLN modulation sits between the norm and the linear layer and the rotation cannot simply be absorbed there.
  • What speed to expect. ViDiT-Q's 1.71× comes from custom INT8 GEMM CUDA kernels. W4A8 saved memory but gave less speed-up (1.38×) because DiT inference is compute-bound. On Intel CPU/Arc, weight-only int4/int8 mostly reduces memory and bandwidth. Real compute speed-ups need int8 activations that run on AMX/VNNI or XMX. Report memory and latency separately, the way Fig. 7 does.
Guide

Copy ViDiT-Q's sensitivity method, not its CUDA kernels. Group LTX-2.3's linear layers by role, including the audio branch and audio-video cross-attention, give each group one metric, rank layers by quantizing them to int4 one at a time, then keep the sensitive ones at int8 or in NNCF's ignored scope while compressing the rest with compress weights. Keep the runs cheap with short low-resolution clips, and report memory and latency separately, since weight-only compression on Intel hardware mainly saves memory.

Quantizing diffusion models

SVDQuant: Absorbing Outliers by Low-Rank Components for 4-Bit Diffusion Models

Muyang Li, Yujun Lin, Zhekai Zhang, Tianle Cai, Xiuyu Li, Junxian Guo, Enze Xie, Chenlin Meng, Jun-Yan Zhu, Song Han — MIT, NVIDIA, CMU, Princeton, UC Berkeley, SJTU, Pika Labs · ICLR 2025 (arXiv 2411.05007)

To make big diffusion transformers like 12B FLUX.1 actually faster, both weights and activations must go to 4 bits (W4A4). SVDQuant first pushes activation outliers into the weights (smoothing), then lets a small 16-bit low-rank branch (from an SVD) soak up the weight outliers, so only a flat, easy residual is quantized. A co-designed engine, Nunchaku, fuses that extra branch into the 4-bit kernels so it costs almost nothing.

Precision
W4A4 · INT4 / NVFP4
Low-rank branch
16-bit, rank 32
FLUX.1 size
22.2 → 6.1 GiB (3.6×)
Speed vs NF4 W4A16
3.0× (4090), 3.1× (5090)
Laptop 4090 vs BF16
10.1× (no offload)
FLUX.1-dev LPIPS
0.223 vs 0.272 (NF4)
Reading guide

SVDQuant asks how to make a twelve billion parameter diffusion transformer like FLUX.1 genuinely faster, not just smaller. Its answer is W four A four, four-bit weights and activations, made possible by smoothing activation outliers into the weights and then letting a small sixteen-bit low-rank branch from an SVD absorb the weight outliers, so only a flat residual is quantized. A companion engine, Nunchaku, fuses that branch into the four-bit kernels. The model ends up 3.6 times smaller and about three times faster than weight-only NF4, with better images. The tab runs from big picture and problem through the method, every equation and proof, every figure and the results tables, to a thesis box on OpenVINO. Among the sixteen papers it follows Q-Diffusion, PTQ4DiT and ViDiT-Q, builds on SmoothQuant and GPTQ, and is extended to video by the SVDQuant-GPTQ note on Wan 2.2.

§0Before reading

SVDQuant rests on one piece of linear algebra: any weight matrix can be split into a few big "directions" plus a small leftover, and the singular value decomposition (SVD) finds the best such split. It also assumes knowing why four-bit weights and four-bit activations (W4A4) are needed for real speed, and why an extra side branch costs memory traffic rather than arithmetic. It is in the atlas because it gives outliers their own small high-precision path instead of rounding them, an idea that can be tried with NNCF on LTX-2.3.

Terms used in this paper

SVD (singular value decomposition)
Writes any matrix as a sum of rank-one pieces, each scaled by a singular value, sorted from largest to smallest. Truncating it after \(r\) pieces gives the best rank-\(r\) approximation.
Rank, low-rank
The rank is how many independent directions a matrix really uses. A low-rank matrix can be stored as the product of two thin matrices, which is cheap.
Smoothing
SmoothQuant's trick: divide each activation channel by a factor and multiply the matching weight row by it. The output is unchanged, but activation outliers move into the weights.
W4A4, W4A16, W8A8
Bits for weights (W) and activations (A). W4A16 is weight-only 4-bit; W4A4 quantizes both, which is what allows 4-bit arithmetic.
NF4
"NormalFloat 4", a 4-bit weight format from QLoRA whose 16 levels follow a bell curve. The paper's weight-only baseline; it saves memory but not compute.
NVFP4
NVIDIA's 4-bit floating-point format, where each small group of values shares a scale. Supported natively by Blackwell-generation GPUs such as the RTX 5090.
Compute-bound vs memory-bound
A task is compute-bound if the arithmetic is the bottleneck, and memory-bound if moving data is. Diffusion steps are mostly compute-bound, so weight-only quantization helps little.
Tensor Core
Specialised matrix-multiply units in NVIDIA GPUs. Lower-precision inputs run faster on them, but only for formats the hardware supports.
RTX 4090, RTX 5090
Consumer NVIDIA GPUs used for the speed tests; the laptop 4090 has 16 GB of memory, too little for the 16-bit FLUX.1 without offloading to the CPU.
Nunchaku
The authors' inference engine, which fuses the low-rank branch into the 4-bit kernels so it adds little time. It is CUDA-only.
LoRA
Low-Rank Adaptation: fine-tuning a model by adding a small low-rank update to its weights. Because SVDQuant already has a 16-bit low-rank branch, LoRAs can be attached directly.
FLUX.1, PixArt-Σ, SDXL
The text-to-image models tested: FLUX.1 is a 12-billion-parameter diffusion transformer, PixArt-Σ a smaller one, and SDXL a UNet-based model.
LPIPS, PSNR
How close a quantized image is to the 16-bit model's image. LPIPS is a learned perceptual distance (lower is better); PSNR is a pixel-level score (higher is better).
FID, ImageReward, MJHQ
FID compares the statistics of many generated images with a reference set (lower is better); ImageReward is a learned human-preference score (higher is better). MJHQ-30K is the Midjourney prompt set used for testing.
Guide

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. The most important are the singular value decomposition, rank, and smoothing, because together they are the method. W four A four versus weight-only, and compute-bound versus memory-bound, explain why the authors want four bit activations. NF4 and NVFP4 are the four bit formats compared, Nunchaku is their fused engine, and LPIPS, ImageReward and FID are the quality scores in the results.

§2Big picture

Guide

The whole method fits in one picture. Smoothing first divides the activations by a per-channel factor lambda, which pushes their outliers into the weights. A small sixteen bit low-rank branch, L one times L two, then takes over those weight outliers. What is left, the residual R, is flat enough to quantize to four bits, and a four bit GEMM multiplies it with the four bit activations. Every later section explains one part of this diagram.

Every linear layer becomes two parallel paths on the same smoothed input X̂: a tiny 16-bit low-rank path (L₁ then L₂) that carries the weight outliers, and a 4-bit GEMM on the residual R. Their outputs are added. Everything is post-training; no fine-tuning.

§3The problem

Guide

Two problems motivate the paper. On the left, a single outlier sets the quantization range, so most values fall into only one or two of the sixteen four bit levels. On the right, weight-only four bit saves memory but still runs a sixteen bit multiply, so it gives no speed-up. Real speed needs both weights and activations in four bits, which is why outliers must be handled first.

Guide

Proposition 4.1 splits the W4A4 error into four factors: the size of the input, the size of the weight, and the quantization error of each. SVDQuant attacks them in pairs. Smoothing shrinks the input and its quantization error, and replacing W by the small residual R shrinks the weight term. Read this diagram as the reason for each of the method's steps.

  • Diffusion is compute-bound even at batch 1 (Fig. 2), so W4A16 only saves memory: NF4 FLUX runs 660 ms/step vs 657 ms BF16 (Fig. 8c). Real speed needs W4A4 on 4-bit tensor cores.
  • At 4 bits both sides break: X and W both have outlier channels. Smoothing only moves outliers from X to W (Fig. 3b, Fig. 4d).
  • Rotation (QuaRot-style) is ruled out: adaptive LayerNorm (adaLN) scales are computed at runtime from the timestep/text, so rotations cannot be folded into the weights offline, and online rotation is too slow. QAT is too expensive at 12B.
  • A separate low-rank branch is slow if run naïvely: it re-reads and re-writes full 16-bit activations, adding ~57% latency to the 4-bit path (Fig. 6a).

§4Method

  1. Smooth (SmoothQuant): X̂ = X·diag(λ)⁻¹, Ŵ = W·diag(λ), with λᵢ = max|X:,ᵢ|^α / max|Wᵢ,:|^(1−α); α searched per layer on calibration prompts. Activations become easy; weights get worse.
  2. Decompose: truncated SVD of Ŵ gives L₁ = UΣ:,:r and L₂ = V:r,: (optimal rank-r fit, Eckart–Young). Because smoothing makes Ŵ's spectrum spiky (Fig. 5), r = 16–32 removes most of its energy.
  3. Quantize only the residual R = Ŵ − L₁L₂ to 4 bits (per-group symmetric; INT4 group 64 with 16-bit scales, or NVFP4 group 16 with FP8 scales), using GPTQ; activations X̂ are quantized per group on the fly.
  4. Refine: re-decompose Ŵ − Q(R) a few times, keep the split with smallest error.
  5. Run with Nunchaku: kernel 1 = Quantize(X̂) + down-projection X̂L₁ (shared input); kernel 2 = 4-bit GEMM + up-projection (shared output). Overhead drops to 5–10%.
  6. Keep sensitive bits in 16-bit: for FLUX the adaLN linear inputs stay W4A16; for other models cross-attention K/V projections stay 16-bit (<5% of runtime). W8A8 variant: per-token dynamic A, per-channel W, rank 16.
Guide

Smoothing makes activations easy by pushing their outliers into the weights, and the SVD then pulls the few dominant directions of that harder weight into a small sixteen-bit branch; since smoothing made the spectrum spiky, rank sixteen to thirty-two suffices. Only the flat residual goes to four bits with GPTQ, after a short refinement loop re-balances the split. Nunchaku fuses the branch into the kernels, and a few sensitive layers stay in sixteen bits.

Guide

The offline recipe runs once per layer. A small set of COCO prompts serves as calibration data. The method searches the smoothing strength alpha by output error, smooths the weight, takes the top r singular vectors as the sixteen bit branch, and quantizes the residual with GPTQ. It can then repeat the decomposition on what quantization left behind and keep the best result.

Why it works (Sec. 4.1–4.2 in one line each)

  • Eq. (6): the layer's error is exactly the 4-bit error of X̂R, so only R and X̂ matter.
  • Eq. (8): the 4-bit error of R is bounded by ‖R‖F, and SVD is the optimal way to minimize ‖R‖F for a given r.
  • Contrast with LoRC / QLoRA-style methods: they quantize W first and fit a low-rank branch to the error, whose spectrum is flat, so low rank cannot fix it (Fig. 10: LoRC IR −0.965).
Offline SVDQuant for one linear layer (reconstructed from Sec. 4.2 + App. D; the paper has no Algorithm box) input : W (m x n), calibration activations X from COCO-caption prompts, rank r (32 for W4A4, 16 for W8A8) for alpha in search_grid: # per-layer migration strength lam[i] = max|X[:,i]|^alpha / max|W[i,:]|^(1-alpha) # smoothing factor, i = 1..m W_hat = diag(lam) @ W ; X_hat = X @ diag(lam)^-1 U,S,V = svd(W_hat) L1, L2 = U[:, :r] * S[:r], V[:r, :] # 16-bit low-rank branch R = W_hat - L1 @ L2 repeat k times: # refinement, keep best Rq = Q(R) # 4-bit, GPTQ, per-group (INT4 g=64 / NVFP4 g=16) L1, L2 = svd_r(W_hat - Rq) ; R = W_hat - L1 @ L2 track err = || X_hat W_hat - (X_hat L1 L2 + Q(X_hat) Q(R)) || keep (lam, L1, L2, Q(R)) with smallest output MSE runtime: Y = (X/lam) @ L1 @ L2 + deq( Q4(X/lam) @ Q(R) ) # fused by Nunchaku into 2 kernels
Guide

This pseudocode is reconstructed from Section 4.2 and Appendix D, since the paper prints no algorithm box. For each candidate migration strength alpha, it smooths the layer, takes a rank r SVD of the smoothed weight, and quantizes the residual. The inner loop re-fits the low-rank part to whatever the quantized residual missed, and the version with the smallest output error on calibration prompts wins. At runtime the layer is just a sixteen-bit path plus a four-bit path, added together.

§5Every equation

All 14 numbered equations (Eqs. 9–11 restate 4, 7, 8 in the appendix) plus the key unnumbered display math, in paper order.

(1)\[ \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}=\operatorname{round}\left(\frac{\mathbf{X}}{s_{\mathbf{X}}}\right),\qquad s_{\mathbf{X}}=\frac{\max(|\mathbf{X}|)}{q_{\max}} \]

Symmetric max-scaled quantization: integer tensor \(\mathbf{Q}_\mathbf{X}\), scale \(s_\mathbf{X}\).

Guide

This is the basic quantizer used throughout the paper. Take a tensor X, divide it by a scale s X, and round to the nearest integer to get the integer tensor Q X. The scale is the largest absolute value in X divided by q max, the largest integer the format allows. One big outlier therefore stretches the scale and wastes levels for every other value, which is the whole problem SVDQuant attacks.

—\[ q_{\max}=2^{k-1}-1\ \text{(signed INT}k\text{)},\qquad q_{\max}=6\ \text{(FP4 E2M1)},\qquad Q(\mathbf{X})=s_{\mathbf{X}}\cdot\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}} \]

Range per data type (INT4 → 7) and the dequantized tensor.

Guide

q max is the largest representable magnitude: two to the power k minus one, minus one, for a signed k-bit integer, so seven for INT4, and six for the FP4 format E2M1 used by NVFP4. Multiplying the integers back by the scale gives Q of X, the dequantized tensor. With only seven positive levels at four bits, how the scale is set decides almost everything.

(2)\[ \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}\approx Q(\mathbf{X})Q(\mathbf{W})=s_{\mathbf{X}}s_{\mathbf{W}}\cdot\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{W}} \]

A linear layer in low precision: integer GEMM, then one rescale. Needs both operands at the same bit-width for a speed-up.

Guide

A linear layer multiplies activations X by weights W. In low precision, both are quantized, the integer matrices are multiplied on fast integer hardware, and one final rescale by s X times s W restores the magnitude. The key point is that both operands must be at the same low bit-width to get the speed-up, which is why the paper insists on W4A4 rather than four-bit weights only.

(3)\[ E(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{W})=\left\lVert \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}-Q(\mathbf{X})Q(\mathbf{W})\right\rVert_F \]

Quantization error of a linear layer, \(\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times m}\), \(\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), Frobenius norm.

Guide

This defines the error the paper tries to shrink: the Frobenius norm, meaning the square root of the sum of squared entries, of the gap between the true output X times W and the quantized output. X has b rows of tokens and m input channels, W maps m inputs to n outputs. Every later equation is a way to bound or reduce this number.

(4)\[ E(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{W})\le\lVert \mathbf{X}\rVert_F\lVert \mathbf{W}-Q(\mathbf{W})\rVert_F+\lVert \mathbf{X}-Q(\mathbf{X})\rVert_F\left(\lVert \mathbf{W}\rVert_F+\lVert \mathbf{W}-Q(\mathbf{W})\rVert_F\right) \]

Prop. 4.1 (error decomposition): error bounded by magnitudes of X, W and their own quantization errors.

Guide

Proposition 4.1 splits the layer error into pieces. The first term is the size of X times the weight quantization error; the second is the activation quantization error times the size of W plus its own error. So the output error stays small only if both X and W are small in magnitude and both quantize well. That is why outliers on either side hurt, and it motivates attacking both.

—\[ \hat{\mathbf{X}}=\mathbf{X}\cdot\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{-1},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{W}}=\mathbf{W}\cdot\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\lambda}),\qquad \boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} \]

Smoothing (SmoothQuant): per-input-channel factor; \(\hat{\mathbf{X}}\hat{\mathbf{W}}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}\) exactly (λ scales the m input rows of W, i.e. diag(λ)W in strict matrix order).

Guide

Smoothing, borrowed from SmoothQuant, divides each input channel of X by a factor lambda i and multiplies the matching row of W by the same factor. X hat times W hat equals X times W exactly, so nothing changes mathematically. What changes is where the outliers live: X hat becomes flat and easy to quantize, while W hat inherits the spikes, the problem seen in Figure 3b.

—\[ \hat{\mathbf{W}}=\mathbf{L}_1\mathbf{L}_2+\mathbf{R},\qquad \mathbf{L}_1\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\ \mathbf{L}_2\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} \]

Split the smoothed weight into a rank-r part and a residual.

Guide

Here the smoothed weight W hat is split into two parts: L one times L two, a rank r product where L one is m by r and L two is r by n, plus a residual R. With r much smaller than m or n, the low-rank part is cheap to store and run in sixteen bits. The next equation shows why only R then needs quantizing.

(5)\[ \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}=\hat{\mathbf{X}}\hat{\mathbf{W}}=\hat{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{L}_1\mathbf{L}_2+\hat{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{R}\approx\underbrace{\hat{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{L}_1\mathbf{L}_2}_{\text{16-bit low-rank branch}}+\underbrace{Q(\hat{\mathbf{X}})Q(\mathbf{R})}_{\text{4-bit residual}} \]

The SVDQuant layer: only the residual branch is quantized.

Guide

Equation five is the SVDQuant layer itself. The output X times W equals X hat times the low-rank part plus X hat times the residual. The first term runs in sixteen bits and carries the outliers; only the second term is quantized, as four-bit X hat times four-bit R. This is the two-path picture from the big-picture diagram.

—\[ \text{overhead}=\frac{mr+nr}{mn},\qquad r\ll\min(m,n),\ r\in\{16,32\} \]

Extra parameters/compute of the low-rank branch (e.g. m = n = 3072, r = 32 → 2.1%).

Guide

The cost of the extra branch is m times r plus n times r values, divided by the m times n values of the full weight. For a 3072 by 3072 layer with rank thirty-two that is about 2.1 percent more parameters and compute. The branch is cheap in arithmetic; Figure 6 shows the real cost is memory traffic, which Nunchaku fixes.

(6)\[ \left\lVert \hat{\mathbf{X}}\hat{\mathbf{W}}-\left(\hat{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{L}_1\mathbf{L}_2+Q(\hat{\mathbf{X}})Q(\mathbf{R})\right)\right\rVert_F=\left\lVert \hat{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{R}-Q(\hat{\mathbf{X}})Q(\mathbf{R})\right\rVert_F=E(\hat{\mathbf{X}},\mathbf{R}) \]

The error of the whole layer equals the plain quantization error of the residual GEMM.

Guide

Equation six says the error of the whole SVDQuant layer is exactly the plain quantization error of the residual product, X hat times R. The sixteen-bit branch adds no error at all. So the question reduces to making X hat and R easy to quantize, and equation eight then says how to do that for R.

(7)\[ \mathbb{E}\left[\max(|\mathbf{R}|)\right]\le c\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\lVert \mathbf{R}\rVert_F\right] \]

Regularity condition of Prop. 4.2 (no extreme outliers relative to overall energy).

Guide

This is a mild regularity assumption for Proposition 4.2: the expected largest entry of R is at most a constant c times the expected Frobenius norm of R. In words, R has no extreme outliers compared with its total energy. The paper checks it for Gaussian entries two blocks down.

(8)\[ \mathbb{E}\left[\lVert \mathbf{R}-Q(\mathbf{R})\rVert_F\right]\le\frac{c\sqrt{\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R})}}{q_{\max}}\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\lVert \mathbf{R}\rVert_F\right] \]

Prop. 4.2: residual quantization error is bounded by the residual's magnitude, so minimize ‖R‖F.

Guide

Proposition 4.2: under that assumption, the expected quantization error of R is at most c times the square root of the number of entries, divided by q max, times the expected size of R. The practical message is simple: a smaller residual means a smaller four-bit error. Minimising the norm of R is therefore the goal, and the SVD is the optimal tool for it.

—\[ c=\sqrt{\frac{\log(\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R}))\,\pi}{\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R})}}\quad\text{(Gaussian entries)} \]

Constant for which Eq. (7) holds when R is normally distributed.

Guide

For a residual with normally distributed entries, the constant c in equation seven is the square root of log of the number of entries times pi, divided by the number of entries. It shrinks as the matrix grows, so the regularity condition is easy to satisfy for large layers. The proof in Appendix A.2, equations twelve to fourteen, derives this value.

—\[ \hat{\mathbf{W}}=\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V},\qquad \mathbf{L}_1=\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{:,:r},\qquad \mathbf{L}_2=\mathbf{V}_{:r,:} \]

Eckart–Young–Mirsky: truncated SVD is the optimal rank-r minimizer of ‖Ŵ − L₁L₂‖F.

Guide

The SVD writes W hat as U times Sigma times V. Keeping the first r columns of U times Sigma gives L one, and the first r rows of V give L two. The Eckart, Young, Mirsky theorem guarantees this truncated SVD is the best possible rank r approximation, so it leaves the smallest residual R, exactly what equation eight asks for.

—\[ \lVert \mathbf{R}\rVert_F=\sqrt{\sum_{i=r+1}^{\min(m,n)}\sigma_i^2}\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad \lVert \hat{\mathbf{W}}\rVert_F=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{\min(m,n)}\sigma_i^2} \]

Removing the top-r singular values \(\sigma_i\) of Ŵ removes most of its energy (Fig. 5).

Guide

The size of the residual equals the square root of the sum of the squared singular values from index r plus one onward, while the full weight includes all of them. If the first few singular values sigma i are huge, removing them removes most of the energy. Figure 5 shows smoothing makes W hat exactly like that, which is why rank thirty-two is enough.

—\[ \lambda_i=\frac{\max(|\mathbf{X}_{:,i}|)^{\alpha}}{\max(|\mathbf{W}_{i,:}|)^{1-\alpha}} \]

App. D: smoothing factor per input channel; migration strength α searched per layer to minimize output MSE after SVD on calibration data.

Guide

This is the smoothing factor for input channel i: the largest activation magnitude in that channel raised to alpha, divided by the largest weight magnitude in that row raised to one minus alpha. Alpha, the migration strength, decides how much difficulty moves from activations to weights. Unlike SmoothQuant, SVDQuant searches alpha per layer to minimise output error measured after the SVD step, using calibration prompts.

(9)\[ E(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{W})\le\lVert \mathbf{X}\rVert_F\lVert \mathbf{W}-Q(\mathbf{W})\rVert_F+\lVert \mathbf{X}-Q(\mathbf{X})\rVert_F\left(\lVert \mathbf{W}\rVert_F+\lVert \mathbf{W}-Q(\mathbf{W})\rVert_F\right) \]

App. A.1 restatement of Prop. 4.1 (= Eq. 4).

Guide

This is the appendix restatement of Proposition 4.1, identical to equation four: the layer error is bounded by the size of X times the weight error, plus the activation error times the size of W plus its error. It is repeated here only to set up the proof that follows.

proof A.1\[ \begin{aligned} &\lVert \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}-Q(\mathbf{X})Q(\mathbf{W})\rVert_F\\ &=\lVert \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{X}Q(\mathbf{W})+\mathbf{X}Q(\mathbf{W})-Q(\mathbf{X})Q(\mathbf{W})\rVert_F\\ &\le\lVert \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{W}-Q(\mathbf{W}))\rVert_F+\lVert(\mathbf{X}-Q(\mathbf{X}))Q(\mathbf{W})\rVert_F\\ &\le\lVert \mathbf{X}\rVert_F\lVert \mathbf{W}-Q(\mathbf{W})\rVert_F+\lVert \mathbf{X}-Q(\mathbf{X})\rVert_F\lVert Q(\mathbf{W})\rVert_F\\ &\le\lVert \mathbf{X}\rVert_F\lVert \mathbf{W}-Q(\mathbf{W})\rVert_F+\lVert \mathbf{X}-Q(\mathbf{X})\rVert_F\lVert \mathbf{W}-(\mathbf{W}-Q(\mathbf{W}))\rVert_F\\ &\le\lVert \mathbf{X}\rVert_F\lVert \mathbf{W}-Q(\mathbf{W})\rVert_F+\lVert \mathbf{X}-Q(\mathbf{X})\rVert_F\left(\lVert \mathbf{W}\rVert_F+\lVert \mathbf{W}-Q(\mathbf{W})\rVert_F\right) \end{aligned} \]

Add-and-subtract X·Q(W), triangle inequality, sub-multiplicativity, then triangle inequality on Q(W) = W − (W − Q(W)).

Guide

The proof of Proposition 4.1 uses one trick and two standard inequalities. Add and subtract X times Q of W, split the norm with the triangle inequality, then use the fact that the norm of a product is at most the product of norms. Finally, Q of W is written as W minus its error, and the triangle inequality is applied once more. Nothing here is specific to diffusion models.

(10)\[ \mathbb{E}\left[\max(|\mathbf{R}|)\right]\le c\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\lVert \mathbf{R}\rVert_F\right] \]

App. A.2 restatement of Eq. (7).

Guide

This restates equation seven in Appendix A.2: the expected maximum entry of the residual R is at most a constant c times its expected Frobenius norm. It is the no-extreme-outliers assumption on which the residual error bound of Proposition 4.2 rests.

(11)\[ \mathbb{E}\left[\lVert \mathbf{R}-Q(\mathbf{R})\rVert_F\right]\le\frac{c\sqrt{\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R})}}{q_{\max}}\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\lVert \mathbf{R}\rVert_F\right] \]

App. A.2 restatement of Eq. (8).

Guide

This restates equation eight in Appendix A.2: the expected quantization error of R is bounded by c times the square root of its size, over q max, times its expected norm. The proof block that follows derives it.

proof A.2\[ \begin{aligned} \lVert \mathbf{R}-Q(\mathbf{R})\rVert_F&=\lVert \mathbf{R}-s_{\mathbf{R}}\cdot\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{R}}\rVert_F=\left\lVert s_{\mathbf{R}}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{R}}{s_{\mathbf{R}}}-s_{\mathbf{R}}\cdot\operatorname{round}\left(\frac{\mathbf{R}}{s_{\mathbf{R}}}\right)\right\rVert_F=|s_{\mathbf{R}}|\left\lVert\frac{\mathbf{R}}{s_{\mathbf{R}}}-\operatorname{round}\left(\frac{\mathbf{R}}{s_{\mathbf{R}}}\right)\right\rVert_F\\ \mathbb{E}\left[\lVert \mathbf{R}-Q(\mathbf{R})\rVert_F\right]&\le\mathbb{E}\left[|s_{\mathbf{R}}|\right]\sqrt{\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R})}=\frac{\sqrt{\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R})}}{q_{\max}}\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\max(|\mathbf{R}|)\right]\le\frac{c\sqrt{\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R})}}{q_{\max}}\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\lVert \mathbf{R}\rVert_F\right] \end{aligned} \]

Each element's rounding error is ≤ 1 step (the paper bounds it by 1 per element), so the error ≤ |s_R|·√size(R); then s_R = max|R|/q_max and Eq. (10).

Guide

The proof of Proposition 4.2 factors the scale out of the error and bounds each element's rounding error by one step, giving the scale times the square root of the number of entries. The scale is the maximum of R over q max, and the regularity assumption turns that maximum into the norm of R. One step is a loose bound, since rounding error is at most half a step, but the conclusion holds.

(12)\[ \mathbb{E}\left[\max(|\mathbf{R}|)\right]\le\sigma\sqrt{2\log(\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R}))} \]

Gaussian maximal inequality (Massart 2007, Lemma 2.3), σ = std of the entries.

Guide

For Gaussian entries with standard deviation sigma, the expected largest absolute entry grows only like sigma times the square root of two times log of the number of entries. This is a standard maximal inequality from Massart, and it is the first ingredient for computing the constant c.

(13)\[ \mathbb{E}\left[\lVert \mathbf{R}\rVert_F\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sqrt{\sum_{x\in \mathbf{R}}x^2}\right]\ge\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sum_{x\in \mathbf{R}}|x|}{\sqrt{\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R})}}\right] \]

Cauchy–Schwarz lower bound on the Frobenius norm.

Guide

The Cauchy, Schwarz inequality gives a lower bound on the Frobenius norm of R: it is at least the sum of absolute entries divided by the square root of the number of entries. This is the second ingredient for the Gaussian constant c.

(14)\[ \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sum_{x\in \mathbf{R}}|x|}{\sqrt{\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R})}}\right]=\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\,\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R})}{\pi}} \]

Mean of the half-normal distribution, \(\mathbb{E}|x|=\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}\).

Guide

For a normal entry, the expected absolute value is sigma times the square root of two over pi, the mean of a half-normal distribution. Summing over all entries turns the lower bound from equation thirteen into sigma times the square root of two times the size over pi.

—\[ \mathbb{E}\left[\max(|\mathbf{R}|)\right]\le\sigma\sqrt{2\log(\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R}))}\le\sqrt{\frac{\log(\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R}))\,\pi}{\operatorname{size}(\mathbf{R})}}\;\mathbb{E}\left[\lVert \mathbf{R}\rVert_F\right] \]

Combining (12)–(14): Eq. (10) holds with the Gaussian c given above.

Guide

Chaining equations twelve to fourteen shows that the expected maximum of R is at most the Gaussian constant c times the expected norm of R. So the regularity condition of Proposition 4.2 holds for Gaussian residuals, closing the proof that a smaller residual gives a smaller four-bit error.

§6Every figure

§7Results

Guide

Lower LPIPS means closer to the full-precision image. On FLUX dev, both four bit SVDQuant variants beat NF4 weight-only quantization, which is not faster anyway. On PixArt Sigma the contrast is sharper: ViDiT-Q at W4A4 collapses to an LPIPS of 0.854, while SVDQuant at W4A4 reaches 0.323, better even than ViDiT-Q at W4A8.

Guide

The left chart is the ablation from Table 3: the low-rank branch gives the biggest gain in PSNR, and GPTQ adds a little more on top. The right chart is the cost from Table 4. Run naively, the extra branch adds about eighteen percent to step time, 250 against 212 milliseconds. The fused Nunchaku kernels cut that to 218. For the thesis, expect the unfused cost, since OpenVINO has no such fused kernel.

The ablation isolates the two tools applied to the residual, the low-rank branch and GPTQ, with four on-off rows per model and format. The low-rank branch is the bigger win, especially on PixArt Sigma INT4, where ImageReward jumps from about minus 1.2 to 0.858. GPTQ adds a smaller gain, and the combination gives the best LPIPS in most groups, though NVFP4 with GPTQ alone edges it on FLUX.1-dev. NNCF offers GPTQ, while the low-rank split would be done by hand.

Table 4 (App. E.4) — Single-step FLUX latency on a desktop RTX 4090 (the text body says laptop; caption says desktop). Naïve INT4 is 1.3× faster than INT8; an unfused low-rank branch adds 18%; Nunchaku brings it back to ≈ naïve INT4.
MethodBF16INT8Naïve INT4SVDQuantSVDQuant + Nunchaku
Latency (ms)657282212250218
Guide

Per-step FLUX latency on a desktop RTX 4090 shows what fusion buys: BF16 takes 657 milliseconds, INT8 282 and naive INT4 212. Adding the low-rank branch unfused raises it to 250, about eighteen percent more, and Nunchaku brings it back to 218. The text body says laptop while the caption says desktop. For the thesis, the unfused figure is the relevant warning, since OpenVINO runs the branch as separate MatMuls.

  • 8-bit SVDQuant is essentially lossless everywhere (PSNR > 21; 27.0 on FLUX.1-dev MJHQ) and beats ViDiT-Q, MixDQ and TensorRT W8A8.
  • NVFP4 beats INT4 thanks to smaller groups (16 vs 64); the gap is largest on the small PixArt-Σ (600M).
  • Memory: 12B FLUX.1 22.2 → 6.1 GiB incl. 0.3 GiB for the low-rank branches.

§8Why it matters for this thesis

Guide

This is how one SVDQuant layer would look inside an OpenVINO model. Every piece is a standard operation: a Multiply by one over lambda, two small MatMuls for the low-rank branch, a compressed four bit MatMul for the residual, and an Add. So the layer can be exported without custom ops. What is missing is a W4A4 matrix multiply and a fused kernel, so on Intel hardware the gain would be quality at four bit weights, not speed.

Takeaways for LTX-2.3 on OpenVINO / NNCF

  • Expressible, but unfused. The low-rank branch is just MatMul(X̂, L₁) → MatMul(·, L₂) in f16 plus an Add, next to an int4 weight-compressed MatMul on R. No custom op is needed, but each layer pays for an extra read of X̂ and write of Y. That is exactly the overhead the paper measured before fusion (+57% on one QKV layer, +18% end-to-end, Fig. 6a / Table 4). LTX video latents mean long token sequences, so benchmark this overhead on Arc/CPU instead of assuming 5–10%.
  • The W4A4 speed-up does not carry over. OpenVINO has no 4-bit activation GEMM. Int4 weights are weight-only (decompressed, or run with dynamic int8 activation quantization on CPU/GPU), and Arc XMX units accelerate int8, not int4. The realistic use of SVDQuant here is better quality for int4 weight-only or W8A8. The rank-32 branch soaks up weight outliers that plain int4 group-wise compression struggles with.
  • Close NNCF equivalents. nncf.compress_weights(..., lora_correction=True) adds a low-rank adapter that corrects the int4 error (LoRC-style: quantize first, then fix the error). The paper shows decomposing first works better (Fig. 10). NNCF's SmoothQuant (in nncf.quantize), AWQ, scale estimation and GPTQ cover the other ingredients. A clean thesis experiment: do the SVD split in PyTorch (smooth → SVD → keep L₁, L₂ in f16), compress only R with NNCF, export, and compare against NNCF int4 with and without lora_correction.
  • Calibration and adaLN. SVD itself needs no data, but the per-layer α search (and GPTQ) needs calibration prompts, i.e. a few LTX denoising trajectories. LTX-2.3 is a DiT with timestep-dependent adaLN, so the paper's argument against rotation applies directly. Also, 1/λ can only be folded offline when the producer op is a static Linear; after adaLN modulation it stays an explicit Multiply.
  • Overhead is small and LoRA-friendly. Rank 32 adds (m+n)·r f16 values per layer: for a 4096×4096 layer that is 1.6% of the parameters, or about 6% of its int4 bytes. Keeping the branch separate lets style/control LoRAs be concatenated into it without re-quantization (Fig. 9), which fits OpenVINO GenAI's runtime LoRA adapters.
Guide

Treat SVDQuant as a quality tool for int4 weight-only or W8A8 on OpenVINO, not a speed-up. The clean experiment is to smooth and split each layer in PyTorch, keep L one and L two in f16, compress only the residual with NNCF, and compare against NNCF int4 with and without lora correction. Calibrate on a few LTX denoising trajectories, and measure the unfused branch overhead on Arc and CPU instead of assuming five to ten percent.

Quantizing diffusion models

DVD-Quant: Data-free Video Diffusion Transformers Quantization

Zhiteng Li, Hanxuan Li, Junyi Wu, Kai Liu, Haotong Qin, Linghe Kong, Guihai Chen, Yulun Zhang, Xiaokang Yang (Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ., Zhejiang Univ., ETH Zürich) · ICLR 2026 · arXiv 2505.18663 (2025)

Post-training quantization of a video DiT with no calibration data at all. Weights get better INT4 grids from a closed-form search (BGR). Activations are rotated with a Hadamard matrix and scaled online at every step (ARQ). A cheap per-step signal then picks 4-bit or 8-bit activations for each denoising step (δ-GBS).

Calibration data
None
Bit-widths
W4A8 · W4A6 · W4A4
Model
HunyuanVideo, 50 steps
Speed-up (RTX 4090)
1.75× / 1.93× / 2.12×
Memory
3.68× smaller
W4A4 Imaging Q.
61.82 (BF16 64.78)
Reading guide

The question behind DVD-Quant is whether a video diffusion transformer can be quantized to four-bit weights and low-bit activations without any calibration data at all. The answer is yes, on HunyuanVideo with 50 steps: at W four A four, meaning four-bit weights and four-bit activations, it reaches an Imaging Quality of 61.82 against 64.78 for the full-precision model, runs 2.12 times faster on an RTX 4090, and uses 3.68 times less memory. It has three parts: a closed-form weight grid search called BGR, a rotation plus live scaling for activations called ARQ, and a per-step switch between four-bit and eight-bit activations called delta-GBS. The tab moves from the big picture to the two problems, then the method, every equation, every figure, the results tables, and a thesis box. It is the tenth of the sixteen papers, in the diffusion quantization group after SVDQuant and before QVGen.

§0Before reading

Following this paper takes three ideas: why most quantizers need calibration data, what a four-bit grid with a step size and zero-point is, and how a rotation can tame outliers. DVD-Quant is in the atlas because it quantizes a video diffusion transformer with no calibration data at all, and its weight method produces an ordinary INT4 grid that OpenVINO can already run.

Terms used in this paper

Post-training quantization (PTQ)
Shrinking a model that is already trained, by storing its numbers with fewer bits, without retraining it. DVD-Quant is a PTQ method.
Calibration data
A small set of example inputs run through the full-precision model to measure typical activation ranges. DVD-Quant uses none: it works from the weights and from the live activations only.
W4A4, W4A8, W4A6
W is the bit-width of the weights, A of the activations. W4A6 in this paper is not a fixed format: each step uses A4 or A8, averaging about six bits.
BF16
A 16-bit floating-point format used for the full-precision reference model. It is the quality every quantized result is compared against.
Step size and zero-point
The two numbers that define a grid: the step size \(\Delta\) is the gap between levels, and the integer zero-point \(z\) says which level stands for zero.
MinMax
The simplest way to set a grid: stretch it from the smallest to the largest value. It is the starting point that BGR improves.
Frobenius norm
The square root of the sum of all squared entries of a matrix. Here it measures the total gap between the original and the quantized weights.
Hadamard matrix
A square matrix of +1 and −1 entries (scaled) whose rows are all perpendicular. Multiplying by it is a rotation, and a fast transform makes it cheap to apply.
Online (dynamic) scaling
Measuring the scale from the tensor that is actually being quantized, at run time, instead of reading a number fixed in advance.
Massive vs channel-wise outliers
Massive outliers are a few single values far larger than all others. Channel-wise outliers are whole channels that run larger than the rest. ARQ rotates away the first and rescales the second.
HunyuanVideo
A large open text-to-video diffusion transformer from Tencent, and the main model tested here. The paper also reports Wan2.1 in its supplement.
RTX 4090
An NVIDIA consumer (gaming) GPU. All speed and memory numbers in the paper are measured on one of them, with custom low-bit kernels.
Tensor Core
The matrix-multiply units inside NVIDIA GPUs that give the speed-up for low-bit integer math. Intel Arc GPUs have a counterpart called XMX, but the paper's kernels do not run there.
VBench
A benchmark suite that scores generated videos on many dimensions. This paper reports eight, such as Imaging Quality, Aesthetic Quality and Motion Smoothness.
Guide

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. The most important are calibration data, which DVD-Quant avoids, and the step size and zero-point, which define every grid it builds. Hadamard matrix and online scaling are the two halves of ARQ. The hardware and benchmark entries matter for reading the results: all speed numbers come from an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with custom Tensor Core kernels, and quality is measured with VBench.

§2Big picture

Three parts: BGR for weights, ARQ for activations, δ-GBS for choosing activation bits per timestep. None needs a single calibration prompt.

§3The problem

  • Calibration for video DiTs is slow (50 steps × long token sequences) and still misses part of the range.
  • With 4-bit activations, existing PTQ collapses: VBench metrics fall 27.5%–61.3% (Tab. 1, Fig. 1).
  • Rotation alone (QuaRot-style) removes big spikes but can push many other values up (Fig. 4).
  • Denoising steps are not equally important, so one fixed bit-width for all steps wastes bits.

§4Method

A. Bounded-init Grid Refinement (weights, offline)

Algorithm 1 Bounded-init Grid Refinement Input: W ∈ R^{n×m}, n ∈ N, ϵ ∈ R Output: Δ* ∈ R^n, z* ∈ Z^n 1: δ_l = δ_u = (max(W) − min(W)) / n 2: E* = ∞, Δ* = z* = 0 3: for i = 1, 2, ..., n do 4: W_c = clamp(W, min(W) + i·δ_l, max(W) − i·δ_u) 5: Δ^(0) = (max(W_c) − min(W_c)) / (2^b − 1), z^(0) = −⌊min(W_c) ⊘ Δ^(0)⌉ 6: W_q^(0) = clamp(⌊W ⊘ Δ^(0)⌉ + z^(0), 0, 2^b − 1) 7: E^(0) = ‖W − Δ^(0) ⊙ (W_q^(0) − z^(0))‖_F, j = 0 8: repeat 9: Δ^(j) = ⟨W_q^(j−1) − z^(j−1), W⟩_row ⊘ ⟨W_q^(j−1) − z^(j−1), W_q^(j−1) − z^(j−1)⟩_row 10: z^(j) = clamp(W̄_q^(j−1) − W̄ ⊘ Δ^(j), 0, 2^b − 1) 11: W_q^(j) = clamp(⌊W ⊘ Δ^(j)⌉ + z^(j), 0, 2^b − 1) 12: E^(j) = ‖W − Δ^(j) ⊙ (W_q^(j) − z^(j))‖_F, j = j + 1 13: until E^(j−1) − E^(j−2) < ϵ 14: if E^(j−1) < E* then 15: E* ← E^(j−1), Δ* ← Δ^(j−1), z* ← z^(j−1) 16: end if 17: end for 18: return Δ*, z*
Guide

Algorithm 1 is BGR written out. It first sets a shrink step equal to the weight range divided by n, then for each i from one to n clips i shrink steps off both tails and builds a MinMax grid on the clipped weights as a starting point. From there it repeats the least-squares step size, the zero-point update and re-rounding, measuring the Frobenius reconstruction error each time, and stops when the improvement falls below epsilon. Across all clipping levels it keeps the step size and zero-point with the smallest error. Everything runs offline on the weights only.

Note: the paper reuses n both as row count of W and as the number of bound-search steps; b is the weight bit-width (4).

B. Auto-scaling Rotated Quantization (activations, online)

C. δ-Guided Bit Switching (per timestep)

  1. Offline: rotate each linear weight by H and quantize to INT4 with BGR (Alg. 1). Weights stay INT4 for every step.
  2. At each step t: rotate activations with a fast Hadamard transform and compute block-wise max scales from the live tensor.
  3. Check δ-GBS: if the accumulated relative output change Σ L1 since the last reset is below δ, quantize activations to 4 bits; otherwise to 8 bits and reset the counter.
  4. Run the W4A4 or W4A8 GEMM kernel (both are standard kernels; no mixed-precision kernel), rescale by Λ.
Guide

The pipeline splits into one offline stage and one per-step loop. Offline, every linear weight is rotated by the Hadamard matrix and quantized to INT4 with BGR, and these weights never change again. At each denoising step, the activations are rotated, their block-wise scales are read from the live tensor, and delta-GBS decides whether this step uses four or eight bits. The chosen standard W4A4 or W4A8 kernel then runs and the result is rescaled. No mixed-precision kernel is needed, only a switch between two existing ones.

§5Every equation

(1)\[ \text{Quant:}\quad \mathbf{W}_q=\operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\lfloor \mathbf{W}\oslash\Delta\rceil+\mathbf{z},\,0,\,2^b-1\right) \]

MinMax per-channel asymmetric quantization; ⊘ element-wise divide, ⌊·⌉ round, b bits.

Guide

Equation 1 is ordinary asymmetric quantization, the baseline everything else builds on. Each weight in W is divided element-wise by the step size delta, rounded to the nearest integer, shifted by the zero-point z, and clamped into the range from zero to two to the b minus one, where b is the bit-width. For four bits that range is zero to fifteen. W q is the resulting integer matrix.

(2)\[ \text{DeQuant:}\quad \widehat{\mathbf{W}}=\Delta\odot(\mathbf{W}_q-\mathbf{z}) \]

Reconstruct weights from integers, step size Δ and zero-point z (⊙ element-wise product).

Guide

Equation 2 goes back from integers to real numbers. The dequantized weight, W hat, is the step size delta times the integer weights W q minus the zero-point z, element by element. The gap between W and W hat is the quantization error that BGR later tries to minimise in equation 3. This is also the form OpenVINO uses when it decompresses INT4 weights at run time.

—\[ \Delta=\frac{\max(\mathbf{W})-\min(\mathbf{W})}{2^b-1}\in\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad \mathbf{z}=-\lfloor \min(\mathbf{W})\oslash\Delta\rceil\in\mathbb{Z}^n \]

MinMax step size and zero-point, one per output channel (row) of W ∈ ℝn×m.

Guide

This is the MinMax recipe for the grid, computed separately for each output row of W. The step size delta is the row's range, max minus min, divided by two to the b minus one, so the levels span exactly the extreme values. The zero-point z is minus the rounded ratio of the minimum to delta, so the smallest weight maps to integer zero. Figure 2 shows why this is wasteful for bell-shaped weights, and BGR uses it only as a starting point.

(3)\[ \Delta^*,\mathbf{z}^*=\arg\min_{\Delta,\mathbf{z}}\lVert \mathbf{W}-\Delta\odot(\mathbf{W}_q-\mathbf{z})\rVert_F \]

The real objective: choose the grid that minimises weight reconstruction error; MinMax is only an initial guess.

Guide

Equation 3 states what BGR really optimises. Among all choices of step size delta and zero-point z, pick the pair that makes the Frobenius norm of W minus its dequantized version as small as possible, the Frobenius norm being the square root of the sum of squared errors. MinMax does not solve this; it is just a first guess. Equations 4 to 6 give the alternating closed-form updates that approximately solve it.

(4)\[ \Delta'=\langle \mathbf{W}_q-\mathbf{z},\mathbf{W}\rangle_{\text{row}}\oslash\langle \mathbf{W}_q-\mathbf{z},\mathbf{W}_q-\mathbf{z}\rangle_{\text{row}} \]

Closed-form least-squares step size with z and Wq fixed; ⟨·,·⟩row is the row-wise inner product.

Guide

Equation 4 updates the step size when the integers and zero-point are held fixed. For each row it divides the inner product of W q minus z with the real weights W by the inner product of W q minus z with itself. That is the textbook least-squares fit of a single scale factor, so it has an exact answer with no iteration or gradients. It is the first update in the inner loop of BGR.

(5)\[ \mathbf{z}'=\operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\overline{\mathbf{W}}_q-\overline{\mathbf{W}}\oslash\Delta',\,0,\,2^b-1\right) \]

Zero-point update with Δ′ fixed: relax z to real values, solve, clamp (then round). The overlines are printed in the paper but not defined there.

Guide

Equation 5 updates the zero-point with the new step size delta prime held fixed. The zero-point is temporarily treated as a real number, solved as the average integer value minus the average weight divided by delta prime, then clamped into the valid integer range and rounded. The overlines are printed in the paper without a definition; reading them as row averages is the natural interpretation, not a stated fact. This is the second update in BGR's inner loop.

(6)\[ \mathbf{W}_q'=\operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\lfloor \mathbf{W}\oslash\Delta'\rceil+\mathbf{z}',\,0,\,2^b-1\right) \]

Re-round the weights on the new grid (same form as Eq. 1).

Guide

Equation 6 re-rounds the weights on the updated grid. It is the same formula as equation 1, only with the new step size delta prime and zero-point z prime: divide, round, add the zero-point, clamp to the four-bit range. With new integers in hand, BGR goes back to equation 4 and repeats until the reconstruction error stops falling.

(7)\[ \mathbf{W}_c=\operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\mathbf{W},\,\min(\mathbf{W})+\delta_l,\,\max(\mathbf{W})-\delta_u\right) \]

Search-bound initialisation: clip the tails by shrink steps δl, δu.

Guide

Equation 7 is the clipping step of BGR's outer loop. W c is W with every value below the minimum plus delta l raised to that bound, and every value above the maximum minus delta u lowered to that bound. Delta l and delta u are the lower and upper shrink amounts. Cutting off the rare extreme weights lets the sixteen levels concentrate on the dense centre shown in figure 2.

(8)\[ \Delta_c=\frac{\max(\mathbf{W}_c)-\min(\mathbf{W}_c)}{2^b-1},\qquad \mathbf{z}_c=-\lfloor \min(\mathbf{W}_c)\oslash\Delta_c\rceil \]

Grid of the clipped weights; this is the start point BGR refines (Alg. 1).

Guide

Equation 8 is simply MinMax applied to the clipped weights W c. Delta c is the clipped range divided by two to the b minus one, and z c is the matching zero-point. This grid is the starting point that the inner loop of Algorithm 1 refines with equations 4 to 6, one start per clipping level.

(9)\[ \mathbf{Y}=\left(\mathbf{X}\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})^{-1}\right)\cdot\left(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s})\mathbf{W}\right)=\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{W}},\qquad s_i=\frac{\max(|\mathbf{X}_i|)^{\alpha}}{\max(|\mathbf{W}_i|)^{1-\alpha}} \]

SmoothQuant-style pre-scaling (what prior video PTQ does): s ∈ ℝC from a calibration set, α migration strength.

Guide

Equation 9 shows what earlier video quantization methods do, borrowed from SmoothQuant. Each input channel of X is divided by a scale s i and the matching weight row is multiplied by it, so the product is unchanged but activation outliers move into the weights. The scale mixes the largest activation and the largest weight with a migration strength alpha. The catch is that the activation maximum comes from a calibration set and stays fixed, which is exactly what figure 3 shows failing across timesteps.

—\[ \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^{\top}=\mathbf{I},\quad |\mathbf{Q}|=\mathbf{I};\qquad \mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{\top}=(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{H})(\mathbf{H}^{\top}\mathbf{W}) \]

Orthogonal rotation (as printed) and Hadamard computational invariance used by ARQ.

Guide

This block states the rotation trick ARQ relies on. An orthogonal matrix Q times its transpose gives the identity, so inserting a Hadamard matrix H and its transpose between the activation X and the weights leaves the output Y unchanged: X times W transpose equals X H times H transpose W. The paper also prints a determinant-style condition that looks garbled, so treat that part loosely. The useful fact is that rotation is free in exact arithmetic and spreads outliers before quantization.

(10)\[ \widehat{\mathbf{X}}=\mathcal{Q}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{H}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}),\quad \widehat{\mathbf{W}}=\mathcal{BGR}(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{H}),\quad \mathbf{Y}=\widehat{\mathbf{X}}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\widehat{\mathbf{W}}^{\top} \] \[ \tilde{\mathbf{X}}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{H},\quad s_j=\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_j\rVert_\infty=\max_i|\tilde{x}_{i,j}|,\quad \boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_c) \]

ARQ: rotate, scale each channel by its live max (no calibration), quantize; weights are rotated then BGR-quantized.

Guide

Equation 10 is ARQ in full. The activation is rotated, X tilde equals X H, and each channel's scale s j is its largest absolute value in the current tensor; lambda is the diagonal matrix of those scales. The quantized activation X hat is the rotated activation divided by lambda and then quantized, while the weights are rotated and quantized with BGR. The output multiplies X hat, lambda and W hat transpose. Because the scales come from the live tensor, no calibration set is needed.

—\[ \mathbf{Y}_{t_0}=\mathbf{X}_{t_0}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{t_0}\mathbf{W},\quad \mathbf{Y}_{t_{49}}=\mathbf{X}_{t_{49}}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{t_{49}}\mathbf{W},\quad \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_t=\operatorname{diag}(s_{t_1},\dots,s_{t_c}) \]

From Fig. 2: the channel scales are time-dependent, recomputed at every step.

Guide

This line comes from the middle panel of figure 2 and makes one point: the scale matrix lambda depends on the timestep. The output at the first step uses lambda at t zero, the output at the last step uses lambda at t forty-nine, and each lambda t is a diagonal of per-channel scales computed at that step. It is the equation form of the drifting curve in figure 3, and the reason ARQ recomputes scales online.

(11)\[ B_{t_i}=\begin{cases} b_{\text{low}} & \sum_{t=t_p}^{t_i-1}\mathcal{L}_1(\mathcal{F},t)\lt\delta\\ b_{\text{high}} & \sum_{t=t_p}^{t_i-1}\mathcal{L}_1(\mathcal{F},t)\ge\delta\end{cases},\qquad \mathcal{L}_1(\mathcal{F},t)=\frac{\lVert\mathcal{F}_t-\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\rVert_1}{\lVert\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\rVert_1} \]

δ-GBS: activation bits for step ti; tp = last reset, 𝓕t = model output at step t; blow = 4, bhigh = 8.

Guide

Equation 11 is the delta-GBS rule. For each step t i, add up the relative L1 change of the model output, the size of the output difference between consecutive steps divided by the size of the previous output, over all steps since the last reset t p. If that sum is below the threshold delta, use b low, four bits; if it reaches delta, use b high, eight bits, and reset. F t is the model output at step t. Figure 6 and figure 2 show it in action.

Table 1 is the main result, VBench scores on HunyuanVideo with higher better. Read it in two blocks. At four-bit weights and higher-bit activations, DVD-Quant at W4A6 nearly matches the full-precision model on Aesthetic and Imaging Quality despite using fewer bits than the W4A8 baselines. At W4A4, the baselines break, MinMax scoring zero on Scene and Dynamic, while DVD-Quant keeps Imaging Quality at 61.82 and Aesthetic at 61.96. Quantization and caching stack. Here DVD-Quant is combined with TeaCache, which skips denoising steps whose output barely changes.
