The paper also reports Wan2.1 results and block-wise ARQ kernel details in a supplementary file that is not part of this PDF.

§8Why it matters for this thesis

DVD-Quant vs LTX-2.3 on OpenVINO / NNCF

  • What is data-free here: all three parts. BGR uses only W. ARQ scales come from the live activation. δ-GBS uses a statistic of the model's own output. So no calibration set is needed, which avoids the thesis cost of hours of CPU time per calibration sample.
  • BGR: directly usable, no custom kernel. The result is a standard asymmetric INT4 grid (u4 values + zero-point + scale per output row), the same format OpenVINO decompresses natively for weight-only INT4. It is a data-free replacement for NNCF's data-aware refinements (scale estimation, AWQ, GPTQ): compute Δ*, z* in PyTorch with Alg. 1 (easy to extend from per-row to NNCF-style group size 64/128) and write them into the compressed constants with a small custom script. Cost: offline CPU time only.
  • ARQ needs custom kernels as published. Reported speed-ups use the authors' block-wise W4A4/W4A8 Tensor Core GEMM kernels plus a fast Hadamard transform on an RTX 4090. OpenVINO has no INT4×INT4 GEMM path on Intel CPU or Arc and no fast Walsh-Hadamard op (a dense MatMul by H costs O(d²) per token). The closest built-in feature is OpenVINO's dynamic INT8 activation quantization for compressed-weight MatMuls: online, group-wise scales, i.e. the A8 half of ARQ without the rotation.
  • δ-GBS is cheap but needs two execution variants. It only swaps between two existing kernels (no mixed-precision kernel). In OpenVINO this means two compiled variants of the transformer chosen per step, with extra weight memory unless weights are shared. Its signal (relative L1 change of outputs) is the same kind used by TeaCache-style caching, so one signal could drive both bit switching and step skipping.
  • Scope caveat: tested on HunyuanVideo (plus Wan2.1 in the supplement) at W4A4–W4A8 on an NVIDIA GPU; no audio, no weight-only W4A16 result, no CPU numbers. For the thesis, BGR is the transferable piece; ARQ and δ-GBS are ideas to check against what OpenVINO can run.
Guide

Take BGR into the thesis and treat the rest as ideas to test. BGR produces an ordinary INT4 grid, one scale and zero-point per row, which OpenVINO already decompresses, so it can be computed in PyTorch with Algorithm 1, extend it to NNCF-style groups of 64 or 128, write it into the compressed weights, and compare it with NNCF's data-aware options without spending CPU hours on calibration. ARQ needs INT4 activation kernels and a fast Hadamard op that OpenVINO lacks; its closest built-in match is dynamic INT8 activation quantization. Delta-GBS would need two compiled model variants, but its signal could also drive TeaCache-style step skipping.

Quantizing diffusion models

QVGen: Pushing the Limit of Quantized Video Generative Models

Yushi Huang, Ruihao Gong, Jing Liu, Yifu Ding, Chengtao Lv, Haotong Qin, Jun Zhang · HKUST, Beihang, SenseTime, Monash, NTU, ETH Zürich · ICLR 2026 (arXiv 2505.11497, 2025)

Quantization-aware training (QAT) for video diffusion transformers at 4 and 3 bits for both weights and activations. A theory result says QAT converges better when the gradient norm is small, so each quantized layer gets a temporary low-rank helper Φ that absorbs quantization error; a rank-decay schedule (SVD + fading the smallest components) then shrinks Φ to nothing, leaving a plain W4A4 model.

Precision
W4A4 · W3A3
Models
CogVideoX 2B/5B, Wan 1.3B/14B
W4A4 quality
≈ BF16 (VBench)
Size / speed
~4× smaller · 1.21–1.44×
Training cost
9–11 (small) to ~182 (14B) H100 GPU-days
Inference overhead
none (Φ removed)
Reading guide

QVGen asks whether a video diffusion transformer can be squeezed to four bits, or even three, for both weights and activations without the videos falling apart. Its answer is yes at four bits, through quantization-aware training plus a temporary low-rank helper that absorbs quantization error during training and is then faded out completely, so the shipped model is a plain W four A four network that scores close to BF16 on VBench. The tab moves from a big-picture diagram to the problem, the method and algorithm, every equation including the proofs, every figure, the results tables, and a thesis box. Among the sixteen papers it is the training-based member of the diffusion quantization group, after Q-Diffusion, PTQ4DiT, ViDiT-Q, SVDQuant and DVD-Quant, and just before the SVDQuant with GPTQ study on Wan 2.2. For the thesis it marks the floor: even with expensive training, four bits is the limit.

§0Before reading

Every quantization paper so far in the atlas was post-training quantization: take a finished model and round it, without changing its weights. QVGen instead retrains the quantized model, so three ideas come first: how training differs from post-training quantization, how backpropagation can pass through rounding at all, and what a low-rank matrix is. It is in the atlas as the upper limit: with a lot of GPU training, how low can a video diffusion transformer go?

Terms used in this paper

QAT vs PTQ
Quantization-aware training retrains the weights while rounding is simulated. Post-training quantization only picks scales for a finished model, with a small calibration set.
W4A4, W3A3
Weights and activations both in 4 bits (or 3). QVGen uses per-channel scales for weights and per-token scales for activations, computed on the fly.
Fake quantization
Round a value to the low-bit grid and immediately convert it back to a float. Training sees the rounding error without needing integer kernels.
Straight-through estimator (STE)
A trick for backpropagating through rounding: treat it as the identity inside the clipping range, and give zero gradient to clipped values.
Knowledge distillation
The quantized "student" is trained to copy the full-precision "teacher" model's noise predictions, instead of learning from the raw training target.
Gradient norm
The overall size of the gradient vector at a training step, \(\lVert g_t\rVert\). QVGen argues that keeping it small makes low-bit training converge better.
Regret
A measure from optimisation theory: the total extra loss accumulated during training compared with the best fixed parameters. Lower average regret means closer to the optimum.
SVD, rank
Singular value decomposition splits a matrix into pieces sorted by importance (singular values). The rank is how many pieces are kept.
LoRA
Low-rank adaptation: training only a small low-rank add-on next to frozen weights. EfficientDM, a baseline here, uses it for quantized diffusion models.
LSQ, Q-DM, EfficientDM
Earlier QAT methods (the first for CNNs, the others for image diffusion models) that the paper adapts to video as baselines.
CogVideoX, Wan
Open-source text-to-video diffusion transformers. The paper tests CogVideoX 2B and 1.5-5B, and Wan 1.3B and 14B.
VBench
A video-generation benchmark that scores separate dimensions such as aesthetic quality, motion smoothness, dynamic degree and scene consistency. It has its own tab at the end of the atlas.
H100, A800
NVIDIA data-centre GPUs. Training ran on H100s; speed was measured on an A800, a variant of the A100 made for the Chinese market with reduced interconnect bandwidth.
Guide

These are the words the paper takes for granted. The most important are quantization-aware training versus post-training quantization, the straight-through estimator, knowledge distillation from a full-precision teacher, and the gradient norm, which the paper's theory links to convergence. SVD and rank describe the helper branch. The rest names the baselines, the CogVideoX and Wan models, the VBench benchmark, and the H100 and A800 GPUs used for training and timing.

§2Big picture

Train the low-bit model with a helper branch that keeps gradients calm, then gradually remove the helper so the shipped model is standard uniform W4A4. The helper is low-rank and disappears one half of its rank at a time.

§3The problem

  • PTQ (ViDiT-Q, SVDQuant) produces no usable video at per-channel W4A4; even at W4A6 it lags far behind.
  • Image-DM QAT methods (LSQ, Q-DM, EfficientDM) degrade at W4A4 and break at W3A3 (Dynamic Degree 0.56 for LSQ on CogX-2B).
  • Activations are the bottleneck: W4A16 is fine, W16A4 is pure noise (Fig. B).
  • Just clipping gradients helps only a little (0.5) and hurts when aggressive (0.1), as Tab. E shows. A more principled fix is needed.

§4Method

  1. Quantize: per-channel asymmetric weights and per-token dynamic activations, Eq. (4); STE for gradients, Eq. (5); LSQ-learned weight scales.
  2. Add Φ to every linear layer: Ŷ = Q(W)Q(X) + WΦQ(X), with WΦ = W − Q(W) at start (Eq. 9).
  3. Factorise: SVD of WΦ truncated to rank r=32 → L (n×r), R (r×m) (Eqs. 10–11).
  4. Train with KD against the BF16 teacher (Eq. 6), updating W, s, z, L, R, while γ fades the lowest λr = r/2 components with a cosine u: 1→0 (Eqs. 12–13).
  5. Truncate to rank (1−λ)r, re-SVD, repeat: 32→16→8→4→2 (Eq. 14).
  6. Final phase: once r ≤ 1/λ, fade everything left (γ=[u]); drop Φ. Ship a plain W4A4/W3A3 model.
Guide

The recipe has two halves. First, set up four-bit fake quantization and attach a helper to every linear layer that starts out equal to the weight's rounding error, compressed by SVD into two thin rank-32 matrices. Second, train by distillation from the BF16 teacher while repeatedly fading the weakest half of the helper's components, cutting them off, and re-factorising: rank 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, then zero. What remains is a plain low-bit model.

Algorithm 1 Procedure of QVGen framework FUNC QVGEN(D, eps_theta, it_per_decay_phase, r, lambda, b) Require: D - training dataset eps_theta(.) - full-precision DiT model it_per_decay_phase - training iterations per decay phase r - initial rank of the auxiliary module lambda - shrinking ratio b - quantization bit-width // Preprocess 1: standard uniform b-bit quantization of eps_theta -> eps_hat (Eq. 4) 2: generate all W_Phi for eps_hat (Eq. 9) // Start QAT 3: while r > 1/lambda do 4: decompose all W_Phi to {L, R} with rank r (Eq. 11) 5: generate gamma (Eq. 13) (u in gamma decays 1 -> 0 over the next it_per_decay_phase iterations) 6: for it in 0 .. it_per_decay_phase do 7: get batch (x0, C) from D 8: eps ~ N(0, I) 9: tau ~ Uniform([1, ..., N]) 10: generate x_tau (Eq. 1) 11: compute loss L (Eq. 6; Eq. 12 used in eps_hat) 12: update all W, s, z and {L, R} by back-prop (STE, Eq. 5) 13: end for 14: truncate {L, R} -> {L', R'}, regenerate W_Phi (Eq. 14) 15: r = (1 - lambda) r 16: end while 17: gamma = [u]_(n x r) (u decays 1 -> 0 over it_per_decay_phase iterations) 18: train eps_hat for it_per_decay_phase iterations (lines 6-13) 19: shrink all W_Phi to empty set (gamma = [0] at the end, so W_Phi can be removed) 20: return eps_hat
Guide

The algorithm is one outer loop wrapped around ordinary training. First, the model is quantized and each helper starts as the quantization error. Each pass of the outer loop factorises the helpers at the current rank, builds the mask gamma, runs a fixed number of distillation steps while the weakest half fades out, then truncates and halves the rank. When the rank is tiny, a last phase fades everything, so the returned model has no helper left.

Setup: 16K captioned OpenVidHQ clips, AdamW (wd 1e-4), cosine LR (3e-5 for ≤2B), 8 epochs on 8×H100 (16 epochs on 16–32×H100 for 5B/14B), equal iterations per decay phase. Attention stays in full-precision flash-attention; only linear layers are quantized.

§5Every equation

(1)\[ \mathbf{x}_\tau = \alpha_\tau \mathbf{x}_0 + \sigma_\tau \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \]

Forward diffusion: clean latent video \(\mathbf{x}_0\in\mathbb{R}^{f\times h\times w\times c}\) mixed with Gaussian noise; \(\alpha_\tau,\sigma_\tau\) set the SNR at timestep \(\tau\in[1,\dots,N]\).

Guide

This is the forward noising step of diffusion. x tau, the noisy latent video at timestep tau, equals alpha tau times the clean latent x zero plus sigma tau times Gaussian noise epsilon. Alpha and sigma set how much signal versus noise remains at that step. QVGen uses it in the training loop to create noisy inputs that both the teacher and the quantized student must denoise.

(2)\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_0,\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\mathcal{C},\tau}\big[\lVert \boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_\tau,\mathcal{C},\tau)\rVert_F^2\big] \]

Standard noise-prediction training loss; \(\mathcal{C}\) = text/image condition. (v-prediction is the common alternative.)

Guide

This is the standard training loss for a diffusion model. The network epsilon theta sees the noisy video, the text condition C and the timestep tau, and tries to predict the noise that was added; the loss is the expected squared difference. QVGen does not train with this directly. It replaces the true noise with the teacher's prediction in equation 6, a distillation version of the same idea.

(3)\[ \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{W})\,\mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{X}) \]

Full-precision vs. quantized linear layer; \(\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\), \(\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}\) (n out-channels, m token dim, k tokens).

Guide

Here is the basic object being compressed: one linear layer. In full precision the output Y is the weight matrix W times the input X. In the quantized version, Y hat is the quantized weight times the quantized input, both at b bits. The gap between Y and Y hat is the quantization error, and every later equation is about keeping that gap from spoiling training and the final video.

(4)\[ \mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{X}) = \Big(\operatorname{clip}\big(\big\lfloor \tfrac{\mathbf{X}}{s}\big\rceil + z,\,0,\,2^b-1\big) - z\Big)\times s,\quad s=\frac{\max(\mathbf{X})-\min(\mathbf{X})}{2^b-1},\quad z=-\Big\lfloor \frac{\min(\mathbf{X})}{s}\Big\rceil \]

Asymmetric uniform (min–max) fake-quantizer with scale \(s\) and zero-point \(z\) — exactly the INT-asym format OpenVINO/NNCF use.

Guide

This is the quantizer itself: asymmetric uniform min-max quantization. The step size s is the value range divided by two to the b minus one levels, and the zero-point z shifts the grid so the minimum maps to zero. Each value is divided by s, rounded, shifted by z, clipped to the allowed integer range, then mapped back. It is exactly the INT asymmetric format OpenVINO and NNCF use, so nothing exotic is needed on the thesis side.

(5)\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{X})}{\partial \mathbf{X}} = \mathbb{I}_{\,0\le \lfloor \mathbf{X}/s\rceil + z \le 2^b-1} \]

Straight-through estimator: gradient passes through rounding as 1 inside the clipping range, 0 outside.

Guide

Rounding has zero gradient almost everywhere, so training through it needs a trick: the straight-through estimator. The derivative of the quantizer is simply taken as one when the scaled value falls inside the clipping range and zero when it is clipped. This lets gradients reach the weights and the learned scales during quantization-aware training, and the gradient norms the paper worries about are measured through this path.

(6)\[ \mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_0,\mathcal{C},\tau}\big[\lVert \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_\tau,\mathcal{C},\tau) - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_\tau,\mathcal{C},\tau)\rVert_F^2\big] \]

Knowledge-distillation QAT loss: quantized student \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_\theta\) matches the BF16 teacher's output.

Guide

This is the loss QVGen actually trains with, a knowledge distillation loss. The quantized student, epsilon hat, and the full-precision teacher, epsilon theta, see the same noisy video, condition and timestep, and the loss is the squared difference of their outputs. The student therefore learns to copy the BF16 model rather than fit raw data, which is the usual choice in diffusion quantization-aware training such as Q-DM and EfficientDM.

(7)\[ R(T) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} f_t(\theta_t) - f_t(\theta^*) \]

Regret over \(T\) iterations; \(\theta^*=\arg\min_{\theta\in\mathbb{S}^d}\sum_t f_t(\theta)\) in a convex compact set.

Guide

Regret is the yardstick for the convergence theory. R of T sums, over T training iterations, how much worse the loss at the current parameters theta t is than the loss at the best fixed parameters theta star. If average regret, R of T divided by T, goes to zero, training is converging. Theorem 3.1 bounds exactly this quantity.

(8)\[ \theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta_t\, \mathbf{g}_t \]

Gradient-descent update with learning rate \(\eta_t\) and gradient \(\mathbf{g}_t\).

Guide

This is plain gradient descent. The next parameters theta t plus one equal the current parameters minus the learning rate eta t times the gradient g t. It is the update rule assumed in the convergence analysis, and it is why the size of g t appears in the bound that follows.

(Thm 3.1)\[ \frac{R(T)}{T} \le \frac{d D_\infty^2}{2T\eta_T^m} + \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\eta_t^M}{2}\lVert \mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 \]

If \(f_t\) convex and \(\lVert\theta_i-\theta_j\rVert_\infty\le D_\infty\): for large \(T\) the first term vanishes, so the average squared gradient norm controls convergence → reduce \(\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2\). (\(\eta^M_t,\eta^m_t\) = max/min learning rates.)

Guide

Theorem 3.1 is the paper's key theoretical motivation. Average regret is at most two terms: the first shrinks as training length T grows, and the second is the average over iterations of the learning rate times the squared gradient norm. So after long training, convergence is governed by how large the gradients are. The takeaway is simple: shrink the gradient norm and quantization-aware training converges better, which the helper phi is designed to do.

(9)\[ \hat{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{W})\mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{X}) + \Phi(\mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{X})),\qquad \Phi(\mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{X}))=\mathbf{W}_\Phi\,\mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{X}) \]

Auxiliary module: an extra FP branch; \(\mathbf{W}_\Phi\) initialised to the weight quantization error \(\mathbf{W}-\mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{W})\).

Guide

This introduces the helper. The quantized layer's output becomes the usual quantized weight times quantized input, plus phi applied to the quantized input, where phi is just an extra full-precision weight W phi times that input. W phi starts as the weight's rounding error, W minus its quantized version, so at the start the layer behaves almost like full precision. That softer start is what lowers the gradient norm.

(10)\[ \mathbf{W}_\Phi = \sum_{s=1}^{d} \sigma_s\, \mathbf{u}_s \mathbf{v}_s^{\top} \]

SVD of the helper weight; \(d=\min\{n,m\}\), \(\sigma_1\ge\dots\ge\sigma_d\). Most \(\sigma_s\) are tiny and get tinier during QAT (Fig. 4).

Guide

This is the singular value decomposition of the helper weight. W phi is written as a sum of d rank-one pieces, each a singular value sigma s times an outer product of vectors u s and v s, sorted from largest to smallest sigma. Figure 4 shows most sigmas are tiny and get tinier during training. That observation is what makes it safe to keep only the top few and later discard them.

(11)\[ \Phi(\mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{X})) = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{R}\,\mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{X}),\quad \mathbf{L}=[\sqrt{\sigma_1}\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\sqrt{\sigma_r}\mathbf{u}_r]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r},\ \mathbf{R}=[\sqrt{\sigma_1}\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\sqrt{\sigma_r}\mathbf{v}_r]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times m} \]

Rank-\(r\) factorisation (\(r\ll d\), \(r=32\) used); column/row \(s\) carries the \(s\)-th largest contribution.

Guide

The helper is stored in factorised form: phi equals L times R times the quantized input. L collects the top r left singular vectors and R the top r right ones, each scaled by the square root of its singular value. With r equal to 32, far below the full dimension, the helper is cheap. Column s of L carries the s-th strongest direction, which lets the next equations fade the weakest columns first.

(12)\[ \hat{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{W})\mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{X}) + (\boldsymbol{\gamma}\odot\mathbf{L})\,\mathbf{R}\,\mathcal{Q}_b(\mathbf{X}) \]

Training-time forward with the rank-based regularizer \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\) masking columns of \(\mathbf{L}\).

Guide

This is the training-time forward pass with the rank regularizer. It is the same layer as before, except L is multiplied element by element by the mask gamma before being combined with R. Gamma lets training gradually switch off selected columns of L, so the helper's contribution shrinks smoothly instead of vanishing abruptly. Equation 13 defines what gamma looks like.

(13)\[ \boldsymbol{\gamma} = \operatorname{concat}\big([1]_{n\times(1-\lambda)r},\ [u]_{n\times\lambda r}\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} \]

Keep the top \((1-\lambda)r\) components; the lowest \(\lambda r\) are multiplied by \(u\), cosine-annealed 1 → 0. \(\lambda=\tfrac12\).

Guide

Gamma is built from two blocks. The first one minus lambda times r columns are all ones, keeping the strongest components untouched. The last lambda times r columns are set to u, a number annealed from one to zero with a cosine schedule. With lambda equal to one half, the weakest half of the helper fades out during each phase while the model learns to compensate.

(14)\[ \begin{cases}\mathbf{L}'=\mathbf{L}[:,\,:(1-\lambda)r]\\ \mathbf{R}'=\mathbf{R}[:(1-\lambda)r,\,:]\end{cases}\ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf{W}_\Phi=\mathbf{L}'\mathbf{R}' \]

When \(u\) hits 0, truncate: rank drops \(r\to(1-\lambda)r\). Repeat (re-SVD, decay, truncate) until \(r=0\), i.e. \(\Phi=\varnothing\).

Guide

Once u reaches zero, the faded columns are removed for real. L prime keeps only the first one minus lambda times r columns of L, and R prime the matching rows of R, and their product becomes the new, smaller helper weight. The rank halves, from 32 to 16 and so on. The loop then re-factorises and repeats until the rank is zero and phi no longer exists.

(A)\[ \theta_{t+1,p} = \theta_{t,p} - \eta_{t,p}\, g_{t,p} \]

Proof of Thm 3.1 — per-entry update of parameter \(p\).

Guide

The appendix proof of Theorem 3.1 starts here. This is gradient descent written for one single entry p of the parameter vector, with its own learning rate eta t p and gradient g t p. Working entry by entry lets the proof handle adaptive, per-parameter learning rates like those in AdamW.

(B)\[ (\theta_{t+1,p}-\theta_p^*)^2 = (\theta_{t,p}-\eta_{t,p}g_{t,p}-\theta_p^*)^2 = (\theta_{t,p}-\theta_p^*)^2 - 2(\theta_{t,p}-\theta_p^*)\eta_{t,p}g_{t,p} + \eta_{t,p}^2 g_{t,p}^2 \]

Expand the squared distance to the optimum.

Guide

The proof now measures how far one parameter entry is from its optimum. Squaring the distance after one update and expanding gives three parts: the old squared distance, minus a cross term of two times distance times learning rate times gradient, plus the learning rate squared times the gradient squared. That last term is where the gradient norm enters the bound.

(C)\[ g_{t,p}(\theta_{t,p}-\theta_p^*) = \frac{1}{2\eta_{t,p}}\big[(\theta_{t,p}-\theta_p^*)^2-(\theta_{t+1,p}-\theta_p^*)^2\big] + \frac{\eta_{t,p}}{2}g_{t,p}^2 \]

Rearranged and divided by \(2\eta_{t,p}\).

Guide

Rearranging the previous expansion isolates the gradient times the distance to the optimum. It equals the drop in squared distance over one step, divided by two times the learning rate, plus half the learning rate times the gradient squared. The first part will telescope across iterations; the second is the gradient-norm penalty that survives into Theorem 3.1.

(D)\[ f_t(\theta_t) - f_t(\theta^*) \le \mathbf{g}_t^{\top}(\theta_t-\theta^*) \]

Convexity (Assumption B.1).

Guide

This is where convexity is used. For a convex loss, the gap between the current loss and the optimal loss is at most the gradient dotted with the distance to the optimum. It links regret to the expression rearranged in the previous step. It is an idealising assumption: real diffusion training is not convex, which is why Appendix C repeats the argument without it.

(E)\[ \begin{aligned}R(T) &\le \sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{p=1}^{d}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t,p}}\big[(\theta_{t,p}-\theta_p^*)^2-(\theta_{t+1,p}-\theta_p^*)^2\big] + \sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{p=1}^{d}\frac{\eta_{t,p}}{2}g_{t,p}^2\\ &= \sum_{p=1}^{d}\Big[\frac{1}{2\eta_{1,p}}(\theta_{1,p}-\theta_p^*)^2-\frac{1}{2\eta_{T,p}}(\theta_{T+1,p}-\theta_p^*)^2\Big] + \sum_{t=2}^{T}\sum_{p=1}^{d}\Big(\frac{1}{2\eta_{t,p}}-\frac{1}{2\eta_{t-1,p}}\Big)(\theta_{t,p}-\theta_p^*)^2 + \sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{p=1}^{d}\frac{\eta_{t,p}}{2}g_{t,p}^2\end{aligned} \]

Sum over dimensions and iterations; telescope.

Guide

Summing over all parameter entries and all iterations bounds the total regret. The distance terms telescope, meaning consecutive terms cancel, leaving the starting distance, a correction for changing learning rates, and the accumulated sum of learning rate times gradient squared. The gradient sum is untouched by the telescoping, which is why it ends up dominating.

(F)\[ R(T) \le \sum_{p=1}^{d}\frac{D_\infty^2}{2\eta_{1,p}} + \sum_{t=2}^{T}\sum_{p=1}^{d}\Big(\frac{1}{2\eta_{t,p}}-\frac{1}{2\eta_{t-1,p}}\Big)D_\infty^2 + \sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{p=1}^{d}\frac{\eta_{t,p}}{2}g_{t,p}^2 \]

Bounded domain (Assumption B.2).

Guide

Assuming parameters stay in a bounded region, every distance to the optimum is replaced by the largest possible distance, D infinity. Now the first two terms depend only on the learning rates and the problem size, while the last term is still the sum of learning rate times squared gradient. That split is exactly the shape of Theorem 3.1.

(G)\[ R(T) \le \frac{dD_\infty^2}{2\eta_T^m} + \sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\eta_t^M}{2}\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 \]

Replace per-entry rates by their min/max.

Guide

To tidy up, every per-entry learning rate is replaced by the smallest rate at the end, eta T m, in the first term, and by the largest rate at each step, eta t M, in the gradient term. The result is a compact bound: a constant depending on dimension d and distance D, plus the sum of the maximum learning rate times the squared gradient norm.

(H)\[ \frac{R(T)}{T} \le \frac{dD_\infty^2}{2T\eta_T^m} + \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\eta_t^M}{2}\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 \]

Average regret = Theorem 3.1 / B.3.

Guide

Dividing by T gives average regret and completes the proof; this line is Theorem 3.1 itself. The first term fades like one over T, so for long training the average squared gradient norm is what limits convergence. This is the formal reason QVGen adds the helper phi: it lowers the gradient norm, as Figure 3 then confirms empirically.

(I)\[ \theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta_t\mathbf{g}_t,\qquad \mathbf{g}_t := \nabla F(\theta_t) \]

Non-convex analysis (App. C): fixed objective \(F\).

Guide

Appendix C redoes the analysis without assuming convexity. Here the objective is a single fixed function F, and the update is ordinary gradient descent, with g t defined as the gradient of F at the current parameters. This setting is closer to real deep-network training and checks that the gradient-norm argument does not depend on the convexity idealisation.

(J)\[ \lVert\nabla F(\theta)-\nabla F(\theta')\rVert_2 \le L\lVert\theta-\theta'\rVert_2 \]

Assumption C.1: \(L\)-smoothness (here \(L\) is a constant, not the low-rank matrix).

Guide

This is the L-smoothness assumption. The gradient cannot change faster than a constant L times the distance between two parameter points. Careful with the letter: this L is a smoothness constant, not the low-rank matrix L from the method. Smoothness is the standard condition that makes a small gradient step reliably reduce the loss.

(K)\[ F(\theta') \le F(\theta) + \nabla F(\theta)^{\top}(\theta'-\theta) + \frac{L}{2}\lVert\theta'-\theta\rVert_2^2 \]

Equivalent descent inequality.

Guide

This descent inequality is an equivalent form of smoothness. The loss at a new point is at most the loss at the old point, plus the gradient dotted with the step, plus L over two times the squared step length. It upper-bounds the loss with a simple bowl-shaped curve, which the proof uses to show every gradient step makes progress.

(L)\[ 0 \lt \eta^m \le \eta_t \le \eta^M \le \frac{1}{L}\quad\forall t \]

Assumption C.2: bounded learning rates.

Guide

This assumption keeps learning rates in a safe range. Every learning rate eta t lies between a positive minimum eta m and a maximum eta M, and the maximum is at most one over the smoothness constant L. Rates that are too large could overshoot, so this cap guarantees each gradient step actually lowers the loss.

(M)\[ \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 \le \frac{2\big(F(\theta_1)-F^\star\big)}{T\eta^m} \]

Theorem C.4 (with \(F\ge F^\star\), Assumption C.3): average squared gradient norm is \(O(1/T)\).

Guide

Theorem C.4 is the non-convex counterpart of Theorem 3.1. The average squared gradient norm over T steps is at most two times the gap between the starting loss and the best possible loss, divided by T times the minimum learning rate. So it falls like one over T. The paper reads it the same way: smaller gradient norms mean a tighter bound after a finite number of steps.

(N)\[ \min_{1\le t\le T}\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 \le \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 \xrightarrow{T\to\infty} 0 \]

Convergence to a first-order stationary point.

Guide

The smallest squared gradient norm seen during training is no larger than the average, and the average goes to zero as training gets longer. So training reaches a first-order stationary point, a place where the gradient vanishes. This is the standard convergence guarantee for non-convex optimisation, restated here to support the paper's gradient-norm focus.

(O)\[ F(\theta_{t+1}) \le F(\theta_t) + \nabla F(\theta_t)^{\top}(\theta_{t+1}-\theta_t) + \frac{L}{2}\lVert\theta_{t+1}-\theta_t\rVert_2^2 = F(\theta_t) - \eta_t\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 + \frac{L}{2}\eta_t^2\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 = F(\theta_t) - \eta_t\Big(1-\frac{L\eta_t}{2}\Big)\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 \]

Plug the update into the descent inequality.

Guide

The proof of Theorem C.4 begins by plugging the gradient descent step into the descent inequality. After simplifying, the new loss is at most the old loss minus eta t times one minus L eta t over two, times the squared gradient norm. In words, each step lowers the loss by an amount proportional to the squared gradient, as long as the learning rate is not too large.

(P)\[ F(\theta_{t+1}) \le F(\theta_t) - \frac{\eta_t}{2}\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 \]

Since \(\eta_t\le 1/L\Rightarrow 1-L\eta_t/2\ge 1/2\).

Guide

Because the learning rate is capped at one over L, the factor one minus L eta over two is at least one half. So each step lowers the loss by at least half the learning rate times the squared gradient norm. It is a clean per-step guarantee of progress that the next line adds up over all of training.

(Q)\[ \sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\eta_t}{2}\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 \le F(\theta_1) - F^\star \]

Telescoping sum with \(F(\theta_{T+1})\ge F^\star\).

Guide

Summing the per-step decrease over all T steps makes the intermediate losses cancel, a telescoping sum. The total of half the learning rate times squared gradient norm is at most the starting loss minus the lowest achievable loss, F star. The loss cannot drop forever, so the gradients cannot stay large forever.

(R)\[ \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 \le \frac{2\big(F(\theta_1)-F^\star\big)}{T\eta^m} \]

Using \(\eta_t\ge\eta^m\) — proves (M).

Guide

Replacing each learning rate by its minimum and dividing by T turns the previous sum into an average. The average squared gradient norm is at most two times the loss gap divided by T times the minimum learning rate. This line proves Theorem C.4, the statement shown earlier as equation M.

(S)\[ \min_{1\le t\le T}\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 \le \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert_2^2 \le \frac{2\big(F(\theta_1)-F^\star\big)}{T\eta^m} \xrightarrow{T\to\infty} 0 \]

Proves (N). Remark C.5: lowering \(\lVert\mathbf{g}_t\rVert\) tightens the finite-\(T\) bound in both settings.

Guide

This closes the non-convex proof. The minimum squared gradient norm is bounded by the average, which is bounded by a quantity that shrinks like one over T, so it tends to zero. Remark C.5 draws the practical link: in both the convex and non-convex settings, lowering the gradient norm tightens the finite-time bound, which justifies the helper phi.

(T)\[ \mathbf{W}_\Phi = \mathcal{Q}_4(\mathbf{W}_\Phi) + \mathcal{Q}_4(\mathbf{E}_1) + \mathcal{Q}_4(\mathbf{E}_2) + \mathcal{Q}_4(\mathbf{E}_3) \]

“Res. Q.” baseline decay (App. F): \(\mathbf{E}_1=\mathbf{W}_\Phi-\mathcal{Q}_4(\mathbf{W}_\Phi)\), \(\mathbf{E}_{i+1}=\mathbf{E}_i-\mathcal{Q}_4(\mathbf{E}_i)\); terms removed one per phase.

Guide

This is one of the alternative ways to remove the helper that the paper compares against, called residual quantization. W phi is written as a four-bit copy of itself plus four-bit copies of successive leftover errors E one, E two and E three, and one term is dropped per phase. Table N shows it scores below rank decay and costs about 2.6 times the GPU time.

(U)\[ \text{TOPS} = \frac{2MNK}{t_{\text{INT4GEMM}}} \div 10^{12} \]

Effective INT4 GEMM throughput for an \([M,K]\times[K,N]\) product (App. N).

Guide

This defines the throughput figure in Table R. For a matrix product of sizes M by K and K by N, the number of operations is two times M times N times K; dividing by the measured INT4 GEMM time and by ten to the twelfth gives tera-operations per second. It shows how close the kernel gets to hardware peak, separate from quantize and dequantize overhead.

(V)\[ \rho \approx \frac{1}{G + (1-G)(1-r)} \]

Amdahl-style projected speed-up if fusion removes a fraction \(r\) of non-GEMM (quant/dequant) time; \(G\) = GEMM time fraction. \(r=0.6\Rightarrow 1.18\text{–}1.38\times\); \(r\approx0.8\Rightarrow 1.25\text{–}1.57\times\).

Guide

This Amdahl-style formula projects speed-up if the quantize and dequantize steps were fused into the matrix multiply. G is the fraction of time spent in the GEMM, and r is the fraction of the remaining non-GEMM time that fusion removes. With r at 0.6 the paper projects about 1.18 to 1.38 times, and with r near 0.8 about 1.25 to 1.57 times. Kernel engineering, not only bit width, sets the real speed-up.

This table compares ways of removing the helper. Linear simply scales all of it down, sparse variants prune entries, with Wanda and MaskLLM as smarter pruning criteria, and residual quantization peels off quantized layers of it. Rank decay wins on every column, 23.01 overall versus at most 22.57 for the others, while the pruning methods also need 1.8 to 2.1 times the training time. Removing whole weak singular directions is both better and cheaper.

An obvious alternative to the helper is simply clipping gradients to keep them small. This table tests it on Wan 1.3B at four bits, where a threshold of 1.0 is the Q-DM baseline. Clipping at 0.5 changes almost nothing, and 0.1 makes things worse. So artificially capping gradients is no substitute; the gradient norm has to come down because the model is easier to fit, which is what phi achieves.

This ablation asks which helper components should be faded. Fading the smallest singular directions, the paper's choice, gives 23.01 overall consistency. Fading random directions, averaged over three runs, gives about 21.9, and fading the largest directions gives 22.24. The ordering from the SVD matters: dropping the weakest directions first lets the model absorb their loss gently.

Self-attention is the single biggest cost in the block, and quantizing linear layers does nothing for it. That is why the paper pairs quantization with sparse attention.

App. O: with SVG sparse attention (self-attn 31.48 → 18.23 ms, 1.73×) and fused “other” ops (14.64 → 2.62 ms, 5.59×), linear layers become 41.38% of block time; W4A4 speeds them up 2.52× (15.14 → 5.991 ms).

§8Why it matters for this thesis

LTX-2.3 on OpenVINO / NNCF

  • Out of scope, but a lower bound. QVGen is full QAT (≈11 H100 GPU-days for 1.3B, ~182 for Wan 14B, with 16K training videos). A bachelor thesis cannot do this for LTX-2.3. What it does give is a reference point: even with training, W4A4 is the limit, and W3A3 fails on large models (Tab. 2, Figs. E–F). PTQ on CPU/Arc should not aim below 4-bit weights.
  • Weight-only is the safe route. Fig. B shows W4A16 stays close to BF16 while W16A4 destroys the video. This supports NNCF compress_weights (INT8 / INT4_ASYM, group-wise) with activations kept in FP16/BF16, or at most INT8.
  • Same number format as OpenVINO. Eq. (4) is plain asymmetric uniform min-max quantization with scale and zero-point, so no custom ops are needed. The low-rank error-compensation idea (WΦ = W − Q(W), rank 32) is close to NNCF’s data-aware INT4 options (e.g. lora_correction, AWQ/scale estimation). These need a small calibration set of LTX prompts or latents.
  • Keep speed-up expectations realistic. Linear layers are only 24.5% of Wan-block time and attention is 51.8% (Tab. S). Even a real W4A4 kernel gives only 1.21–1.44× end-to-end. On Intel, weight-only INT4 mainly cuts memory and bandwidth. Wall-clock gains will need caching or sparse attention as well (Fig. 6c).
  • Reusable evaluation protocol. The paper uses 8 VBench dimensions plus PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS against BF16 outputs from the same seed (Tab. G). This is cheap to replicate on a small prompt set to compare int8, int4 and mixed-precision LTX variants.
Guide

Treat QVGen as a boundary, not a recipe. Full training costs 11 to 182 GPU-days, so for LTX-2.3 use post-training compression and do not aim below four-bit weights. Use NNCF weight-only compression, INT8 or group-wise INT4 asymmetric, with activations in FP16 or at most INT8, since Figure B shows four-bit activations destroy video. Try data-aware options like LoRA correction or AWQ with a small calibration set, expect memory savings more than speed, and reuse its VBench plus PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS protocol.

Quantizing diffusion models

Timestep-Aware SVDQuant-GPTQ for W4A4 Quantization of Wan2.2-I2V

Junhao Wu, Dezhong Yao, Hai Jin · Huazhong University of Science and Technology · arXiv:2605.27003, May 2026

This paper quantizes a 14B-per-expert video diffusion transformer (Wan2.2 image-to-video) to 4-bit weights and 4-bit activations. It combines three known tools: an SVDQuant low-rank branch that soaks up outliers, GPTQ rounding for the 4-bit residual weights, and a per-layer activation clipping ratio that is looked up by timestep bin, searched separately for each of the two MoE experts. The result is 59% less memory for a 0.9% drop in VBench score, but no speed-up, because the H100 had no native FP4 kernel for it.

Reading guide

Can a fourteen billion parameter per expert video diffusion transformer, Wan 2.2 image to video, run with four bit weights and four bit activations, called W four A four, without retraining? The answer is yes for quality and memory: combining an SVDQuant low-rank branch, GPTQ rounding and a clip ratio looked up per timestep bin cuts peak memory by 59 percent for a VBench drop of under one percent, but it runs 1.8 times slower because the H100 had no fused FP4 kernel. The tab moves from the big picture, to the three problems of outliers, timestep drift and two experts, then the method, every equation, every figure, the results tables and a thesis box. Among the sixteen papers it is the last of the diffusion quantization group, after QVGen, stitching GPTQ, SVDQuant and timestep-aware calibration together on a large video model, which makes it the closest analogue to the LTX-2.3 project.

§0Before reading

This paper takes a very large image-to-video model whose denoiser is split into two experts, and squeezes both weights and activations to four bits in the MXFP4 format. Following it takes three ideas: how the two experts share the denoising steps, what a four-bit block format looks like, and why saving memory does not automatically save time. It is in the atlas because it is the closest published analogue to the LTX-2.3 project: a big video transformer, compressed after training, with timestep-aware calibration.

Terms used in this paper

Image-to-video (I2V)
Generating a video that starts from a given image, usually together with a text prompt, instead of from text alone.
Wan2.2-I2V-A14B
An open-source image-to-video model from Alibaba. "A14B" means about 14 billion parameters are active at each step.
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)
A model with several sub-networks ("experts") where only one or a few run for a given input. In Wan2.2 the expert is chosen by the denoising step.
High-noise / low-noise expert
Wan2.2's two denoisers: the first handles the early, very noisy steps, the second the late steps. The paper finds the low-noise expert more fragile under quantization.
Timestep bin
A small group of consecutive denoising steps treated alike. The paper stores one activation scale per layer and bin, instead of one for all 40 steps.
W4A4
Weights and activations both in 4 bits. Much harder than weight-only W4A16, because activations change with every input and step.
MXFP4
A "microscaling" 4-bit floating-point format: blocks of 32 values share one power-of-two scale, and each value has only 16 possible codes.
BF16
16-bit "brain float", the usual full-precision format for large models and the reference every quantized result is compared against.
Clipping ratio \(\rho\)
A factor below 1 that shrinks the activation range before quantizing. Rare large values get cut off, and the common values get finer steps.
Low-rank branch (SVDQuant)
A thin 16-bit matrix pair, found with the SVD, that keeps the hardest part of each weight in high precision while the rest goes to 4 bits.
GPTQ
A weight-rounding method that uses a little calibration data to round weights so the layer's output error stays small, instead of simple round-to-nearest (RTN).
Pseudo-quantization
Storing low-bit numbers but converting them back to 16-bit before the math. It saves memory and shows the quality effect, but gives no speed-up.
NVIDIA H100
A data-centre GPU (Hopper generation) whose Tensor Cores support FP16, BF16, FP8 and INT8 but not FP4, so the paper could not run 4-bit math natively.
OpenS2V-Eval and VBench
OpenS2V-Eval is the test set here: 180 image-to-video cases. VBench is the scoring protocol, with scores such as Imaging Quality, Subject Consistency and Motion Smoothness.
Guide

These fourteen terms are the vocabulary the paper takes for granted. The most important are the mixture of experts, meaning Wan two point two's two denoisers; the timestep bin, a group of steps that shares one activation scale; MXFP4, the four bit block format; and pseudo-quantization, which saves memory but not time. Keep this list open while reading the method and results sections of the tab.

§1Big picture

SVDQuant deals with outliers, GPTQ deals with the rounding of the residual weights, and the timestep lookup table deals with activation ranges that drift over time. Because Wan2.2 swaps from a high-noise expert to a low-noise expert partway through sampling, the search runs once per expert.

§2The problem

  • At 4-bit, activations are the weak link. They depend on the input, so their outliers cannot be fixed offline the way weight outliers can.
  • Wan2.2 activations are non-stationary across the 40 steps (Fig. 1), so a single scale either over-clips early steps or blurs late ones.
  • The MoE split of Wan2.2 (a high-noise expert, then a low-noise expert) makes the two experts' statistics differ.
  • Plain RTN W4A4 drops Imaging Quality from 0.705 to 0.389 (Table I).

§3Method

  1. Smooth each linear layer: divide activation channels by \(D_l\) and multiply the weight by it (Eq. 5). This moves outlier magnitude onto the static weight.
  2. SVD split the smoothed weight into a low-rank part \(L_1^lL_2^l\), kept in high precision, plus a residual \(R_l\) (Eq. 6).
  3. GPTQ the residual to 4-bit, using second-order (Hessian) information and calibration activations instead of round-to-nearest. This gives \(\hat R_l^{\text{GPTQ}}\) (Eq. 7).
  4. Bin the trajectory: split the denoising steps into a few timestep bins \(B_k\), separately for each expert (e.g. high_early, high_mid, boundary_pre / low_mid, low_late, boundary_post in Fig. 3).
  5. Search ρ for every (layer, bin): threshold \(\alpha=\rho\,m_{l,k}\) (Eq. 8), scale \(s=\alpha/q_{\max}\) (Eq. 9). Keep the ρ with the smallest output MSE against BF16 on calibration samples (Eq. 10).
  6. Infer: map the current \(t\) to its bin, fetch \(s^A_{l,k}\) and run Eq. 11. No online search is needed.
Guide

The method runs in two phases. Offline, each layer is first smoothed so activation outliers move into the weight, then the weight is split into a high precision low-rank part and a residual, and that residual is rounded to four bits with GPTQ instead of plain rounding. Next the denoising trajectory is cut into a few bins per expert, and for every layer and bin a clip ratio is chosen by comparing outputs against BF16. At inference the current step simply picks its bin and fetches the stored scale.

Procedure (transcribed from §III; the paper has no Algorithm box) for expert in {high_noise, low_noise}: for each quantized linear layer l in expert: X̂l, Ŵl = smooth(Xl, Wl, Dl) # Eq. 5 L1, L2, Rl = SVD_lowrank(Ŵl) # Eq. 6, low-rank kept 16-bit R̂l = GPTQ_4bit(Rl, calib activations X̂l) # Eq. 7 for each timestep bin Bk of this expert: m[l,k] = reference |activation| on calib t ∈ Bk ρ*[l,k] = argmin_{ρ∈R} E_t ||Yl(t) − Ŷl(t;ρ)||² # Eq. 8–10 s[l,k] = ρ*[l,k]·m[l,k] / q_max inference step t: k = bin(t); Ŷl = X̂l·L1·L2 + Q_A(X̂l; s[l,k])·R̂l # Eq. 11
Guide

The procedure is a loop over the two experts, then over their layers. For each layer the weight work happens once: smooth, split by SVD, and round the residual with GPTQ. Only then does the inner loop over timestep bins run, measuring a reference activation magnitude and picking the best clip ratio, which becomes a stored scale. The final line is inference, where the bin lookup and equation eleven are all that remain. This listing is transcribed from the text, since the paper gives no algorithm box.

§4Every equation

(1)\[ Y = XW,\qquad X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C_{\text{in}}},\; W\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{\text{in}}\times C_{\text{out}}} \]

Full-precision linear layer: \(N\) tokens, \(C_{\text{in}}\)/\(C_{\text{out}}\) channels (q, k, v, o, gate, FFN …).

Guide

The starting point is an ordinary linear layer. Y equals X times W, where X holds N tokens with C in input channels, and W maps those to C out output channels. Every projection in the transformer, the query, key, value and output projections and the feed-forward layers, has this form, so it is the object all later equations quantize.

(2)\[ \hat{Y} = Q_A(X)\,Q_W(W) \]

W4A4: both activation quantizer \(Q_A\) and weight quantizer \(Q_W\) are 4-bit; PTQ must keep \(\hat Y\approx Y\) on calibration data without retraining.

Guide

Quantized inference replaces both factors with four bit versions. Y hat is Q A of X times Q W of W, where Q A is the activation quantizer and Q W the weight quantizer. The goal of post-training quantization is to keep Y hat close to Y on calibration data without any retraining. The rest of the method is about making these two quantizers lose as little as possible.

(3)\[ Q(z;s,z_0) = s\cdot\left(\operatorname{clip}\left(\left\lfloor \frac{z}{s}\right\rceil + z_0,\; q_{\min},\; q_{\max}\right) - z_0\right) \]

Uniform quantize-dequantize: scale \(s\), zero-point \(z_0\), integer range \([q_{\min},q_{\max}]\), \(\lfloor\cdot\rceil\) = round to nearest. (Experiments actually use MXFP4, a block-scaled FP4 format.)

Guide

This is the basic quantize then dequantize step. Divide the value z by the scale s, round to the nearest integer, add the zero point z zero, clip to the integer range from q min to q max, then subtract the zero point and multiply back by s. Rounding and clipping are the two sources of error. The experiments actually use MXFP4, a block-scaled four bit float format, but the idea is the same.

(4)\[ s = \frac{\alpha}{q_{\max}} \]

Symmetric case (\(z_0=0\)): the clipping threshold \(\alpha\) fixes the step size. Too small over-clips, too large wastes resolution.

Guide

With a symmetric grid and zero point zero, the step size is set by one number. The scale s equals the clipping threshold alpha divided by q max. Choosing alpha is the whole trade-off: too small and large values get clipped, too large and the sixteen levels are spread thin. Equations eight and nine turn this choice into something searched per layer and per timestep bin.

(5)\[ X_lW_l = (X_lD_l^{-1})(D_lW_l) = \hat{X}_l\hat{W}_l \]

Channel-wise smoothing with diagonal \(D_l\): shrinks activation outlier channels and moves their magnitude into the weight. The output is mathematically unchanged.

Guide

Smoothing is a free rearrangement. X l times W l equals X l times D l inverse, times D l times W l, where D l is a diagonal matrix of per-channel factors. Dividing the activations by D l shrinks outlier channels, and multiplying the weight by it moves that magnitude into the static weight. The output is mathematically unchanged; only where the difficulty lives has moved, and that fix is the SmoothQuant idea.

(6)\[ \hat{W}_l = L_1^lL_2^l + R_l \]

SVDQuant split: low-rank branch \(L_1^lL_2^l\) (high precision, holds outlier directions) + residual \(R_l\) (to be 4-bit).

Guide

The smoothed weight is then split in two. W hat l equals L one times L two, a low-rank product, plus a residual R l. The low-rank branch is kept in sixteen bits and captures the dominant outlier directions, so the residual that must go to four bits is much tamer. This is the SVDQuant decomposition, and it answers the outlier problem shown in the first problem figure.

(7)\[ \hat{Y}_l = \hat{X}_lL_1^lL_2^l + Q_A(\hat{X}_l)\,\hat{R}_l^{\text{GPTQ}} \]

Final layer: the 16-bit low-rank path sees unquantized \(\hat X_l\); the residual path uses a 4-bit activation and GPTQ-rounded 4-bit weights.

Guide

This is the finished quantized layer. Y hat l is X hat l times the low-rank branch, plus the four bit quantized X hat l times R hat l GPTQ. The low-rank path sees unquantized activations and sixteen bit weights, while the residual path runs on four bit activations and four bit weights rounded with GPTQ, which uses second order information to compensate rounding error. The timestep-aware part will only change the activation quantizer in the second term.

(8)\[ \alpha_{l,k}(\rho) = \rho\cdot m_{l,k} \]

Clip threshold for layer \(l\), timestep bin \(k\): candidate ratio \(\rho\) times the reference activation magnitude \(m_{l,k}\) from calibration.

Guide

The clip threshold is expressed as a fraction of a measured size. Alpha for layer l and bin k equals rho times m l k, where m l k is a reference activation magnitude recorded on calibration data in that bin, and rho is a candidate ratio such as 0.8 or 0.9. Searching over rho rather than alpha makes one small candidate set work for every layer.

(9)\[ s^A_{l,k}(\rho) = \frac{\alpha_{l,k}(\rho)}{q_{\max}} \]

The corresponding activation scale (Eq. 4 applied per layer and bin).

Guide

Each candidate threshold becomes an activation scale. The scale s A for layer l and bin k is alpha divided by q max, which is just equation four applied separately to every layer and timestep bin. These are the numbers that end up in the lookup table used at inference.

(10)\[ \rho^{*}_{l,k} = \arg\min_{\rho\in\mathcal{R}}\; \mathbb{E}_{t\in B_k}\left[\left\lVert Y_l(t) - \hat{Y}_l(t;\rho)\right\rVert_2^2\right] \]

Search objective: over candidate set \(\mathcal R\), minimise the expected output MSE of the SVDQuant-GPTQ layer vs. BF16 across steps in bin \(B_k\).

Guide

The search objective picks the best ratio. Rho star for layer l and bin k is the rho from the candidate set that minimises the expected squared difference between the BF16 output Y l of t and the quantized output Y hat l of t, averaged over the steps t in bin B k. Because the full SVDQuant-GPTQ layer is inside the loss, the chosen clip accounts for the weight error too.

(11)\[ \hat{Y}_l(t) = \hat{X}_lL_1^lL_2^l + Q_A\!\left(\hat{X}_l;\, s^A_{l,k}\right)\hat{R}_l^{\text{GPTQ}},\qquad t\in B_k \]

Inference: the current step selects bin \(k\), and its precomputed scale is fetched from a lookup table, so runtime overhead is negligible.

Guide

At inference the layer is equation seven with one change. The activation quantizer now uses the stored scale s A for the bin k that contains the current step t. Finding k and fetching the scale is a table lookup, so the timestep awareness adds almost no runtime cost. This is the bottom lane of the big picture diagram.

—\[ H\times W\times T = 720\times1280\times61 \]

Unnumbered: the generation setting used for all methods (height × width × frames).

Guide

All methods generate videos of the same size: 720 by 1280 pixels and 61 frames. This fixes the workload behind every quality and efficiency number in the results tables, so memory and latency comparisons are like for like.

—\[ \frac{64.4-26.2}{64.4} = 59.3\%\ \text{(peak memory)},\qquad \frac{64.0-25.9}{64.0}=59.5\%\ \text{(model size)} \]

Headline savings, computed from Table II.

Guide

The headline savings come straight from Table II. Peak memory drops from 64.4 to 26.2 gigabytes, a 59.3 percent cut, and model size from 64.0 to 25.9 gigabytes, a 59.5 percent cut. Notice this is well short of the four times one might expect from sixteen to four bits. The paper does not break this down, but the likely reasons are the sixteen bit low-rank branches, the block scales and any layers left unquantized.
