Wan 2.2 and LTX-2.3 are similar in scale but differ in how much runs at once. Wan has two experts of about fourteen billion parameters with only one active per step, while LTX-2.3 runs roughly fourteen billion video and five billion audio parameters together. The paper does W4A4 on an H100; the thesis targets INT8 and INT4 weight-only compression through NNCF on CPU and Arc. The LTX figures come from the thesis brief, and its quality loss is still to be measured.

§7Why it matters for this thesis

Closest analogue to the LTX-2.3 project: a large video DiT, PTQ only, with timestep-aware calibration

  • Take the sensitivity map, not the W4A4 recipe. Here self_attn.o (attention output projection) and ffn.2 (FFN down projection) carry most of the 4-bit error, and keeping only those in higher precision (Ours†) recovers almost all quality (0.803 vs 0.806). For LTX-2.3 in NNCF, a natural first experiment is INT4 weights everywhere except the attn.to_out / FFN down-projection layers, which stay at INT8. Use ignored_scope or a mixed-precision ratio / sensitivity metric in nncf.compress_weights, then check whether LTX shows the same pattern.
  • GPTQ and low-rank correction exist in NNCF, but only for weights. nncf.compress_weights(..., dataset=..., gptq=True) and the data-aware options (AWQ, scale estimation, lora_correction) are the OpenVINO counterparts of "GPTQ residual + low-rank branch". They need calibration data, which means capturing transformer inputs from real LTX sampling runs across all timesteps. No custom kernels are needed.
  • Timestep bins only matter if activations are quantized. In the thesis's weight-only INT8/INT4 setting, activations stay FP16/FP32 (or use OpenVINO's CPU dynamic per-token quantization), so the clip-ratio lookup table is not needed. It becomes relevant only for a static W8A8 attempt. There the lesson is to calibrate with samples drawn from every step (LTX distilled uses few steps, so few bins), because one static scale per layer in an OpenVINO IR cannot switch with t unless the graph is split.
  • Memory ≠ speed. This paper saves 59% memory but runs 1.8× slower because it has no fused low-bit kernel. OpenVINO already ships fused INT4/INT8 weight-decompression matmuls for CPU and Arc GPU, so the thesis should report memory and wall-clock time per step on real hardware, and not claim speed-ups from model size alone.
  • Scale sanity check. Wan2.2 activates one ~14B expert per step. LTX-2.3 runs its ~14B video and ~5B audio streams together, so about 19B parameters are live. The W4A16 row (64 → 26.4 GB) shows that 4-bit weight-only compression alone gives roughly a 2.4× footprint cut for a whole pipeline. That is a realistic target for INT4 LTX-2.3, which should end up around 10–12 GB of transformer weights with some INT8 layers.
Guide

Borrow the sensitivity map, not the W4A4 recipe. A first NNCF experiment is INT4 weights everywhere except the attention output and feed-forward down projections, kept at INT8 through an ignored scope or a mixed-precision setting in compress weights, then check whether LTX shows the same pattern. GPTQ, AWQ and LoRA correction in NNCF are the weight-only counterparts and need calibration inputs captured from every timestep. Skip the clip lookup table unless static W8A8 is tried, and report real memory and time per step, since memory savings are not speed.

Acceleration beyond quantization

FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning

Tri Dao (Princeton & Stanford) · arXiv:2307.08691 technical report · July 2023 (ICLR 2024)

Attention is slow mostly because of memory traffic, not arithmetic: the N×N score matrix is written to and read back from slow GPU memory. FlashAttention computes the exact same result tile by tile in fast on-chip memory using an “online softmax”; FlashAttention-2 reorganises the loops and the GPU work split so that the chip spends most of its time in fast matrix multiplies, doubling speed again.

Output
Exact (no approx.)
Extra memory
O(N) instead of O(N²)
vs FlashAttention
≈2× (1.7–3.0×)
Forward, A100
up to 230 TFLOPs/s (73%)
Backward, A100
up to 63% of peak
GPT training
225 TFLOPs/s/GPU (72% MFU)
Reading guide

Why is attention so slow on a GPU, and how close can it get to the speed of a plain matrix multiply? Tri Dao's answer is that attention is limited by memory traffic and by poor work splitting, not by arithmetic, and that reorganising the loops of FlashAttention roughly doubles its speed again while giving exactly the same output. The tab opens with the big picture of data movement, then the hardware problem, then the method: the swapped loops, the online softmax, and the new split of work across thread blocks and warps. After that come every equation, every figure from the paper, the benchmark results, and a thesis box. Among the sixteen papers, this one sits in the acceleration group with DeepCache and TeaCache. It speeds up attention without touching any weights, so it complements the quantization papers from GPTQ to SVDQuant rather than competing with them.

§0Before reading

This paper is not about compression at all: it makes attention faster by changing how data moves inside a GPU, while the result stays exactly the same. Following it takes three things: what attention and softmax compute, why the N×N score matrix is the expensive part, and a rough picture of a GPU (threads, warps, thread blocks, SMs, fast SRAM versus slow HBM). It is in the atlas because in a video transformer like LTX-2.3 attention over thousands of tokens can dominate each step, and weight quantization cannot speed it up.

Terms used in this paper

Attention (Q, K, V)
Each token makes a query, a key and a value. Queries are compared with all keys, and the resulting weights average the values into the output O.
Sequence length N, head dimension d
N is the number of tokens attending to each other; d is the length of each query or key vector in one head (64 or 128 in this paper's benchmarks).
Softmax
Turns a row of scores into positive weights that sum to one: exponentiate each score and divide by the total. Subtracting the row maximum first keeps the numbers safe.
Online softmax
Computing softmax block by block with a running maximum and running sum, rescaling the old sum when a larger maximum appears. Gives exactly the same result.
Kernel
One program launched on the GPU, such as a matrix multiply. Standard attention uses several kernels; FlashAttention fuses everything into one.
HBM
High Bandwidth Memory: the GPU's large main memory (tens of gigabytes) that sits off the compute chip. Big, but slow compared with on-chip memory.
SRAM (shared memory)
Small, very fast memory inside each SM. FlashAttention loads tiles of Q, K and V here so the N×N scores never go to HBM.
Streaming multiprocessor (SM)
One of the many processor cores of an NVIDIA GPU; each runs thread blocks and has its own SRAM. The A100 has 108. Intel Arc's closest equivalent is the Xe-core.
Thread block and warp
A thread block is a group of threads placed on one SM; it is split into warps of 32 threads that execute the same instruction together. FlashAttention-2 re-plans the work at both levels.
Tensor Core
Special NVIDIA hardware units for fast matrix multiplies in low precision such as FP16/BF16. Other operations (exp, max, division) run much slower, so the paper minimises them.
FLOPs and TFLOPs/s
FLOPs count floating-point operations; TFLOPs/s is trillions per second, the speed measure in every chart. "Percent of peak" compares it with the hardware maximum.
A100 and H100
NVIDIA data-centre GPUs (A100 is the older generation, H100 the newer). The paper's main benchmarks are on an A100 80GB; a few are on an H100.
Forward and backward pass
Forward computes the output; backward computes gradients for training. Inference, as in this thesis, uses only the forward pass.
Causal mask
In text language models a token may only look at earlier tokens, so half the score matrix is skipped. Video DiTs like LTX-2.3 attend in all directions, without this mask.
Guide

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The most important pairs are HBM and SRAM, the slow big memory and the fast small one, and thread block and warp, the two levels at which the paper splits work. Tensor Cores make matrix multiplies fast, so every exponential or division counts. Remember too that the thesis needs only the forward pass, and that video transformers use no causal mask.

§1Big picture

FlashAttention (v1) already did the right-hand picture. FlashAttention-2 keeps the idea and fixes how the GPU is used: (1) fewer non-matmul FLOPs, (2) parallelism over the sequence length, (3) no shared-memory reduction between warps.

§2The problem

  • Standard attention materialises S and P (N×N) in HBM: O(N²) memory and O(N²) slow memory traffic; for N ≫ d (N ≈ 1k–8k, d ≈ 64–128) this dominates run time. P must also be saved for backward.
  • FlashAttention v1 fixed memory, but (i) rescales the output by diag(ℓ)⁻¹ at every inner step (extra non-matmul FLOPs), (ii) only parallelises over batch × heads, so long sequences with small batch leave SMs idle, (iii) splits K, V across warps (“split-K”), forcing a shared-memory reduction.

§3Method

3.1 Tiling loop (Algorithm 1)

3.2 Online softmax as a running state

3.3 What FlashAttention-2 changes

  1. Fewer non-matmul FLOPs. Keep an un-scaled Õ and divide by ℓ once at the end; store only the log-sum-exp L (not m and ℓ separately) for the backward pass.
  2. Parallelise over sequence length. Forward: one thread block per (batch, head, row block i). Backward: one thread block per column block j; the only shared quantity, dQ, is updated with atomic adds.
  3. Better warp partitioning. Inside a thread block (4 or 8 warps), split Q across warps instead of K/V (Fig. 3), so no warp needs another warp’s partial sums.
  4. Causal masking by blocks. Skip blocks entirely above the diagonal; apply the mask only on the diagonal block of each row.
  5. Block sizes {64, 128} × {64, 128}, hand-tuned per head dimension d and shared-memory size (larger = fewer SRAM loads but more registers; too large = register spilling or launch failure).
Guide

These are the paper's four practical changes plus the tuning knob that ties them together. The first two cut expensive non-matmul work: divide by l once at the end, and store only the log-sum-exp. The next two fill the GPU better: give each row block its own thread block, and split queries rather than keys across warps so no warp waits for another's partial sums. With a causal mask, blocks above the diagonal are simply skipped. Block sizes of 64 or 128 are hand-tuned per head dimension, trading fewer memory loads against register pressure.

3.4 Parallelism, causal skipping, backward dataflow

3.5 Algorithms (transcribed)

Algorithm 1 FlashAttention-2 forward pass Require: Matrices Q, K, V ∈ ℝ^(N×d) in HBM, block sizes B_c, B_r. 1: Divide Q into T_r = ⌈N/B_r⌉ blocks Q_1,…,Q_Tr of size B_r × d each, and divide K, V into T_c = ⌈N/B_c⌉ blocks K_1,…,K_Tc and V_1,…,V_Tc, of size B_c × d each. 2: Divide the output O ∈ ℝ^(N×d) into T_r blocks O_1,…,O_Tr of size B_r × d each, and divide the logsumexp L into T_r blocks L_1,…,L_Tr of size B_r each. 3: for 1 ≤ i ≤ T_r do 4: Load Q_i from HBM to on-chip SRAM. 5: On chip, initialize O_i^(0) = (0)_(B_r×d) ∈ ℝ^(B_r×d), ℓ_i^(0) = (0)_(B_r) ∈ ℝ^(B_r), m_i^(0) = (−∞)_(B_r) ∈ ℝ^(B_r). 6: for 1 ≤ j ≤ T_c do 7: Load K_j, V_j from HBM to on-chip SRAM. 8: On chip, compute S_i^(j) = Q_i K_jᵀ ∈ ℝ^(B_r×B_c). 9: On chip, compute m_i^(j) = max(m_i^(j−1), rowmax(S_i^(j))) ∈ ℝ^(B_r), P̃_i^(j) = exp(S_i^(j) − m_i^(j)) ∈ ℝ^(B_r×B_c) (pointwise), ℓ_i^(j) = e^(m_i^(j−1) − m_i^(j)) ℓ_i^(j−1) + rowsum(P̃_i^(j)) ∈ ℝ^(B_r). 10: On chip, compute O_i^(j) = diag(e^(m_i^(j−1) − m_i^(j)))⁻¹ O_i^(j−1) + P̃_i^(j) V_j. 11: end for 12: On chip, compute O_i = diag(ℓ_i^(T_c))⁻¹ O_i^(T_c). 13: On chip, compute L_i = m_i^(T_c) + log(ℓ_i^(T_c)). 14: Write O_i to HBM as the i-th block of O. 15: Write L_i to HBM as the i-th block of L. 16: end for 17: Return the output O and the logsumexp L. [note] line 10 as printed has diag(·)⁻¹; the factor that is actually applied is diag(e^(m_old − m_new)) ≤ 1 (no inverse), consistent with line 9.
Guide

Algorithm 1 is the whole forward pass in one place. It cuts Q into row blocks and K and V into column blocks. Then, for each query block, and these can run in parallel, it initialises the running maximum, sum and output, and walks through all key blocks. Each step computes a score tile, updates the maximum, exponentiates, rescales the old sum and output, and adds the new contribution. At the end it normalises the output once and writes the log-sum-exp. This is the only algorithm that matters for inference.

Algorithm 2 FlashAttention-2 Backward Pass Require: Matrices Q, K, V, O, dO ∈ ℝ^(N×d) in HBM, vector L ∈ ℝ^N in HBM, block sizes B_c, B_r. 1: Divide Q into T_r = ⌈N/B_r⌉ blocks Q_1,…,Q_Tr of size B_r × d each, and divide K, V into T_c = ⌈N/B_c⌉ blocks K_1,…,K_Tc and V_1,…,V_Tc, of size B_c × d each. 2: Divide O into T_r blocks O_1,…,O_Tr of size B_r × d each, divide dO into T_r blocks dO_1,…,dO_Tr of size B_r × d each, and divide L into T_r blocks L_1,…,L_Tr of size B_r each. 3: Initialize dQ = (0)_(N×d) in HBM and divide it into T_r blocks dQ_1,…,dQ_Tr of size B_r × d each. Divide dK, dV ∈ ℝ^(N×d) in to T_c blocks dK_1,…,dK_Tc and dV_1,…,dV_Tc, of size B_c × d each. 4: Compute D = rowsum(dO ∘ O) ∈ ℝ^d (pointwise multiply), write D to HBM and divide it into T_r blocks D_1,…,D_Tr of size B_r each. 5: for 1 ≤ j ≤ T_c do 6: Load K_j, V_j from HBM to on-chip SRAM. 7: Initialize dK_j = (0)_(B_c×d), dV_j = (0)_(B_c×d) on SRAM. 8: for 1 ≤ i ≤ T_r do 9: Load Q_i, O_i, dO_i, dQ_i, L_i, D_i from HBM to on-chip SRAM. 10: On chip, compute S_i^(j) = Q_i K_jᵀ ∈ ℝ^(B_r×B_c). 11: On chip, compute P_i^(j) = exp(S_ij − L_i) ∈ ℝ^(B_r×B_c). 12: On chip, compute dV_j ← dV_j + (P_i^(j))ᵀ dO_i ∈ ℝ^(B_c×d). 13: On chip, compute dP_i^(j) = dO_i V_jᵀ ∈ ℝ^(B_r×B_c). 14: On chip, compute dS_i^(j) = P_i^(j) ∘ (dP_i^(j) − D_i) ∈ ℝ^(B_r×B_c). 15: Load dQ_i from HBM to SRAM, then on chip, update dQ_i ← dQ_i + dS_i^(j) K_j ∈ ℝ^(B_r×d), and write back to HBM. 16: On chip, compute dK_j ← dK_j + dS_i^(j)ᵀ Q_i ∈ ℝ^(B_c×d). 17: end for 18: Write dK_j, dV_j to HBM. 19: end for 20: Return dQ, dK, dV. [note] as printed: D ∈ ℝ^d should read D ∈ ℝ^N (one value per row); S_ij in line 11 means S_i^(j). Line 15 is done with atomic adds when column blocks run in parallel (Sec. 3.2).
Guide

Algorithm 2 computes the gradients for training. It first computes D, the row-wise sum of the output gradient times the output, which makes the softmax derivative cheap. Then, for each key and value block, it loops over query blocks, recomputes the scores and probabilities from the stored log-sum-exp, accumulates the gradients for V and K on chip, and adds its share of the query gradient into HBM with atomic adds. Recomputation trades extra arithmetic for never storing an N by N matrix.

MQA / GQA are supported by index manipulation (no duplication of K/V heads); in backward, dK and dV are summed over the implicitly duplicated heads.

§4Every equation

The paper has no numbered equations; all display math is listed below in paper order, tagged by section. Following the paper, the 1/√d scaling of QKᵀ, masking and dropout are omitted for clarity.

§2.2a\[ \mathbf S=\mathbf Q\mathbf K^{\top}\in\mathbb R^{N\times N},\qquad \mathbf P=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf S)\in\mathbb R^{N\times N},\qquad \mathbf O=\mathbf P\mathbf V\in\mathbb R^{N\times d} \]

Standard attention; Q, K, V ∈ ℝ^(N×d), N = sequence length, d = head dimension, softmax row-wise.

Guide

Standard attention takes three steps. S equals Q times K transposed, where Q, K and V are N by d matrices, N is the sequence length and d the head dimension, so S is N by N. P is the row-wise softmax of S, and the output O is P times V. The problem the paper attacks is that S and P are N by N, so for long sequences they are huge and end up in slow memory.

§2.2b\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{dV}&=\mathbf P^{\top}\mathbf{dO}\in\mathbb R^{N\times d}\\ \mathbf{dP}&=\mathbf{dO}\,\mathbf V^{\top}\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}\\ \mathbf{dS}&=\operatorname{dsoftmax}(\mathbf{dP})\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}\\ \mathbf{dQ}&=\mathbf{dS}\,\mathbf K\in\mathbb R^{N\times d}\\ \mathbf{dK}&=\mathbf Q\,\mathbf{dS}^{\top}\in\mathbb R^{N\times d} \end{aligned} \]

Backward pass by the chain rule; dO is the loss gradient w.r.t. O. Five matmuls (vs. two in forward).

Guide

These five lines are the backward pass by the chain rule, where dO is the gradient of the loss with respect to the output. The gradient for V is P transposed times dO; dP is dO times V transposed; dS applies the softmax derivative to dP; and the gradients for Q and K are dS times K and Q times dS transposed. That is five matrix multiplies against two in the forward pass, which is why backward is harder to make fast.

§2.2c\[ p=\operatorname{softmax}(s)\;\Rightarrow\; ds=\big(\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^{\top}\big)\,dp \]

Row-wise softmax Jacobian (“dsoftmax”). Row by row this equals p ∘ (dp − pᵀdp), which is where D in Alg. 2 comes from.

Guide

Here is the derivative of softmax for one row. If p is the softmax of the scores s, then a small change dp in the probabilities maps back to ds equal to the diagonal matrix of p minus p times p transposed, all times dp. Row by row this simplifies to p times the quantity dp minus one number per row, the dot product of p and dp. That number is exactly the D vector that Algorithm 2 precomputes.

§2.3.1a\[ \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf S^{(1)} & \mathbf S^{(2)}\end{bmatrix},\;\; \mathbf S^{(1)},\mathbf S^{(2)}\in\mathbb R^{B_r\times B_c};\qquad \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf V^{(1)}\\ \mathbf V^{(2)}\end{bmatrix},\;\; \mathbf V^{(1)},\mathbf V^{(2)}\in\mathbb R^{B_c\times d} \]

One row block of S split into two column blocks; V split accordingly. B_r, B_c = row / column block sizes.

Guide

This sets up the toy example for the online softmax. One row block of scores S is split into two column blocks, S one and S two, each B r rows by B c columns, and V is split to match into V one and V two. B r and B c are the row and column block sizes. The next two equations compute the same output, first the standard way, then block by block.

§2.3.1b\[ \begin{aligned} m&=\max\big(\operatorname{rowmax}(\mathbf S^{(1)}),\operatorname{rowmax}(\mathbf S^{(2)})\big)\in\mathbb R^{B_r}\\ \ell&=\operatorname{rowsum}\big(e^{\mathbf S^{(1)}-m}\big)+\operatorname{rowsum}\big(e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m}\big)\in\mathbb R^{B_r}\\ \mathbf P&=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf P^{(1)} & \mathbf P^{(2)}\end{bmatrix}=\operatorname{diag}(\ell)^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}e^{\mathbf S^{(1)}-m} & e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{B_r\times 2B_c}\\ \mathbf O&=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf P^{(1)} & \mathbf P^{(2)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf V^{(1)}\\ \mathbf V^{(2)}\end{bmatrix}=\operatorname{diag}(\ell)^{-1}e^{\mathbf S^{(1)}-m}\mathbf V^{(1)}+e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m}\mathbf V^{(2)}\in\mathbb R^{B_r\times d} \end{aligned} \]

Standard (safe) softmax needs the max m and sum ℓ over the whole row before normalising. (As printed, diag(ℓ)⁻¹ is meant to apply to both terms of O.)

Guide

Here is the standard, numerically safe softmax on the two blocks. It first needs m, the maximum over the whole row, and l, the sum of exponentials of the scores minus m across both blocks. Only then can the division give P and multiply by V to get O. The catch is that m and l depend on the whole row, so every block must be seen before normalising. The next equation removes that requirement. As the tab notes, the division by l is meant to apply to both terms.

§2.3.1c\[ \begin{aligned} m^{(1)}&=\operatorname{rowmax}(\mathbf S^{(1)})\in\mathbb R^{B_r}\\ \ell^{(1)}&=\operatorname{rowsum}\big(e^{\mathbf S^{(1)}-m^{(1)}}\big)\in\mathbb R^{B_r}\\ \tilde{\mathbf P}^{(1)}&=\operatorname{diag}(\ell^{(1)})^{-1}e^{\mathbf S^{(1)}-m^{(1)}}\in\mathbb R^{B_r\times B_c}\\ \mathbf O^{(1)}&=\tilde{\mathbf P}^{(1)}\mathbf V^{(1)}=\operatorname{diag}(\ell^{(1)})^{-1}e^{\mathbf S^{(1)}-m^{(1)}}\mathbf V^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{B_r\times d}\\ m^{(2)}&=\max\big(m^{(1)},\operatorname{rowmax}(\mathbf S^{(2)})\big)=m\\ \ell^{(2)}&=e^{m^{(1)}-m^{(2)}}\ell^{(1)}+\operatorname{rowsum}\big(e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m^{(2)}}\big)=\operatorname{rowsum}\big(e^{\mathbf S^{(1)}-m}\big)+\operatorname{rowsum}\big(e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m}\big)=\ell\\ \tilde{\mathbf P}^{(2)}&=\operatorname{diag}(\ell^{(2)})^{-1}e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m^{(2)}}\\ \mathbf O^{(2)}&=\operatorname{diag}(\ell^{(1)}/\ell^{(2)})^{-1}\mathbf O^{(1)}+\tilde{\mathbf P}^{(2)}\mathbf V^{(2)}=\operatorname{diag}(\ell^{(2)})^{-1}e^{\mathbf S^{(1)}-m}\mathbf V^{(1)}+\operatorname{diag}(\ell^{(2)})^{-1}e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m}\mathbf V^{(2)}=\mathbf O \end{aligned} \]

Online softmax as used in FlashAttention v1: local softmax per block, then rescale. The rescale factor for O⁽¹⁾ must be diag(ℓ⁽²⁾)⁻¹ diag(e^(m⁽¹⁾−m⁽²⁾) ℓ⁽¹⁾); the paper’s shorthand omits the exponential and writes the ratio inverted.

Guide

The original FlashAttention's online softmax processes block one alone, getting its own max m one, sum l one, and a correctly normalised partial output O one. When block two arrives, the new max m two and the rescaled sum l two turn out to equal the full-row m and l. The partial output is then corrected by the ratio of old to new sums, so after the last block the result is exact, without ever holding the whole row.

§3.1\[ \frac{312\ \text{TFLOPs/s (FP16/BF16 matmul)}}{19.5\ \text{TFLOPs/s (FP32 non-matmul)}}\approx 16 \]

A100: each non-matmul FLOP costs ~16× a matmul FLOP, motivating tweak 1 and 2 below.

Guide

This ratio motivates the paper's first two tweaks. On the A100, half-precision matrix multiplies run at 312 teraflops per second, but single-precision operations that are not matrix multiplies, like exp, max and division, run at only 19.5. Divided, that is about sixteen, so each non-matmul flop costs as much as sixteen matmul flops. Even a small amount of softmax bookkeeping can therefore eat a large share of the runtime.

§3.1.1a\[ \mathbf O^{(2)}=\operatorname{diag}(\ell^{(1)}/\ell^{(2)})^{-1}\mathbf O^{(1)}+\operatorname{diag}(\ell^{(2)})^{-1}e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m^{(2)}}\mathbf V^{(2)} \]

Tweak 1, before: v1 rescales both terms by diag(ℓ⁽²⁾)⁻¹ at every step.

Guide

Here is the version one update that FlashAttention-2 improves. To merge block two, v1 rescales the old output O one by the ratio of old to new sums, and also divides the new term by l two. Both terms are divided by the current sum at every block, so this expensive rescaling is repeated T c times per row. The next equation shows how to postpone it.

§3.1.1b\[ \tilde{\mathbf O}^{(2)}=\operatorname{diag}(\ell^{(1)})^{-1}\mathbf O^{(1)}+e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m^{(2)}}\mathbf V^{(2)} \]

Tweak 1, after: keep an “un-scaled” Õ plus the statistic ℓ⁽²⁾; only at the end scale Õ^(last) by diag(ℓ^(last))⁻¹. (As printed; in the un-scaled form the first term is e^(m⁽¹⁾−m⁽²⁾)Õ⁽¹⁾, see §3.1.1d.)

Guide

Tweak one: keep an un-scaled output, O tilde, carry the sum l alongside it, and divide only once after the last block. The equation is reproduced as printed in the paper; in the fully un-scaled form the first term should be e to the power of m one minus m two, times O tilde one, as the tab's equation 3.1.1d shows. The idea is the same either way: fewer non-matmul operations inside the inner loop.

§3.1.1c\[ L^{(j)}=m^{(j)}+\log\big(\ell^{(j)}\big) \]

Tweak 2: store only the row-wise log-sum-exp for backward (one vector instead of m and ℓ); then P = exp(S − L).

Guide

Tweak two. The backward pass needs each row's softmax statistics, and instead of storing both the maximum m and the sum l, FlashAttention-2 stores just L equals m plus the log of l, called the log-sum-exp. Backward can then rebuild the probabilities directly as exp of S minus L. That is one vector per row instead of two, and a simpler recomputation.

§3.1.1d\[ \begin{aligned} m^{(1)}&=\operatorname{rowmax}(\mathbf S^{(1)})\in\mathbb R^{B_r}\\ \ell^{(1)}&=\operatorname{rowsum}\big(e^{\mathbf S^{(1)}-m^{(1)}}\big)\in\mathbb R^{B_r}\\ \tilde{\mathbf O}^{(1)}&=e^{\mathbf S^{(1)}-m^{(1)}}\mathbf V^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{B_r\times d}\\ m^{(2)}&=\max\big(m^{(1)},\operatorname{rowmax}(\mathbf S^{(2)})\big)=m\\ \ell^{(2)}&=e^{m^{(1)}-m^{(2)}}\ell^{(1)}+\operatorname{rowsum}\big(e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m^{(2)}}\big)=\operatorname{rowsum}\big(e^{\mathbf S^{(1)}-m}\big)+\operatorname{rowsum}\big(e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m}\big)=\ell\\ \tilde{\mathbf P}^{(2)}&=\operatorname{diag}(\ell^{(2)})^{-1}e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m^{(2)}}\\ \tilde{\mathbf O}^{(2)}&=\operatorname{diag}\big(e^{m^{(1)}-m^{(2)}}\big)^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf O}^{(1)}+e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m^{(2)}}\mathbf V^{(2)}=e^{\mathbf S^{(1)}-m}\mathbf V^{(1)}+e^{\mathbf S^{(2)}-m}\mathbf V^{(2)}\\ \mathbf O^{(2)}&=\operatorname{diag}(\ell^{(2)})^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf O}^{(2)}=\mathbf O \end{aligned} \]

FlashAttention-2 online softmax (2-block case). The right-hand equality of Õ⁽²⁾ holds with factor diag(e^(m⁽¹⁾−m⁽²⁾)) — the printed “⁻¹” is a typo (same in Alg. 1 line 10).

Guide

Here is the full two-block example redone with FlashAttention-2's un-scaled output. Block one gives m one, l one and O tilde one without any division. Block two updates the max and sum, and O tilde two is the old O tilde shrunk by e to the power of m one minus m two, plus the new block's contribution. Only at the very end is O tilde divided by l to give the exact output. Compare with equations 3.1.1a and b to see the division leave the loop.

Alg. 1\[ \begin{aligned} T_r&=\Big\lceil \tfrac{N}{B_r}\Big\rceil,\quad T_c=\Big\lceil \tfrac{N}{B_c}\Big\rceil,\qquad \mathbf S_i^{(j)}=\mathbf Q_i\mathbf K_j^{\top}\\ m_i^{(j)}&=\max\big(m_i^{(j-1)},\operatorname{rowmax}(\mathbf S_i^{(j)})\big),\quad \tilde{\mathbf P}_i^{(j)}=\exp\big(\mathbf S_i^{(j)}-m_i^{(j)}\big),\quad \ell_i^{(j)}=e^{m_i^{(j-1)}-m_i^{(j)}}\ell_i^{(j-1)}+\operatorname{rowsum}\big(\tilde{\mathbf P}_i^{(j)}\big)\\ \mathbf O_i^{(j)}&=\operatorname{diag}\big(e^{m_i^{(j-1)}-m_i^{(j)}}\big)^{-1}\mathbf O_i^{(j-1)}+\tilde{\mathbf P}_i^{(j)}\mathbf V_j,\qquad \mathbf O_i=\operatorname{diag}\big(\ell_i^{(T_c)}\big)^{-1}\mathbf O_i^{(T_c)},\qquad L_i=m_i^{(T_c)}+\log\big(\ell_i^{(T_c)}\big) \end{aligned} \]

General forward recurrences (lines 1, 8–13), initialised with O = 0, ℓ = 0, m = −∞.

Guide

These are the general forward recurrences of Algorithm 1, for any number of blocks. T r and T c count the row and column blocks: N over B r and N over B c, rounded up. For query block i and key block j, the score tile S equals Q i times K j transposed, the max m and sum l are updated as in the two-block case, and the un-scaled output is rescaled and extended. At the end, O i is divided by l once and L i is stored.

§3.1.1e\[ \mathbf O=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf Q\mathbf K^{\top})\mathbf V,\qquad \text{FLOPs}=O(N^2d),\qquad \text{extra memory}=O(N) \]

Correctness and cost of Algorithm 1: exact output; the only extra storage is L.

Guide

Algorithm 1 guarantees an exact result: the output equals softmax of Q times K transposed, times V, with no approximation. The work is still proportional to N squared times d, the same as standard attention, but extra memory beyond inputs and output is only proportional to N, since the only stored statistic is L. The speed comes from fewer memory trips and better scheduling, not from skipping computation.

Alg. 2\[ \begin{aligned} D&=\operatorname{rowsum}(\mathbf{dO}\circ\mathbf O),\qquad \mathbf S_i^{(j)}=\mathbf Q_i\mathbf K_j^{\top},\qquad \mathbf P_i^{(j)}=\exp\big(\mathbf S_i^{(j)}-L_i\big)\\ \mathbf{dV}_j&\leftarrow\mathbf{dV}_j+(\mathbf P_i^{(j)})^{\top}\mathbf{dO}_i,\qquad \mathbf{dP}_i^{(j)}=\mathbf{dO}_i\mathbf V_j^{\top},\qquad \mathbf{dS}_i^{(j)}=\mathbf P_i^{(j)}\circ\big(\mathbf{dP}_i^{(j)}-D_i\big)\\ \mathbf{dQ}_i&\leftarrow\mathbf{dQ}_i+\mathbf{dS}_i^{(j)}\mathbf K_j,\qquad \mathbf{dK}_j\leftarrow\mathbf{dK}_j+\mathbf{dS}_i^{(j)\top}\mathbf Q_i \end{aligned} \]

Backward recurrences (lines 4, 10–16). D = rowsum(dO∘O) = rowsum(P∘dP) makes dsoftmax cheap; ∘ is element-wise product.

Guide

These are the backward recurrences of Algorithm 2. D is the row sum of dO times O, element by element. For each tile, the probabilities are recomputed as exp of S minus L, the V gradient gains P transposed times dO, dP equals dO times V transposed, and dS equals P times the quantity dP minus D, element by element. Then dS updates the gradients for Q and K. Precomputing D turns the softmax derivative into a cheap element-wise step.

§4.1\[ \text{FLOPs}_{\text{fwd}}=4\cdot\text{seqlen}^2\cdot\text{head dimension}\cdot\text{number of heads},\qquad \text{FLOPs}_{\text{bwd}}=2.5\cdot\text{FLOPs}_{\text{fwd}} \]

Benchmark accounting (per sequence); halved with a causal mask; ×2.5 for backward (5 vs 2 matmuls).

Guide

Benchmarks count work this way. Forward flops equal four times sequence length squared, times head dimension, times number of heads. With a causal mask the count is halved, and backward is counted as 2.5 times forward, matching five matrix multiplies against two. Figures 4 to 7 divide these flop counts by measured time to get teraflops per second, so a taller bar means a faster kernel on the same work.

§4.2\[ \text{FLOPs}=6\cdot\text{seqlen}\cdot\text{number of params}+12\cdot\text{number of layers}\cdot\text{hidden dim}\cdot\text{seqlen}^2 \]

Megatron-LM training-FLOPs formula used for Table 1 (weights term + attention term; attention not halved for causal, for consistency).

Guide

The Megatron-LM formula for total training flops is used to report Table 1. The first term, six times sequence length times number of parameters, covers the weight matrix multiplies; the second, twelve times layers times hidden size times sequence length squared, covers attention. The attention term is not halved for causal masking, to stay consistent with earlier work. Dividing by time per GPU gives the utilisation figures in the table.

Guide

This summary is derived by the tab from the bar labels of Figures 4 to 7. For each figure it gives the best FlashAttention-2 throughput and the range of speed-ups over the original FlashAttention across all 24 settings. The A100 forward pass shows the widest gain, up to about 3.4 times, at 227 teraflops. That forward row is the one relevant to diffusion inference, where the backward pass never runs.

  • Paper’s headline: FA2 is 1.7–3.0× faster than FlashAttention, 1.3–2.5× faster than FlashAttention in Triton, 3–10× faster than standard PyTorch attention; ≈2× vs FlashAttention/xformers overall.
  • End-to-end GPT training: up to 1.3× vs FlashAttention and 2.8× vs no FlashAttention; H100 without Hopper-specific instructions still reaches ≈335 TFLOPs/s, with a further 1.5–2× expected from TMA / 4th-gen Tensor Cores (future work, later FlashAttention-3).

§7Why it matters for this thesis

LTX-2.3 on Intel Arc / CPU with OpenVINO

  • Long sequences make attention the bottleneck. A video DiT attends over all spatio-temporal latent tokens at once (bidirectional, no causal mask). Attention FLOPs grow as 4·N²·d·heads (§4.1) while linear layers grow as N, so for longer or higher-resolution clips attention can dominate the step time — and weight-only int8/int4 (NNCF) does not speed it up, because attention has no weights.
  • Use the fused op, don’t write a kernel. OpenVINO has a ScaledDotProductAttention operation, and recent GPU/CPU plugins execute it with tiled, online-softmax (FlashAttention-style) kernels. What matters for the thesis is that the converted LTX-2.3 IR actually contains SDPA nodes (PyTorch F.scaled_dot_product_attention converts to it; hand-written MatMul→Softmax→MatMul patterns need to be fused by OpenVINO transformations). Check the runtime/execution graph and compare latency with the fused op on vs. off.
  • Only Algorithm 1 matters. Inference needs just the forward pass (O and optionally L); the backward pass, atomic dQ updates and causal-block skipping are irrelevant for DiT denoising. Sequence-length parallelism (Fig. 2) is exactly what helps batch-1 generation fill all Xe-cores.
  • Exact, so no calibration and no quality risk. Unlike quantization, FlashAttention changes only data movement; it combines freely with NNCF weight compression and with caching methods. It needs no calibration data — but block sizes are tuned for the hardware’s on-chip memory, which differs between A100 and Arc, so treat A100 speed-ups as qualitative.
  • Precision interplay. The exp/rowmax/rescale path is the “non-matmul” part the paper minimises; on Arc, keeping SDPA in FP16 (XMX matmul) with FP32 statistics is the natural setting. Quantizing attention activations (Q, K, V, P to int8) is a separate, riskier experiment that the fused kernel may or may not support.
Guide

For the thesis, the job is to verify, not to implement. Export LTX-2.3 so that its attention becomes OpenVINO's ScaledDotProductAttention operation, check in the execution graph that these fused nodes really appear, and measure latency with the fused op on and off. NNCF's weight-only int8 or int4 compression does nothing for attention, which has no weights, so this is a separate, exact speed-up that stacks with quantization and caching. Treat A100 numbers as qualitative, and keep attention in FP16 with FP32 statistics on Arc.

Acceleration beyond quantization

DeepCache: Accelerating Diffusion Models for Free

Xinyin Ma, Gongfan Fang, Xinchao Wang (National University of Singapore) · CVPR 2024 (arXiv 2312.00858)

From one denoising step to the next, the deep, high-level features of a diffusion U-Net barely change. DeepCache runs the full U-Net once, caches the deep feature that enters a shallow up-block, and for the next N−1 steps recomputes only the cheap shallow skip path. No training, no calibration data, just a change to the sampling loop.

Training / data
none (training-free)
SD v1.5 (PLMS-50)
2.3× faster, CLIP −0.05
LDM-4-G ImageNet
4.1×, FID 3.39→3.59
Max tested speed-up
10.5× (N=20)
Knob
cache interval N, branch m
Architecture
U-Net skip branches
Reading guide

DeepCache asks a simple question: if a diffusion model's deep features barely change from one denoising step to the next, why recompute them every time? It answers: run the full U-Net once, cache the deep feature, and for the next few steps run only the cheap shallow path that plugs into that cache. It needs no training and no data, and reaches 2.3 times faster Stable Diffusion with almost the same CLIP score, and over four times faster ImageNet generation with FID moving only from 3.39 to 3.59. The tab goes from the big picture and the problem, to the method, every equation, every figure, the result tables with three charts, and finally a thesis box. Among the sixteen papers it belongs to the acceleration group with FlashAttention-2 and TeaCache: it saves steps' worth of compute rather than bits, so it can stack on top of the quantization papers.

§0Before reading

DeepCache is built on two ideas worth knowing first: the U-Net, an image network whose shallow and deep layers are joined by skip connections, and the sampling loop, which calls that same network at every denoising step. It is in the atlas because it saves time without touching bits: it reuses work across steps, so it can stack on top of int8/int4 compression, and it is the direct ancestor of TeaCache, which brings the same idea to transformers like LTX-2.3.

Terms used in this paper

U-Net
An image network with a down path that shrinks the image into abstract features, a middle block, and an up path that grows it back. Stable Diffusion and the other models in this paper use one to predict noise.
Skip connection (skip branch)
A shortcut that sends the output of down block Di directly to up block Ui. The paper numbers the branches from 1 (shallowest) upward.
Feature map
The intermediate output of a block: a stack of small images, one per channel. "High-level" features from deep blocks describe layout and objects, not pixels.
Timestep \(t\)
The position in the denoising process, counting down from pure noise to the clean image. Each timestep costs one call of the network.
Sampler: DDPM, DDIM, PLMS
The rule that turns the network's noise prediction into the next, less noisy image. DDPM is the original slow sampler; DDIM and PLMS reach good images in fewer steps (here 50 to 250).
Feature similarity
A score of how alike two feature maps are, where values near 1 mean almost identical. The paper finds many step pairs above 0.95.
Cache interval \(N\)
How often the full network runs: one full step, then \(N-1\) cheap steps reusing the cache. Larger \(N\) means faster sampling and more drift from the original image.
Branch \(m\)
Which skip branch the cheap steps keep. Only blocks D1..Dm and Um..U1 run; a smaller \(m\) is faster but less accurate.
MACs
Multiply-accumulate operations: a hardware-independent count of the arithmetic a model does. The paper reports the average per step.
Throughput and speed-up
Throughput is images generated per second on real hardware; speed-up is that throughput divided by the original model's. Measured speed-up is usually smaller than the drop in MACs.
RTX 2080
An NVIDIA consumer graphics card from 2018, the single GPU used for all throughput numbers. An Intel CPU or Arc GPU will give different absolute times, so re-measure.
FID (and sFID, IS)
Fréchet Inception Distance compares features of real and generated images; lower is better. sFID is a variant sensitive to spatial layout, and Inception Score (IS) is higher-is-better. Used for ImageNet, CIFAR-10 and LSUN results.
CLIP score
How well an image matches its text prompt, measured with a CLIP model (here ViT-g/14); higher is better. Used for Stable Diffusion on PartiPrompts and MS-COCO 2017 prompts.
Stable Diffusion v1.5 and LDM-4-G
Two latent diffusion models: Stable Diffusion makes images from text, LDM-4-G makes ImageNet images from a class label. Both run their U-Net on a compressed latent, not on pixels.
Guide

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The two knobs to remember are the cache interval N, how often the full network runs, and the branch m, how deep the cheap path goes. FID and CLIP score measure quality, MACs and throughput measure cost, and all timings come from a single RTX 2080 graphics card, so Intel numbers will differ.

§1Big picture

Diffusion sampling calls the same network 25–250 times. DeepCache removes most of the work inside the retrieve steps rather than removing steps.

§2The problem

  • Retraining-based compression (Diff-Pruning, BK-SDM, Spectral DPM) is costly for large models like Stable Diffusion.
  • Adjacent-step deep features are highly similar; for every timestep, ≥10% of other steps have similarity > 0.95 (up to 80% for DDPM LSUN-Churches).
  • Similarity is not constant: for LDM it drops by ~40% of the progress (Fig. 2c), so a fixed long cache interval hurts.

§3Method

  1. Cache step (step t): run the whole U-Net, store F_cache = Um+1(·) (Eq. 4), and update x.
  2. Retrieve steps (next N−1 steps): run only D1…Dm on the new x, feed Concat(Dm, F_cache) into Um (Eq. 5), run Um…U1.
  3. Repeat every N steps (uniform, Eq. 6) or at the steps in I from the non-uniform rule (Eq. 7).
  4. Pick m (depth of the kept shallow path) and N (interval): larger N or smaller m gives more speed and lower quality. Paper uses branch 3 / 1 / 2 for DDPM / LDM-4-G / SD.
Guide

The procedure alternates two kinds of step. A cache step runs the whole network and saves the deep feature. The following N minus one retrieve steps run only the first m down blocks on the new input, join them with the saved feature, and finish with the first m up blocks. A larger interval N or a shallower branch m means more speed and less quality. The paper uses branch three for DDPM, one for LDM, and two for Stable Diffusion.

Algorithm 1: DeepCache (Appendix A, DDPM sampler shown)

Input: U-Net with down blocks {D_i}_{i=1..d}, up blocks {U_i}_{i=1..d}, middle block M Input: caching interval N, branch index m Input: output from step x_t, timestep t Output: predicted output at t - N step ▷ 1. Cache step - compute eps_theta(x_t, t) and x_{t-1} h_0 ← x_t ▷ h_i for down-sampling features for i = 1..d do h_i ← D_i(h_{i-1}) u_{d+1} ← M(h_d) ▷ u_i for up-sampling features for i = d..1 do if i = m then store u_{i+1} in Cache u_i ← U_i(Concat(u_{i+1}, h_i)) x_{t-1} = 1/sqrt(alpha_t) * ( x_t - (1-alpha_t)/sqrt(1-alphabar_t) * u_1 ) + sigma_t z ▷ z ~ N(0, I) ▷ 2. Retrieve step - compute {x_{t-n}}_{n=2..N} for n = 2..N do h_0 ← x_{t-n+1} for i = 1..m do h_i ← D_i(h_{i-1}) retrieve u_{m+1} from Cache for i = m..1 do u_i ← U_i(Concat(u_{i+1}, h_i)) x_{t-n} = 1/sqrt(alpha_t) * ( x_t - (1-alpha_t)/sqrt(1-alphabar_t) * u_1 ) + sigma_t z ▷ z ~ N(0, I) return x_{t-N}
Guide

The first part of Algorithm 1 is an ordinary U-Net pass: go down through all blocks, through the middle block, then back up, and on the way up save the feature arriving at branch m. The second part loops over the next N minus one steps, runs only the shallow down blocks, pulls the saved feature from the cache, and runs the shallow up blocks. Each pass ends with the usual sampler update, so only the network evaluation changes, not the sampler.

Note: the retrieve-step update in Algorithm 1 is transcribed as printed (it reuses xt, αt); in practice the sampler uses the current step’s x and schedule.

§4Every equation

(1)\[ q\left(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \mathbf{x}_{t-1}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{x}_t;\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,\mathbf{x}_{t-1},\,\beta_t\mathbf{I}\right) \]

Forward diffusion: each step shrinks the previous sample and adds Gaussian noise with variance βt.

Guide

The forward diffusion step. q of x t given x t minus one is a Gaussian: the previous sample x t minus one is scaled by the square root of one minus beta t, and noise with variance beta t is added, where beta t is the noise schedule and I is the identity matrix. Repeating this turns an image into pure noise. It is background only; DeepCache does not change the diffusion process itself.

(2)\[ \mathbf{x}_{t-1}\sim p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\mid \mathbf{x}_t)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{x}_{t-1};\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(\mathbf{x}_t-\frac{1-\alpha_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,t)\right),\,\beta_t\mathbf{I}\right) \]

Reverse step: the network εθ predicts noise and the sampler removes it. Here \(\alpha_t=1-\beta_t\), \(\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{i=1}^{T}\alpha_i\) (as printed).

Guide

The reverse, denoising step that sampling repeats many times. The network epsilon theta looks at the noisy sample x t and the timestep t and predicts the noise; the sampler subtracts a scaled version of it, divides by the square root of alpha t, and adds fresh noise with variance beta t. Alpha t is one minus beta t, and alpha bar t is the running product of the alphas. Every one of these network calls is what DeepCache makes cheaper.

(3)\[ \operatorname{Concat}\left(D_i(\cdot),\,U_{i+1}(\cdot)\right) \]

Input to up-block Ui: low-level skip feature from Di concatenated with the high-level main-branch feature from Ui+1.

Guide

The input to up block U i is the concatenation of two features: the low-level feature from down block D i arriving over the skip branch, and the high-level feature from the deeper up block U i plus one on the main branch. This structural fact is what makes DeepCache possible: the deep half can be replaced by a stored copy while the skip still delivers fresh shallow detail.

(4)\[ F^{t}_{\text{cache}}\leftarrow U^{t}_{m+1}(\cdot) \]

Cache step at time t: store the main-branch feature entering Um.

Guide

The cache step. At time t, F cache is set to the output of up block U m plus one, that is, the deep main-branch feature that is about to enter up block U m. Here m is the chosen skip branch. This stored tensor is the only thing carried between steps, and equation 5 is where it gets reused.

(5)\[ \operatorname{Concat}\left(D^{t-1}_{m}(\cdot),\,F^{t}_{\text{cache}}\right) \]

Retrieve step t−1: fresh shallow feature Dm plus the stale cached deep feature; blocks below m are not executed.

Guide

The retrieve step at time t minus one. Up block U m receives the fresh shallow feature from D m, computed on the new input, concatenated with the stale F cache saved at time t. Nothing deeper than branch m runs. This is equation 3 with the expensive main-branch input swapped for the cached one, and Table 5 shows the cache matters: replacing it with zeros destroys the images.

(6)\[ \mathcal{I}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{N}\mid x=iN,\;0\le i\lt k\right\},\qquad k=\lceil T/N\rceil \]

Uniform 1:N: full inference at every N-th step; k is the number of cache updates.

Guide

The uniform refresh schedule. The set I holds the steps where the full network runs: every multiple of N, i times N, for i from zero up to k minus one, where k is T divided by N rounded up and T is the total number of steps. With fifty steps and N equal to five, that means ten full steps. It is the simple baseline that equation 7 improves on.

(7)\[ \begin{aligned}\mathcal{L}&=\left\{\,l_i \;\middle|\; l_i\in \operatorname{linear\_space}\left((-c)^{\frac{1}{p}},\,(T-c)^{\frac{1}{p}},\,k\right)\right\}\\ \mathcal{I}&=\operatorname{unique\_int}\left(\left\{\,i_k \;\middle|\; i_k=(l_k)^{p}+c,\ \text{where } l_k\in\mathcal{L}\right\}\right)\end{aligned} \]

Non-uniform 1:N: evenly space k points in a p-th-root space centred on step c (end exclusive), map back with power p, round and deduplicate. Full steps are densest near c. Defaults found: c≈15 (SD, 50 steps) or 120 (LDM, 250 steps), p≈1.2–1.5.

Guide

The non-uniform refresh schedule. Take k evenly spaced points between minus c and T minus c, but in a p-th-root space; raise them back to the power p, shift by the centre c, round to integers and remove duplicates. Here c is the step where features change fastest and p controls how strongly refreshes cluster around it. The result is dense full steps near c and sparse ones far away. Tables 7 to 10 tune c and p.

Alg. 1\[ \mathbf{x}_{t-1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(\mathbf{x}_t-\frac{1-\alpha_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\mathbf{u}_1\right)+\sigma_t\mathbf{z},\qquad \mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) \]

Unnumbered sampler update inside Algorithm 1: u1 (final up-block output) plays the role of εθ.

Guide

The sampler update used inside Algorithm 1. It is the same as equation 2, except that u one, the output of the first up block, stands in for the predicted noise epsilon theta; sigma t times z adds fresh Gaussian noise. It makes explicit that on a retrieve step the shallow path's output is treated exactly like a full network prediction.

§4.5\[ \text{work}\;=\;K\ \text{full passes}\;+\;(N-1)\times K\ \text{shallow passes} \]

Ablation framing (in text): DeepCache = K DDIM steps plus (N−1)×K shallow-network steps.

Guide

A way to count the work in the ablation of section 4.5. DeepCache equals K full network passes, the same as K DDIM steps, plus N minus one times K extra shallow passes. Framed like this, the question becomes whether those cheap shallow passes add quality on top of plain DDIM with K steps, which Table 6 answers with a clear yes.

§7Why it matters for this thesis

DeepCache → LTX-2.3 on OpenVINO / NNCF

  • Orthogonal to quantization and needs no calibration. Caching changes the sampling loop, not the weights, so it stacks on top of NNCF int8/int4 weight compression. But errors compound (quantization noise plus stale features): measure the combination, not each part alone.
  • Recipe does not transfer literally. LTX-2 is a DiT, a flat stack of transformer blocks with residual adds and no U-Net long skips, so there is no ‘cheap shallow branch’. The DiT counterpart is caching the residual of a block span (FORA / Δ-DiT style) or of the whole model with an adaptive trigger (TeaCache-style). Speed-up ≈ share of blocks skipped × share of steps that are retrieve steps.
  • OpenVINO feasibility: pure pipeline work, no custom kernels. Export the transformer as two or three IR sub-models (first blocks, middle span, last blocks), or one model that also outputs the residual. The Python loop then decides per step whether to run the middle span or add the cached residual. Keeping the cache tensor on the device (Arc GPU remote tensors) avoids host copies. A video latent has many tokens, so the cache can take hundreds of MB, which matters on CPU/iGPU memory.
  • Few-step regimes cut the gain. DeepCache shines at 50–250 steps. The distilled LTX variants use only a handful of steps, and adjacent-step similarity drops as steps get farther apart. Expect caching to help mainly the full (non-distilled) multi-step model, and use a non-uniform schedule (Eq. 7 idea: refresh more often where features change fastest).
  • Evaluation to copy. Run speed-vs-quality sweeps over N (Tables 13–14) against the ‘just use fewer steps’ baseline (Fig. 6). For video, add temporal-consistency metrics (e.g. FVD, CLIP score per frame) and an audio check, since stale features may show up as flicker.
Guide

Treat caching as a separate layer on top of NNCF weight compression, and measure the two together, since quantization noise and stale features add up. For LTX-2.3, cache the residual of a middle span of transformer blocks, or the whole model output TeaCache-style, by exporting the model as two or three OpenVINO sub-models and letting the Python loop decide per step. Watch cache memory on CPU and Arc, expect little gain on the few-step distilled model, and compare against simply using fewer steps.

Acceleration beyond quantization

Timestep Embedding Tells: It’s Time to Cache for Video Diffusion Model

Feng Liu, Shiwei Zhang, Xiaofeng Wang, Yujie Wei, Haonan Qiu, Yuzhong Zhao, Yingya Zhang, Qixiang Ye, Fang Wan · UCAS, Alibaba, CASIA, Fudan, NTU · arXiv 2411.19108 (v2, Mar 2025), CVPR 2025

Consecutive denoising steps of a video DiT often produce almost the same output, so some steps can simply reuse the previous result. TeaCache decides which steps to skip by watching a cheap signal, how much the timestep-modulated input changed, rescales it with a small polynomial, and skips until the accumulated change crosses a threshold. No training; it works alongside quantization.

Type
Training-free step caching
Best speed-up
4.41× (−0.07 VBench)
Max speed-up
6.83× OpenSora-Plan
Latte / Open-Sora
1.86× / 1.55× lossless
Knobs
δ = 0.1 / 0.2 · poly order
Overhead
1 modulation + 1 L1 norm / step
Reading guide

TeaCache asks a simple question: if consecutive denoising steps of a video diffusion transformer give almost the same output, can we skip some of them without training anything? The answer is yes, as long as the steps to skip are chosen from a cheap signal, the change in the timestep-modulated input, rescaled by a small polynomial and summed until it crosses a threshold. The tab starts with the big picture and the problem of fixed skipping, then walks through the method, every equation, every figure, the results tables, and a thesis box on LTX-2.3. Headline numbers are 1.86 times faster on Latte and 1.55 times on Open-Sora with no VBench loss, and up to 4.41 times on OpenSora-Plan for a loss of 0.07 points. Among the sixteen papers it is the last of the acceleration group, after FlashAttention-2 and DeepCache, and just before VBench. It cuts how often the model runs, so it stacks with int8 or int4 weights.

§0Before reading

Following TeaCache takes three ideas: a diffusion model makes a video by running the whole transformer once per denoising step, the timestep reaches every block through a small scale-and-shift, and "how much a tensor changed" can be measured with one ratio. The paper is in the atlas because it does not make each step cheaper. It skips whole steps, and that stacks with the int8/int4 weights from the quantization papers.

Terms used in this paper

Denoising (sampling) step
One iteration of the sampler that removes a bit of noise from the latent video. Each step calls the full model once; Latte uses 50, Open-Sora 30 and OpenSora-Plan 150 in this paper.
DiT (diffusion transformer)
The denoising network built from transformer blocks (attention plus feed-forward) instead of a U-Net. LTX-2.3 is one.
Timestep embedding
The vector made from the step number \(t\) (sinusoidal features, then an MLP). It tells every block how noisy the input is.
adaLN modulation
Adaptive LayerNorm: normalise the tokens, then scale and shift them with values computed from the timestep embedding. TeaCache's indicator is the output of the first one.
Relative L1 distance
Sum of absolute differences between two tensors divided by the sum of absolute values of the reference one. A unit-free "percentage change".
Residual caching
Storing "output minus input" of the whole transformer stack at a computed step, and adding it to the fresh input on skipped steps.
Threshold \(\delta\)
How much accumulated change is tolerated before recomputing. The paper's "slow" setting uses 0.1 (higher quality), "fast" uses 0.2 (more skipping).
PAB, Δ-DiT, T-GATE
Earlier training-free caching methods, the baselines here. They reuse attention outputs or block features on a fixed schedule rather than deciding per step.
Open-Sora 1.2, OpenSora-Plan, Latte
Open-source text-to-video diffusion transformers used as test models. None of them is LTX; the method must be re-fitted per model.
NVIDIA A800
A data-centre GPU of the Ampere generation, essentially an A100 with reduced GPU-to-GPU link bandwidth; the 80 GB version is used here. It is far faster than an Intel CPU, so compare speed-up ratios, not seconds.
VBench
A benchmark that scores generated videos on many quality and consistency dimensions without needing a reference video. Higher is better; paper 16 of the atlas.
LPIPS, PSNR, SSIM
Reference-based metrics: they compare the cached video with the uncached one. Lower LPIPS, higher PSNR and SSIM mean closer to the original.
Dynamic Sequence Parallelism
A way to split one video's tokens across several GPUs, switching the split between spatial and temporal layers. Used in Table 4 to show caching stacks with multi-GPU runs.
Guide

These are the terms the paper assumes. The most important ones are the denoising step, the timestep embedding and its adaptive LayerNorm modulation, the relative L1 distance and the threshold delta that controls how much is skipped. Also note the two kinds of quality metric: VBench judges a video on its own, while LPIPS, PSNR and SSIM measure how close the cached video stays to the uncached one. All timings are on an NVIDIA A800, a data-centre GPU.

§1Big picture

Quantization makes each DiT pass cheaper; TeaCache runs fewer passes. The decision comes from the input side, so it costs almost nothing.

§2The problem

  • Sampling is sequential: 30–150 full DiT passes per video.
  • Earlier caches (PAB, Δ-DiT, T-GATE) reuse on a fixed schedule, but how much the output changes varies a lot from step to step (Fig. 3).
  • The ideal criterion (output change, Eq. 4) needs the output, which is the expensive part. What is needed is a predictor that is available before running the model.
  • Just using fewer sampler steps is worse: it coarsens αt (Fig. 6).

§3Method

  1. Pick the indicator. Text embedding is constant; the raw noisy input barely changes; the timestep embedding ignores content. Use the timestep-embedding-modulated noisy input Ft at the first block (Fig. 4, Table 2).
  2. Measure change. Compute L1rel(F, t) against the previous step (Eq. 4).
  3. Rescale. Map it to an estimated output change with a polynomial f fitted offline (Eq. 6, Fig. 5, Table 3).
  4. Accumulate and compare. Add f(·) to a running sum; while sum ≤ δ reuse, otherwise compute and reset (Eq. 7).
  5. Reuse the residual. Cache output − input of the DiT stack; on a skipped step add it to the fresh input (§3.4).
Guide

The method is a chain of five decisions. First choose an indicator that is cheap yet tracks the output: the timestep-modulated noisy input at the first block wins over the text embedding, the raw input, and the timestep embedding alone. Then measure its relative change from the previous step, correct that number with an offline-fitted polynomial, and add it to a running sum. When the sum crosses the threshold delta, run the full model and reset; otherwise reuse the cached residual, output minus input.

TeaCache sampling loop (no Algorithm box in the paper — written from §3.3/§3.4 + Eq. 7) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ input : sampler steps t_1..t_T, DiT blocks B_1..B_N, threshold δ, poly coeffs a_0..a_n acc ← 0 ; F_prev ← None ; Δ ← None for t in t_1 .. t_T: T_t ← MLP(sinusoidal(t)) # Eq. 3, cheap h_in ← patchify+embed(x_t) F_t ← modulate(LN(h_in), T_t) # 1st block's shift/scale only if F_prev is None: compute ← True # first step always computed else: acc ← acc + f( ‖F_t − F_prev‖₁ / ‖F_prev‖₁ ) # Eq. 4 on F, rescaled by Eq. 6 compute ← (acc ≥ δ) # Eq. 7 if compute: h_out ← B_N(…B_1(h_in, T_t, text)…) # full DiT Δ ← h_out − h_in # cache the residual acc ← 0 else: h_out ← h_in + Δ # reuse: skip all N blocks F_prev ← F_t x_{t−1} ← sampler_step(x_t, head(h_out), t) # Eq. 2 / DDIM / flow step return x_0
Guide

The whole method fits in a normal sampling loop; the paper has no algorithm box, so this is reconstructed from its sections three point three and three point four. Each step computes the cheap timestep embedding and the first block's modulated input, then updates the accumulated rescaled change. The first step is always computed. If the sum has reached delta, all transformer blocks run, the residual is cached and the sum resets; otherwise the cached residual is added to the input. Either way the sampler takes its normal step, so the schedule is untouched.

§4Every equation

(1)\[ \mathbf{x}_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,\mathbf{x}_{t-1}+\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\mathbf{z}_t \quad\text{for}\quad t=1,\dots,T \]

Forward diffusion: each step shrinks the signal by \(\sqrt{\alpha_t}\) and adds Gaussian noise \(\mathbf{z}_t\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\); \(\alpha_t\in[0,1]\).

Guide

Equation 1 is the forward diffusion process that adds noise. x t, the sample at step t, equals the square root of alpha t times the previous sample x t minus one, plus the square root of one minus alpha t times fresh Gaussian noise z t. Alpha t is between zero and one and sets how much signal survives each step. TeaCache does not change this; it is background for the reverse loop in equation 2.

(2)\[ p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_t)=\mathcal{N}\big(\mathbf{x}_{t-1};\,\mu_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,t),\,\Sigma_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,t)\big) \]

Reverse (denoising) step: the network predicts mean \(\mu_\theta\) and covariance \(\Sigma_\theta\). This is the sequential loop TeaCache shortens.

Guide

Equation 2 is the reverse, denoising step. p theta of x t minus one given x t is a Gaussian whose mean mu theta and covariance sigma theta are predicted by the network from the current sample x t and the step t. Generation repeats this step many times in sequence, and each repetition is one full transformer pass. That sequential loop is exactly the cost TeaCache shortens by reusing work between neighbouring steps.

(3)\[ \mathbf{T}_t=\operatorname{MLP}\big(\operatorname{sinusoidal}(t)\big) \quad\text{for}\quad t=1,\dots,T \]

Timestep embedding: scalar \(t\) → sinusoidal features → MLP. It produces the shift/scale that modulates every block (Fig. 4).

Guide

Equation 3 builds the timestep embedding. The scalar step t is turned into sinusoidal features, then passed through a small MLP to give the vector T t. This vector produces the scale and shift that modulate every transformer block, as figure 4 shows. It is cheap to compute, which is why TeaCache can afford to look at it, and at the input it modulates, at every step.

(4)\[ \mathrm{L1}_{\mathrm{rel}}(\mathbf{O},t)=\frac{\lVert\mathbf{O}_t-\mathbf{O}_{t+1}\rVert_1}{\lVert\mathbf{O}_{t+1}\rVert_1} \]

Relative L1 change of a tensor between consecutive steps (\(t+1\) is the previous, noisier step). Large → new information, must compute; small → reuse. Applied to outputs \(\mathbf{O}\) (ideal, unavailable) or to inputs \(\mathbf{F}\) (cheap).

Guide

Equation 4 measures how much a tensor changed between steps. The relative L1 distance of O at step t is the L1 norm of O t minus O t plus one, divided by the L1 norm of O t plus one, where t plus one is the previous, noisier step. A large value means new information, so the model should run; a small value means the output could be reused. Applied to outputs it is the ideal but unavailable criterion; TeaCache applies it to the cheap input F instead.

(5)\[ \sum_{t=t_a}^{t_b-1}\mathrm{L1}_{\mathrm{rel}}(\mathbf{F},t)\;\le\;\delta\;\lt\;\sum_{t=t_a}^{t_b}\mathrm{L1}_{\mathrm{rel}}(\mathbf{F},t) \]

Naive rule: after computing at \(t_a\), keep reusing while the accumulated input change stays \(\le\delta\); the first step \(t_b\) where it exceeds \(\delta\) is recomputed and the sum reset. \(\mathbf{F}\) = timestep embedding or modulated noisy input.

Guide

Equation 5 is the naive skipping rule. After computing at step t a, keep summing the relative input change from equation 4; while the sum up to the step before t b stays at or below delta, reuse. The first step t b where the sum exceeds delta is recomputed, and the sum restarts. F here is the timestep embedding or the modulated noisy input. The flaw is that input change and output change are on different scales, which equation 6 fixes.

(6)\[ y=f(x)=a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2+\cdots+a_nx^n \]

Rescaling polynomial: \(x\) = input difference (modulated noisy input), \(y\) = estimated output difference. Fitted offline with numpy; removes the scaling bias of Fig. 5.

Guide

Equation 6 is the rescaling polynomial. y equals f of x, which is a zero plus a one times x plus a two times x squared, and so on up to a n times x to the n. Here x is the measured change in the modulated input and y is the estimated change in the output. The coefficients a zero to a n are fitted offline, as in the fitting diagram, and they remove the scaling bias visible in figure 5. Table 3 shows first order already captures most of the gain.

(7)\[ \sum_{t=t_a}^{t_b-1}f\big(\mathrm{L1}_{\mathrm{rel}}(\mathbf{F},t)\big)\;\le\;\delta\;\lt\;\sum_{t=t_a}^{t_b}f\big(\mathrm{L1}_{\mathrm{rel}}(\mathbf{F},t)\big) \]

Final TeaCache indicator = Eq. 5 with each term rescaled by \(f\). \(\delta=0.1\) (slow), 0.2 (fast); Fig. 1 also uses 0.15, 0.25.

Guide

Equation 7 is the final TeaCache rule: equation 5 with every term passed through the polynomial f first. So the running sum is of estimated output changes, not raw input changes, and a step is recomputed the moment that sum exceeds delta. Delta is the only knob users turn: 0.1 is the slow, near-lossless setting and 0.2 the fast one, with 0.15 and 0.25 also shown in figure 1.

impl.\[ \mathbf{F}_t=\big(1+\gamma(\mathbf{T}_t)\big)\odot\operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{in}}_t)+\beta(\mathbf{T}_t) \]

Not displayed in the paper — Fig. 4 in formula form: the noisy-input tokens after the first block’s adaLN scale \(\gamma\) and shift \(\beta\). This is the tensor \(\mathbf{F}\) fed to Eq. 4.

Guide

This formula is not printed in the paper; it writes figure 4 as an equation. F t, the indicator, equals one plus gamma of T t, multiplied element by element with the layer-normalised input tokens h in, plus beta of T t. Gamma and beta are the first block's adaptive layer norm scale and shift, both computed from the timestep embedding. This F t is the tensor whose relative change goes into equation 4, and it costs only one modulation layer to get.

impl.\[ \mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{out}}_t\approx\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{in}}_t+\big(\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{out}}_{t_a}-\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{in}}_{t_a}\big),\qquad t_a\lt t\lt t_b \]

Not displayed in the paper — §3.4 in formula form: on a skipped step the cached residual (output minus input) of the last computed step is added to the current input.

Guide

This formula is also not printed in the paper; it restates section three point four. On a skipped step t between t a and t b, the output h out at t is approximated by the current input h in at t plus the residual saved at the last computed step, h out at t a minus h in at t a. Because the fresh input enters the sum, the output keeps moving with the sampler, which is why caching loses less than dropping steps.
