Table 4 gives the raw latencies behind chart B, in seconds with speed-up over the one-GPU baseline in brackets. TeaCache is fastest at every GPU count on both models. On OpenSora-Plan with 221 frames it cuts one-GPU latency from 324.41 seconds to 48.22, already 6.73 times faster before any parallelism, and reaches 32.02 times with eight GPUs. The single-GPU column is the one relevant to a one-machine Intel setup.

  • At δ = 0.1 (slow), VBench equals or beats the full model on Latte and Open-Sora and is within 0.07 points on OpenSora-Plan.
  • The modulated input beats the timestep embedding as an indicator (Table 2); it also adapts per prompt, whereas the timestep embedding picks the same steps for every prompt.
  • Rescaling adds +0.24 VBench (1st order); higher orders help very little (Table 3).
  • PSNR/SSIM drop at δ = 0.2: the video stays plausible but drifts from the uncached reference.

§7Why it matters for this thesis

TeaCache on LTX-2.3 with OpenVINO / NNCF

  • The biggest latency win on CPU, and it stacks. One LTX DiT step on an Intel CPU can take minutes, so skipping 40–50 % of steps saves more wall-clock time than int8 vs. int4 kernels do. It works independently of weight-only int8/int4 (NNCF), so the thesis can report quantization, caching, and both combined as separate ablations.
  • No custom kernels, just control flow. Everything happens in the Python denoising loop (e.g. an optimum-intel / OpenVINO GenAI-style pipeline). Two things are needed in the exported graph: (a) the first block’s modulated input Ft as an extra output, or a tiny separate IR that computes it; (b) access to the pre-block hidden state and the post-block hidden state so the residual can be cached and added. In practice this means splitting the IR into embed+mod | blocks | head. Only standard ops are involved (Abs, ReduceMean, Sub, Add).
  • Recalibrate the polynomial. The coefficients are model-specific. Published TeaCache ports exist for LTX-Video (the TeaCache repo ships an LTX-Video variant), but LTX-2.3 has a different architecture and schedule, and after int4 quantization the input/output change curves can shift. Refit f on the quantized model: run about 20–70 prompts without caching, log (L1rel(F), L1rel(O)) per step, then np.polyfit. This is cheap compared with NNCF calibration.
  • LTX-2 specifics to handle. Classifier-free guidance doubles the passes, so decide once per step for both branches. The audio-video joint model has two token streams, so measure F on the video stream (or both) and cache both residuals. With a few-step distilled checkpoint (about 8 steps) there is little redundancy left, so expect small gains and use a conservative δ.
  • Evaluation. Report speed-up vs. δ together with VBench-style / CLIP scores and PSNR/SSIM against the uncached output (the paper shows these diverge at δ = 0.2). Memory cost is one hidden-state tensor per stream, which is negligible next to the weights.
Guide

Treat caching as a separate ablation next to NNCF quantization: report quantization alone, caching alone, and both together, since skipping transformer passes likely saves more CPU time than int8 versus int4 kernels. To implement it, split the OpenVINO model into embedding plus modulation, the block stack, and the head, so the loop in Python can read F t and cache the residual. Refit the polynomial on the quantized LTX-2.3 with a few dozen uncached prompts, decide once per step for both guidance branches and both audio and video streams, and use a conservative delta on a distilled few-step checkpoint.

Evaluation

VBench: Comprehensive Benchmark Suite for Video Generative Models

Ziqi Huang, Yinan He, Jiashuo Yu, Fan Zhang, Chenyang Si, Yuming Jiang, Yuanhan Zhang, Tianxing Wu, Qingyang Jin, Nattapol Chanpaisit, Yaohui Wang, Xinyuan Chen, Limin Wang, Dahua Lin, Yu Qiao, Ziwei Liu · CVPR 2024 (arXiv 2311.17982)

Instead of one number like FVD, VBench splits “is this generated video good?” into 16 separate scores. Each score has its own prompt set (~100 prompts) and its own off-the-shelf judge model (DINO, CLIP, RAFT, AMT, MUSIQ, LAION aesthetic, GRiT, UMT, Tag2Text, ViCLIP). Human pairwise preferences confirm that every score ranks models the way people do.

Dimensions
16 (7 quality + 9 condition)
Prompts
~100 per dim + 8×100 per category
Human pairs
N × 5 × 6 per dimension
Human alignment
Spearman ρ 0.61–0.998
Models tested
LaVie, ModelScope, VideoCrafter, CogVideo
Output
scores in [0,1] (shown as %)
Reading guide

VBench asks a simple question: how can one tell whether a generated video is good, and in what way? Its answer is to replace one opaque number like FVD with sixteen separate scores, each with its own small prompt set and its own off-the-shelf judge network, and to check every score against human votes. The tab starts with the big picture and the problem, then walks through the method one dimension at a time, lists every equation, redraws every figure, and ends with the results tables and a box on how to use VBench in the thesis. VBench is the sixteenth and last paper in the atlas and the only one about evaluation. The other fifteen describe the model and how to make it cheaper; VBench is the ruler that shows the cheaper model still makes good video.

§0Before reading

VBench does not generate or compress anything: it measures generated video. Following it takes three ideas: a pretrained network can turn a frame into a feature vector compared by angle, optical flow measures how much things move between frames, and a rank correlation shows whether a metric orders models the way people do. It is in the atlas because the thesis must prove that the compressed LTX-2.3 still makes good video, and VBench is the ruler for that.

Terms used in this paper

Text-to-video (T2V) model
A generator that turns a text prompt into a short clip. VBench tests LaVie, ModelScope, VideoCrafter and CogVideo; LTX-2.3 is one too.
FVD, FID, IS
Older one-number metrics that compare feature statistics of generated and real media. They give no diagnosis of what went wrong, which is VBench's motivation.
Dimension
One narrowly defined quality, like Temporal Flickering or Object Class. VBench has 16, split into Video Quality and Video-Condition Consistency.
Prompt suite
The small, purpose-built set of prompts (about 100) used to test one dimension, plus a set sorted into eight content categories.
CLIP
A model that embeds images and text in one shared space, so a frame and a sentence can be compared by cosine similarity.
DINO
A self-supervised image model whose features are sensitive to object identity; VBench uses it to check the subject stays the same.
ViCLIP, UMT
Video models that look at many frames together. ViCLIP scores camera-motion style and overall prompt match; UMT recognises human actions.
Optical flow (RAFT)
A per-pixel motion field between two frames. RAFT is the estimator VBench uses for Dynamic Degree.
Frame interpolation (AMT)
A model that predicts an in-between frame. VBench uses its prediction error to score Motion Smoothness.
MUSIQ, LAION aesthetic
Per-frame image scorers: MUSIQ rates low-level quality (noise, blur, exposure), the LAION predictor rates beauty on a 0 to 10 scale.
GRiT, Tag2Text
GRiT detects and describes objects (used for objects, colour, spatial relations); Tag2Text captions frames to check the scene.
Win ratio
The share of human pairwise comparisons a model wins, counting a tie as half a win.
Spearman's ρ
A correlation computed on ranks, not values: 1 means two lists order things identically, 0 means no relation.
A100
An NVIDIA data-centre GPU. The paper mentions it only for fine-tuning its video language model; the VBench scorers themselves can run on any machine with PyTorch.
Guide

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. Most are names of the judge networks: CLIP and DINO for frame features, ViCLIP and UMT for whole-clip understanding, RAFT for motion, AMT for frame interpolation, MUSIQ and the LAION predictor for image quality and beauty, GRiT and Tag2Text for objects and scenes. Win ratio and Spearman's rho are how the paper checks it agrees with people.

§2Big picture

Each dimension answers one yes/no-style question (“is the subject the same cat throughout?”, “is the style Van Gogh?”). The two top-level questions: Video Quality — does it look good regardless of the prompt? — and Video-Condition Consistency — is it what the user asked for?

§3The problem

  • IS, FID, FVD, CLIPSIM disagree with human judgement and give no diagnosis.
  • Video-quality-assessment models (VQA) were built for real camera footage, not generative artifacts.
  • “Quality” means different things to different users (flicker vs. prompt fidelity) — needs disentangling.
  • T2V sampling is slow (LaVie ~90 s, CogVideo >2 min per video) → test set must be compact (~100 prompts / dim).

§4Method

  1. Prompt Suite per Dimension: ~100 prompts designed to probe exactly one ability (e.g. movable subjects for Subject Consistency; Kinetics-400 actions for Human Action; COCO classes for Object Class). Semantics prompts carry labels (class, colour, relation, style) for automatic checking.
  2. Prompt Suite per Category: human-curated prompts classified by an LLM [130] into 8 YouTube-like categories (Animal, Architecture, Food, Human, Lifestyle, Plant, Scenery, Vehicles); 800 prompts cleaned → 100 per category.
  3. Sample videos from each T2V model with every prompt (seed fixed at 2).
  4. Score each video with the dimension’s judge model (mini-diagrams below); average over videos → model score.
  5. Anchor with reference baselines: Empirical Min, Empirical Max, WebVid-Avg.
  6. Validate each dimension with human pairwise preference win ratios and Spearman ρ.
Guide

The pipeline has four stages. First, build small prompt suites, about a hundred prompts per dimension that each probe one ability, plus eight content categories of a hundred prompts each sorted by a language model. Second, sample one video per prompt from every model with a fixed seed. Third, score each video with that dimension's judge and average into a model score, reading it against reference baselines. Finally, confirm the dimension ranks models the way humans do.

How each dimension is computed

Table A3 — LLM prompt for category classification The assistant gives helpful, detailed, and polite answers to the user's questions. Please act as a language expert, able to choose one or more suitable categories from [Animal, Architecture, Food, Human, Lifestyle, Plant, Scenery, Vehicles] for the given text. Given the input text, you should return the answer without explanation. For example, if the input is [A man eats hamburgers.], the output tag format should be [Food, Human]. The given text is Input text. (classification accuracy ~95%, then manual check)
Guide

This is the exact prompt used to sort the category prompts. A language model is asked to act as a language expert and tag each text with one or more of eight categories, such as Food or Vehicles, with no explanation. The logic is cheap automatic labelling followed by a human check: the tagging was about 95 percent accurate, then corrected by hand to give a hundred clean prompts per category.

Table A4 — VLM chain of thought (dimension selection) <SYSTEM>: You are an assistant with fair and objective standards for video assessment. Given the input statement for the video generation model: {input text}, please select appropriate evaluation dimensions from [16 dimension names]. <USER>: a dilapidated phone booth stood as a relic of a bygone era on the sidewalk, frozen in time. <ASSISTANT>: ... subject consistency, background consistency, temporal flickering, motion smoothness, dynamic degree, aesthetic quality, imaging quality, scene, temporal style, overall consistency
Guide

This chain-of-thought template is how the tuned video language model starts an evaluation. Given a prompt, it first selects which of the sixteen dimensions apply, and only then scores the video on them. In the phone booth example, the model leaves out object and colour checks and keeps the quality, scene, style and overall ones. Choosing dimensions first mirrors how VBench itself matches prompt suites to dimensions.

§5Every equation

(1)\[ S_{subject}=\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=2}^{T}\frac{1}{2}\big(\langle d_1\cdot d_t\rangle+\langle d_{t-1}\cdot d_t\rangle\big) \]

Subject Consistency. \(d_i\): DINO feature of frame \(i\), unit-normalised; \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) = dot product = cosine similarity. Averaged over all videos of a model.

Guide

Equation one is Subject Consistency. S subject is one over T minus one times the sum from frame two to frame T of one half times the dot product of d one and d t, plus the dot product of d t minus one and d t. Here d t is the unit-length DINO feature of frame t, so each dot product is a cosine similarity. It rewards frames that match both the first frame and their neighbour, and is averaged over all of a model's videos.

(2)\[ S_{background}=\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=2}^{T}\frac{1}{2}\big(\langle c_1\cdot c_t\rangle+\langle c_{t-1}\cdot c_t\rangle\big) \]

Background Consistency; \(c_i\): CLIP image feature of frame \(i\), unit-normalised.

Guide

Equation two is Background Consistency, identical in form to equation one. The only change is that c t, the unit-length CLIP image feature of frame t, replaces the DINO feature. Each frame is compared with the first frame and the previous one, the two cosine similarities are averaged, and the result is averaged over the T minus one frame transitions.

(3)\[ S_{flicker}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big(\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\operatorname{MAE}(f_i^{t},f_i^{t+1})\Big) \]

Temporal Flickering: mean absolute pixel difference between consecutive frames, \(N\) videos, \(T\) frames, \(f_i^t\) = frame \(t\) of video \(i\).

Guide

Equation three computes raw flicker. For each of N videos, it takes the mean absolute error between frame t and frame t plus one, averages over the T minus one pairs, and then averages over all videos. Because it is only applied to static scenes, any pixel change is treated as flicker. A larger value means worse flicker, which equation four then flips.

(4)\[ S_{flicker\text{-}norm}=\frac{255-S_{flicker}}{255} \]

Maps to [0,1] (8-bit pixels); higher = less flicker. Motion Smoothness uses the same normalisation on its interpolation MAE.

Guide

Equation four normalises flicker: 255 minus S flicker, all divided by 255. Since eight-bit pixels range from zero to 255, this maps the error into zero to one, with higher meaning less flicker. Motion Smoothness reuses exactly this normalisation. One consequence is that scores cluster near the top, around 96 to 99 percent, so small differences matter.

\[ S_{motion}=\frac{255-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k}\operatorname{MAE}\big(\hat f_{2k-1},f_{2k-1}\big)}{255},\quad \hat f_{2k-1}=\operatorname{AMT}(f_{2k-2},f_{2k}) \]

Motion Smoothness (text, normalised “in the same way as Eq. 4”): drop odd frames of \([f_0,\dots,f_{2n}]\), interpolate them back, compare.

Guide

This is Motion Smoothness written out from the paper's text. Every odd frame is removed, and AMT reconstructs frame f two k minus one from the frames on either side, giving f hat. The mean absolute error between f hat and the real frame, averaged over the n dropped frames, is subtracted from 255 and divided by 255, as in equation four. Low reconstruction error means predictable, smooth motion.

\[ S_{dynamic}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{1}\Big[\operatorname{mean}\big(\text{top }5\%\ \lVert\text{RAFT flow}\rVert\big)_i\gt\tau\Big] \]

Dynamic Degree: proportion of non-static videos (threshold \(\tau\) not given in the paper).

Guide

This is Dynamic Degree. For each video, take the RAFT optical flow magnitudes, average the largest five percent, and check whether that exceeds a threshold tau. The indicator is one for moving videos and zero otherwise, and S dynamic is the average over N videos, so it is the share of non-static clips. The paper does not give the threshold value.

\[ S_{aesthetic}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\operatorname{LAION}(f_t)}{10},\qquad S_{imaging}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\operatorname{MUSIQ}(f_t)}{100} \]

Frame-wise quality: linear normalisation of a 0–10 rating and a 0–100 rating, averaged over frames.

Guide

These two formulas give the frame-wise quality scores. S aesthetic averages the LAION aesthetic rating of each frame divided by ten, and S imaging averages the MUSIQ rating divided by a hundred, both over T frames. They are simple linear rescalings to zero to one, so they inherit whatever the judge models consider good.

\[ S_{obj}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\mathbb{1}\big[o\in\operatorname{GRiT}(f_t)\big],\qquad S_{multi}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\mathbb{1}\big[\{o_1,o_2\}\subseteq\operatorname{GRiT}(f_t)\big] \]

Object Class / Multiple Objects: fraction of frames where the requested object(s) are detected.

Guide

These are the object scores. S obj is the fraction of the T frames in which GRiT detects the requested object o. S multi is the fraction of frames in which both requested objects, o one and o two, are detected together. The indicator makes each frame count as one or zero.

\[ S_{action}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\mathbb{1}\big[a_i\in\{\text{top-5 UMT classes with logit}\gt0.85\}\big] \]

Human Action on 16 uniformly sampled frames.

Guide

Human Action is scored per video. For each of N videos, the indicator is one if the prompted action a i is among UMT's top five classes with a logit above 0.85, and the score is the average of these hits. UMT sees sixteen uniformly sampled frames, so it judges the motion, not a single still.

\[ S_{color}=\frac{\#\{t:\ o\ \text{detected},\ \text{caption}(o,f_t)\ \text{has colour } c\}}{\#\{t:\ o\ \text{detected}\}} \]

Color: only frames containing the object count.

Guide

Color is a ratio of frame counts. The numerator counts frames where the object is detected and its caption contains the requested colour c; the denominator counts all frames where the object is detected. Dividing by detected frames only means a missing object does not lower the colour score, keeping the two dimensions separate.

\[ S_{spatial}(f_t)=\begin{cases}1 & \text{relation correct},\ \operatorname{IoU}\lt\tau\\ \kappa(\operatorname{IoU}) & \text{relation correct},\ \operatorname{IoU}\ge\tau\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} \]

Spatial Relationship: correct if distance along the named axis exceeds that along the other axis; \(\kappa\) = IoU-based coefficient (exact form not given).

Guide

Spatial Relationship is scored per frame in three cases. If the relation is correct and the boxes overlap little, meaning IoU below tau, the frame scores one. If it is correct but the boxes overlap heavily, it gets a reduced score kappa of IoU. Otherwise it scores zero. The exact form of kappa is not given in the paper, so treat this as a sketch of the rule.

\[ S_{scene}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_t\mathbb{1}\big[\text{all scene words}\subseteq\operatorname{Tag2Text}(f_t)\big] \]

Scene: every scene word must appear in the caption, order free.

Guide

Scene is the fraction of the T frames where every word of the scene name appears in Tag2Text's caption. The indicator is strict about vocabulary but ignores word order, so partial matches do not count.

\[ S_{app}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_t\langle\operatorname{CLIP}_I(f_t)\cdot\operatorname{CLIP}_T(s)\rangle,\qquad S_{tstyle},\,S_{overall}=\langle\operatorname{ViCLIP}_V(v)\cdot\operatorname{ViCLIP}_T(p)\rangle \]

Style and overall: cosine similarity between visual and text features (\(s\) = style phrase, \(p\) = prompt).

Guide

These are the style and overall scores, all cosine similarities between a visual and a text embedding. S app averages, over frames, the similarity between the CLIP image feature of frame t and the CLIP text feature of the style phrase s. Temporal Style and Overall Consistency instead compare one ViCLIP embedding of the whole video v with the ViCLIP text embedding of the prompt p.

\[ \#\text{pairs}=N\times5\times6,\qquad \binom{4}{2}=6 \]

Human annotation: 5 groups of 4 model videos per prompt, all 6 pairs compared.

Guide

This counts human comparisons. For each of N prompts there are five groups of four model videos, and four models give four choose two, which is six pairs. So each dimension collects N times five times six pairwise votes. This is the data behind the win ratios in equation fifteen.

\[ \operatorname{WinRatio}(m)=\frac{\sum_{\text{pairs with } m}\big(\mathbb{1}[m\ \text{wins}]+\tfrac12\mathbb{1}[\text{tie}]\big)}{\#\text{pairs with } m} \]

Computed from both human labels and VBench scores; Spearman ρ between the two per dimension (Fig. 5).

Guide

The win ratio of model m is the sum over all pairs involving m of one for a win plus one half for a tie, divided by the number of pairs involving m. It is computed twice, once from human labels and once from VBench scores, and the Spearman rank correlation between the two is the human-alignment number reported for each dimension in figure five.

\[ \tilde s_{m,d}=a+(b-a)\,\frac{s_{m,d}-\min_{m'}s_{m',d}}{\max_{m'}s_{m',d}-\min_{m'}s_{m',d}} \]

Radar normalisation: \((a,b)=(0.3,0.8)\) for Figs. 2, 6, A26; \((0,1)\) over all 32 model×category values for Fig. 7.

Guide

This is only for drawing radar charts. The score s of model m on dimension d is min-max normalised across models, then stretched into the range a to b. Figures two, six and A26 use a of 0.3 and b of 0.8, so the best model sits at 0.8 and the worst at 0.3. Figure seven uses zero to one over all 32 model and category values. It changes the picture, not the underlying scores.

§8Why it matters for this thesis

  • Pick the dimensions that compression can break. Int8/int4 weight-only quantization of LTX-2.3 mainly risks Imaging Quality (noise/blur, MUSIQ), Aesthetic Quality, Temporal Flickering and Subject/Background Consistency; step-caching mainly risks Motion Smoothness and Dynamic Degree. Semantics dims (Object Class, Spatial) check that the text path survived. A 6–8 dimension subset is enough.
  • Always pair consistency with Dynamic Degree. A degraded model that produces near-static clips will gain on consistency/flicker (§3). Report Dynamic Degree next to them, and next to WWB similarity, so “smoother” is not mistaken for “better”.
  • Compare FP16 vs. quantized on the same prompts and seeds. VBench scores are absolute; the thesis needs deltas. Use the per-dimension prompt suites (~70–100 prompts) with fixed seeds, and treat changes smaller than the model-to-model gaps in Table 1 (e.g. <0.5 pt on Motion Smoothness) as noise unless repeated.
  • Evaluation runs off-device in PyTorch. The judges (DINO, CLIP, RAFT, AMT, MUSIQ, GRiT, UMT, ViCLIP) are separate networks; generate videos with OpenVINO on Intel CPU/Arc, save frames, then score on any machine. Nothing needs converting to OpenVINO, but store frames losslessly (PNG) — codec artifacts would contaminate Imaging Quality and Flicker.
  • Audio is not covered. VBench is video-only and 2-second-oriented; LTX-2.3’s audio stream and longer clips need a separate check (e.g. WWB-style similarity or audio metrics), and resolution/length should be stated since the paper sampled 256–512 px, 16–33 frames.
Guide

Use VBench as a before-and-after test, not a leaderboard. Pick six to eight dimensions that compression can break: imaging and aesthetic quality, flicker and consistency for quantization, motion smoothness and dynamic degree for caching, plus one or two semantic checks. Generate FP16 and quantized videos with OpenVINO on the same prompts and seeds, save frames as PNG, and score them in PyTorch on any machine. Always report Dynamic Degree next to consistency, and remember VBench does not cover audio.
